closed base disc and hence compact. Together with the
compact unmodified complement they cover the inverse
image of that disc. This proves properness of the glued
family. All maps are biholomorphic on the overlaps,
so its total space is smooth.

On the central main component the gluing reverses the
same inverse-transform maps used to define $T_0$.
It therefore recovers the original $P$ with every
analytic transition. The chosen fibre-period basis
preserves the linear part of each marked normal cover.
The maps $(z,w)\mapsto(a^{r_i}z,aw)$ commute with both
contractions and with the finite action; as $a$ varies,
they realize every constant translation of the marked
axis. They therefore preserve the given remaining gluing
constants. The full local equation is $s=xw$ in the
free coarse charts, so all central components have
multiplicity one and meet transversely as the given $S$.

Outside this tube the compact family
\eqref{eq:II:compact-twistor-lattice}, pulled back by
$t=s^R$, is unchanged. The proper local replacement and
that compact complement give a smooth compact threefold
over $\PP^1$. Every nonzero fibre is the original smooth
connected two-torus. The central quasibundle has Euler
number zero by \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic};
\cref{lem:II:hopf-curve-restriction} gives Euler number zero
for the Hopf leaves, and each double curve is elliptic. Additivity gives $e(S)=0$, completing
the construction.
\end{proof}

\par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The canonical identity on an arbitrary Hopf leaf.}
We first use an actual reduced smoothing. Let the divisor
of a local canonical evaluation generator be
$k_PP+\sum_i k_iH_i$. Its existence and the fact that it
has only vertical zeroes are the exact direct-image
calculation in \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.38}. Adjunction on one leaf gives
\[
                  K_H=\OO_H(-aJ),\qquad
                  a=k_H-k_P+1\in\Z.                      \tag{C.AS.6}\hypertarget{tag-00AV}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.6}
\]
We classify this equality on the actual pair $(H,J)$,
including the full secondary deck group.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  Take a normal primary cyclic subgroup of the Hopf deck
group $\Gamma$. Its generator $F$ is central: conjugation
can send it only to $F$ or $F^{-1}$, while the nonzero
logarithm of the modulus of its derivative determinant
excludes the latter. This is the exact normal-core
argument of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.43}. We therefore have a finite
unramified primary cover $H'\to H$, and the full inverse
image $D$ of $J$ is a disjoint union of smooth elliptic
curves. The finite quotient acts transitively on these
curves, since $J$ is connected. Pullback gives
\[
                           K_{H'}=-aD.                  \tag{C.AS.7}\hypertarget{tag-00AW}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.7}
\]


\item  For a nonlinear primary contraction the curve computation
of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.38} gives its unique axis, and the full
centralizer computation of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.43} gives exactly the
nonlinear quotient in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}--\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}.
The invariant form $dz\wedge dw/w^{r+1}$ has divisor
$-(r+1)J$, on the quotient as well. Since $\OO_H(J)$ has
infinite order, \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.6} forces $a=r+1$.


\item  Consider a diagonal primary contraction. Its invariant
curve computation can be read directly from an equation
on $\C^2$. Closure across the origin and removal of the
nonconstant unit in its transformation give an eigenfunction
of $F$. Comparison of its power-series monomials gives
the axes in the absence of a multiplicative resonance.
In that case the complete centralizer is diagonal, so
it cannot interchange the axes. Thus $D$ is one axis.
If, for example, it is $w=0$, the exact automorphy
characters in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.7} give
$\alpha\beta=\beta^a$, which is the resonance
$\alpha=\beta^{a-1}$. The contraction moduli make
$a-1>0$. This contradicts the assumed absence of a
resonance and accounts for that case through an actual
character equality.


\item  In the resonant case pass to a further central cyclic
subgroup to remove the finite root-of-unity discrepancy.
Its generator has the form
\[
                 F(z,w)=(\gamma^p z,\gamma^q w),
       \qquad p,q\ge1,\quad\gcd(p,q)=1,\quad |\gamma|<1 .
                                                               \tag{C.AS.8}\hypertarget{tag-00AX}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.8}
\]
Here the axes have defining weights $p,q$, and every
other irreducible curve has equation $z^q=cw^p$ of
weight $pq$. This follows from the same eigenfunction
calculation: after an axis monomial is removed, a
weighted homogeneous polynomial factors into these
binomials over $\C$. Its irreducible factor is unique
because $p,q$ are coprime. The curves are smooth away
from the origin, as required for the elliptic curves
on $H'$.


\item  The canonical weight is $p+q$. If $D$ is an orbit of
$m$ non-axis curves, \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.7} therefore gives
\[
                              ampq=p+q.                 \tag{C.AS.9}\hypertarget{tag-00AY}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.9}
\]
The same calculation with a single axis replaces $mpq$
by $p$ or $q$. These are genuine character equalities:
a purported extra holomorphic unit and its inverse
extend across the origin, and their nonzero value there
forces the identical character. In particular $a>0$.


\item  For $p,q>1$, coprimality gives $pq>p+q$, so \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.9}
is impossible. A single axis would require $p\mid q$
or $q\mid p$, also impossible. In this case the
centralizer preserves each axis, so an orbit containing
both axes cannot occur. For $p=r>1,q=1$, the curves
$z=cw^r$, including $z=0$, all have weight $r$.
The triangular centralizer can permute these curves;
an orbit of $m$ of them has total weight $mr$ and
would require $amr=r+1$, hence $r\mid1$.
The only possibility is the weight-one axis $w=0$,
and then $a=r+1$.


\item  We retain the full deck group in this last calculation.
Commuting with $(\gamma^rz,\gamma w)$ gives exactly
\[
              (z,w)\longmapsto(Az+Cw^r,Bw).             \tag{C.AS.10}\hypertarget{tag-00AH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.10}
\]
Its induced action on $z/w^r$ is affine. The central
cyclic subgroup acts trivially there; hence the image
is a finite affine group. Averaging the orbit of zero
gives an actual common fixed point. The corresponding
coordinate change $z\mapsto z-cw^r$ makes every element
diagonal, while retaining the marked axis. Equation
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.6} then says, for every deck element,
$AB=B^{r+1}$, so $A=B^r$. Thus $\Gamma$ is the
weighted scalar group with an infinite contracting
generator $\beta$ and finite roots of unity
$\mu_n$. Freeness on the marked axis gives
$\gcd(r,n)=1$. This is exactly the diagonal pair in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}--\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}.


\item  It remains to check the scalar case $p=q=1$,
where the full secondary group need not initially
be diagonal. Every component of $D$ lifts to a
line, and \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.7} gives $am=2$. If $m=1$,
the finite projective group fixes that line.
On its affine complement, averaging gives a
second fixed point, so the linear group becomes
diagonal in coordinates retaining the first line.
The character equality $AB=B^2$ forces $A=B$
for every element. We obtain the case $r=1$
of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}, with scalar finite action.
If $m=2$, then $a=1$ and an element of the full
deck group interchanges the two lines. Choose
them as the two coordinate axes. The unique
log-canonical form up to a constant is
\[
                             \frac{dz}{z}\wedge\frac{dw}{w}.
                                                               \tag{C.AS.11}\hypertarget{tag-00AI}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.11}
\]
Every such interchange multiplies this form
by $-1$. A form with exactly the same divisor
differs by a nowhere-zero holomorphic function
on the compact primary Hopf surface, hence by
a constant. It therefore cannot descend.
This contradicts the actual equality
$K_H+J=0$ in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.6}. Thus this last orbit
does not satisfy \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.6}. We have proved,
without an a priori restriction on the secondary
group, precisely the leaf-pair list \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1},
and in every surviving case
\[
                              k_i-k_P=r_i\ge1.          \tag{C.AS.12}\hypertarget{tag-00AJ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.12}
\]


\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Canonical divisors on Hopf leaf pairs}\label{subsec:II:hopf-leaf-pairs}

\begin{lemma}[A canonical divisor supported on one Hopf curve]\hypertarget{tag-P352}{}\label{lem:II:hopf-single-canonical-curve}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:hopf-single-canonical-curve}{proved}{P352}{\cref{lem:II:hopf-curves,lem:II:hopf-curve-restriction,lem:II:central-primary-hopf-cover,lem:II:reduced-anticanonical-hopf,lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary}; \cref{cdp:eq:C.SH.3,cdp:eq:C.SH.4}}
Let $H$ be a compact primary or secondary Hopf surface and
$J\subset H$ a connected smooth curve. An identity
$K_H\simeq\OO_H(-aJ)$ with $a\in\Z$ holds exactly for
the marked pairs in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}, with the full
deck actions \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}; in these coordinates
$a=r+1$. The isomorphism marks $J$ as the image of $w=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The curve $J$ is elliptic by \cref{lem:II:hopf-curves}.
By \cref{lem:II:hopf-curve-restriction} and Serre duality,
$H^0(H,K_H)=0$. For $a\le0$ the canonical section of
$\OO_H(-aJ)$ would be nonzero, so $a>0$.
Apply \cref{lem:II:reduced-anticanonical-hopf} with the
effective divisor $aJ$. Its reduced alternative has two
distinct curve images and cannot equal this single-curve
support. Its other alternative gives $a\ge2$ and a finite
unramified central primary cover $\pi:H'\to H$ on which
$D=\pi^{-1}(J)$ is one marked curve. The unramified
differential and divisor pullback give
\begin{equation}
                           K_{H'}=-aD.                  \hypertarget{tag-00AW}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.7}
\end{equation}
The primary-cover clause of that lemma gives either the
nonlinear contraction $(\beta_0^rz+w^r,\beta_0w)$ or the
diagonal contraction $(\gamma^rz,\gamma w)$, with
$D=\{w=0\}$ and $a=r+1$. Its weight comparison
\cref{cdp:eq:C.AS.8,cdp:eq:C.AS.9} and its logarithmic
form \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.11} are on this same central-cover
construction; thus all inverse images of the marked curve
and all divisor coefficients are fixed in this application.

In the nonlinear case use the full centralizer map
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SH.3} for this same central contraction.
Every member of the full deck group commutes with it.
The quotient and splitting maps \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SH.4}
therefore identify $H$ with
$H_r(\beta)/\mu_n$, with finite action
$(z,w)\mapsto(\zeta^rz,\zeta w)$ and $\gcd(r,n)=1$.
Here $\beta$ is the second-coordinate multiplier of the
primitive contracting generator in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SH.4};
the central generator with multiplier $\beta_0$ is a positive
power of it times a finite deck element. The rescaling of
$z$ used there keeps $w=0$, and the
nonlinear primary curve is unique, so these maps carry
its image precisely to the given $J$.

For the diagonal central contraction, every deck lift
preserves its marked axis. For $r\ge2$, this contraction is
class $\mathrm{III}$ of \cite[arXiv v2, Theorem~2.1(3), p.~5]{Khaled2024Hopf}.
Its source parameters $(a,b,d)=(A,C,B)$ give
\begin{equation}
              (z,w)\longmapsto(Az+Cw^r,Bw).             \hypertarget{tag-00AH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.10}
\end{equation}
with $A,B\ne0$. For $r=1$, class $\mathrm{IV}$ in the same
theorem gives $\operatorname{GL}(2,\C)$; preservation of
$w=0$ sets its lower-left matrix entry to zero and gives
the same formula. Its action on
$z/w^r$ is affine. The central contraction acts trivially
on that coordinate, so the induced affine group is finite.
The average of its finite orbit of zero is a common fixed
point $c$. The maps $z'=z-cw^r$, $w'=w$ and
$z=z'+c(w')^r$, $w=w'$ conjugate the whole group to
diagonal maps while preserving the marked curve and
commuting with the central contraction.

The invariant form $dz\wedge dw/w^{r+1}$ trivializes
$K_{H'}((r+1)D)$. The section pulled back from
$K_H(aJ)$ differs from it by a constant, since $H'$ is
compact and connected. Invariance under every diagonal
deck element gives $AB=B^{r+1}$, hence $A=B^r$.
The full group is consequently the weighted scalar group
given by its second-coordinate multipliers. It has a
cyclic subgroup of finite index, so it is generated by
one contracting multiplier $\beta$, together with its
finite subgroup $\mu_n$. Freeness on $w=0$ gives
$\gcd(r,n)=1$: a root with $\zeta^r=1$ would fix a
nonzero point of that axis. Thus its quotient is exactly
the diagonal pair of \cref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1,cdp:eq:C.AS.2},
with the same marked curve.

Conversely, for each displayed pair the invariant form
and infinite order of $\OO_H(J)$ in the proof of
\cref{lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary} give
$K_H=-(r+1)J$ and uniqueness of the integer $a$.
This proves both directions with the stated pair maps.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Compact insertion of elliptic stars}\label{subsec:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}

\begin{lemma}[Compact insertion with prescribed Hopf leaves]\hypertarget{tag-P353}{}\label{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}{proved}{P353}{\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data,lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor,lem:II:logarithmic-period-family,cdp:st:C.2.UN.42}; \cref{cdp:eq:C.NH.6,cdp:eq:C.NH.7,cdp:eq:C.NH.9,cdp:eq:C.NH.10}}
Let a marked elliptic star have elliptic base $B$, no unmarked
multiple fibres, and
\begin{equation}
                         c(T_0)=0\in H^2(B,\Lambda_F).     \hypertarget{tag-00AT}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.4}
\end{equation}
Suppose there is a positive integer $R$ with
\begin{equation}
 \begin{cases}
 r_i=R,&H_i\text{ is of the nonlinear form in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}},\\
 r_i<R,&H_i\text{ is of the diagonal form in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}}.
 \end{cases}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AU}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.5}
\end{equation}
Then its given reduced surface $S$ is the full fibre over
zero of a proper map $f:Y\to\PP^1$, where $Y$ is a smooth
compact complex threefold and every other fibre is a smooth
connected two-torus. The central main component is the given
$P$, with its entire analytic torsor and marked normal covers;
each leaf and each elliptic gluing map is the prescribed one.
Every reduced fibre support has Euler characteristic zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor} to the
principal torsor $q_0:T_0\to B$ of
\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data}, using $F_1=F$ and its
zero Chern class. Use the coordinate change
$(z,w)_{\mathrm{KX}}=(p,z)$, with
$\Gamma=\Gamma_B$ and $\Lambda_{F_1}=\Lambda_F$.
The resulting full lattice presentation is exactly
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.14}. The local translations by the
zero-cochain in that lemma and their inverse translations
identify this quotient with the original analytic torsor
over the same $B$. Write it as $T_0=\C^2/\Lambda_0$, with
the fibre direction $p=0$ and the disjoint marked fibres $F_i$.

Apply the full rank-four clause of
\cref{lem:II:logarithmic-period-family} to this exact lattice
$\Lambda_0$, and pull its compact family back by $t=s^R$.
Its periods are $V_{s^R}(\Lambda_0)$ and its central fibre
is the same $T_0$. For the $i$th marked fibre, the product
map \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5} identifies its elliptic curve with
$\C^*/\gamma_i^{\Z}$, where $\gamma_i=\beta_i^{n_i}$.
Choose the corresponding oriented fibre-period basis
$\lambda_i=(0,a_i)$, $\mu_i=(0,b_i)$, with
$\gamma_i=\exp(2\pi i b_i/a_i)$. The projection of
$\Lambda_0$ onto the base lattice is surjective with this
fibre lattice as kernel, so these two periods extend to
an integral basis of all four periods.
In the vector coordinates $(P,Z)$ after $V_{s^R}$, set
\begin{equation}
 p^{(i)}=P-s^R\frac{\bar a_i}{a_i}Z,\qquad
 z_i=\frac{2\pi i}{a_i}Z.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.16}
\end{equation}
The period $\lambda_i$ becomes $(0,2\pi i)$, and $\mu_i$ becomes
\begin{equation}
   \bigl(\delta_i(s),\log\gamma_i\bigr),\qquad
   \delta_i(s)=s^R
        \left(\bar b_i-\frac{\bar a_i b_i}{a_i}\right).
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TI}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.17}
\end{equation}
where $d_i=\overline b_i-\overline a_i b_i/a_i\ne0$ by
the real independence of $a_i,b_i$.
The two remaining periods have coordinates
$(P_{ij}(s),Z_{ij}(s))$, $j=1,2$.
At zero their first coordinates are a base-period basis,
so remain real-linearly independent on a smaller disc.
They define the elliptic curve
$B_{i,s}=\C/\langle P_{i1}(s),P_{i2}(s)\rangle$ and the
degree-zero line $M_{i,s}$ with constant factors
$\exp Z_{ij}(s)$.
Quotienting first by these two periods and by $(0,2\pi i)$,
then by the last period, gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_s=M_{i,s}^{\times}/
   \langle(p,\ell)\mapsto(p+d_i s^R,\gamma_i\ell)\rangle,
                    \qquad d_i\ne0 .                  \hypertarget{tag-00AO}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}
\hypertarget{tag-012A}{}
\hypertarget{tag-00TJ}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.8}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.18}}
\end{equation}
This is an isomorphism of holomorphic families: the first
quotient uses $(p,z)\mapsto(p,e^z)$ and the two constant
line factors, and the last quotient uses exactly the
remaining period. The inverse is given by local logarithms
modulo those same four generators. All four periods and
their original flat torsor parameters are therefore preserved.
The line $M_{i,s}$ may be any degree-zero line. In particular
when $T_0=F\times B$ and its complementary periods have zero
fibre coordinate, $M_{i,0}$ is trivial.

Write $p=p^{(i)}$ in this presentation, and choose a constant
lift $p_i^0$ of its marked central base point. At that point
of the smooth elliptic surface family

\begin{lemma}[Effective anticanonical Hopf boundaries]\hypertarget{tag-P325}{}\label{lem:II:reduced-anticanonical-hopf}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:reduced-anticanonical-hopf}{proved}{P325}{\cref{lem:II:central-primary-hopf-cover}; \cite[arXiv v1, \S2.2.2, p.~4; \S2.3.1, p.~8]{AbashevaDeev2024AB}; \cite[arXiv v2, normal forms (1), p.~3; Theorem~2.1 and Remark~2.2, p.~5]{Khaled2024Hopf}}
Let $H$ be a compact Hopf surface and let $D$ be a nonempty
effective integral divisor whose support consists of disjoint smooth
elliptic curves. Suppose $K_H(D)\simeq\OO_H$. Exactly one of the
following alternatives holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $D$ is reduced. The pair $(H,D)$ is a diagonal primary or
secondary Hopf surface with its two axes individually marked.
There are coordinates on $W=\C^2\setminus\{0\}$ in which the
full deck group of $W\to H$ is diagonal and the inverse image
of $D$ is $\{zw=0\}\cap W$. The two axes have distinct images
on $H$, and $dz/z\wedge dw/w$ descends to a nowhere-zero
section of $K_H(D)$.
\item $D=dC$ for one smooth elliptic curve $C$ and an integer $d\ge2$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, a coefficient-one component of $D$ forces the
first alternative.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $H=W/\Gamma$ and apply
\cref{lem:II:central-primary-hopf-cover}. It gives a central
contraction $F$ and a finite unramified primary cover
$\pi:P=W/\langle F\rangle\to H$.
Put $D_P=\pi^*D$. The local unramified differential preserves
each divisor coefficient and gives
$K_P(D_P)\simeq\pi^*(K_H(D))\simeq\OO_P$.

Use the complete primary normal-form list in
\cite[arXiv v2, formula~(1), p.~3; Theorem~2.1, p.~5]{Khaled2024Hopf}.
In the nonlinear case write
$F(z,w)=(\beta^a z+w^a,\beta w)$, $a\ge1$.
Its unique curve is $C_P=\{w=0\}/\langle F\rangle$ by
\cite[arXiv v1, \S2.2.2, p.~4]{AbashevaDeev2024AB},
so $D_P=dC_P$ for a positive integer $d$.
The determinant of $dF$ is $\beta^{a+1}$; thus
$w^{a+1}\partial_z\wedge\partial_w$ is an anticanonical
section with divisor $(a+1)C_P$.
The line $\OO_P(C_P)$ has infinite order: a trivial positive
power would turn its canonical section into a holomorphic
function with a nonempty zero divisor on the compact connected
surface. Therefore $K_P(D_P)\simeq\OO_P$ forces $d=a+1\ge2$.
Unramified descent gives the second alternative on $H$.

In diagonal coordinates $F(z,w)=(\alpha z,\beta w)$,
an anticanonical section lifts to
$g(z,w)\partial_z\wedge\partial_w$. Hartogs extends $g$
across zero, and equivariance gives
\begin{equation}
                        g(\alpha z,\beta w)
                                      =\alpha\beta g(z,w).
\hypertarget{tag-00DP}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.CZ.11}
\end{equation}
If there is no positive multiplicative relation between
$\alpha$ and $\beta$, comparison of monomials gives only $zw$.
Indeed a nonzero coefficient of $z^iw^j$ requires
$\alpha^{i-1}\beta^{j-1}=1$; since both multipliers contract,
any solution other than $(i,j)=(1,1)$ gives such a relation.

Otherwise choose positive integers $u,v$ with
$\alpha^u=\beta^v$, and write $u=dq$, $v=dp$ with $(p,q)=1$.
The central power $F^d$ has multipliers
$\alpha_1=\alpha^d$, $\beta_1=\beta^d$ satisfying
$\alpha_1^q=\beta_1^p$.
Choose integers $s,t$ with $sp+tq=1$ and put
$\gamma=\alpha_1^s\beta_1^t$.
Then $\gamma^p=\alpha_1$, $\gamma^q=\beta_1$, and $0<|\gamma|<1$.
The quotient map $W/\langle F^d\rangle\to W/\langle F\rangle$
is finite unramified, and $F^d$ is still central in $\Gamma$.
Pullback to this cover retains every coefficient of $D_P$.
The monomials of $g$ now have weight $p+q$.
The equation $pi+qj=p+q$ is equivalent to
$i=1+q\ell$, $j=1-p\ell$, with $\ell\in\Z$.
For $p,q>1$, nonnegative exponents force $\ell=0$.
For $p>1,q=1$, the full section is
\begin{equation}
                        g=w(az+bw^p).
\hypertarget{tag-00R0}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.ML.9}
\end{equation}
When $a=0$, its divisor is $(p+1)$ times the single axis.
When $a\ne0$, the two factors are distinct and simple;
$z'=z+(b/a)w^p$, $w'=w$ sends them to the axes and commutes
with the contraction. Its inverse is
$z=z'-(b/a)(w')^p$, $w=w'$.
For $p=1,q>1$ use the exchanged coordinates and the exchanged
triangular map. For $p=q=1$, $g$ is a nonzero quadratic.
A repeated linear factor gives twice one curve; two distinct
linear factors give an invertible linear coordinate map,
with inverse its matrix inverse, commuting with the scalar contraction.
Thus on this finite unramified primary cover the divisor is
either reduced with two curves, or a positive multiple of one
curve with coefficient at least two. Since the cover is
surjective and unramified, the same reducedness alternative
and each coefficient descend to $H$; in the latter case the
image of that single curve is all of the support of $D$.
In particular a coefficient-one component excludes the latter case.

It remains to retain the full marking in the reduced case.
Use the coordinates just constructed, so the pulled-back
boundary is the two axes and the central contraction is diagonal.
Every deck lift preserves their union and commutes with that
central contraction. A lift preserving each axis has form
$(zU(z,w),wV(z,w))$ with holomorphic units $U,V$.
Commutation makes both units invariant under the contraction;
iteration to zero makes them constant.
A lift interchanging the axes has form $(wU,zV)$.
Comparison of linear terms forces the two multipliers of the
central contraction to agree, and the same iteration makes
$U,V$ constant. It is a diagonal map followed by interchange.
The logarithmic form $dz/z\wedge dw/w$ is a nowhere-zero
section of the pulled-back canonical-boundary line, and spans
its section space because the primary surface is compact and connected.
Diagonal lifts fix it; interchange negates it.
The nonzero section pulled back from $K_H(D)$ is invariant,
so every deck lift preserves each axis. The full group
$\Gamma$ is diagonal and the two images are distinct.

A diagonal group containing an infinite cyclic subgroup of finite
index is finitely generated abelian, so
$\Gamma=\langle f\rangle\oplus T$ with $T$ finite.
Choose the sign of $f$ so that a positive power is a positive
power of the central contraction times an element of $T$.
Both multipliers of $f$ then have modulus less than one.
The finite group $T$ acts freely on $W$, so each coordinate
character is injective; consequently $T$ is cyclic.
The equality $H=(W/\langle f\rangle)/T$ gives the stated
diagonal primary or secondary presentation with its marked axes.
The logarithmic form descends through this free quotient.
\end{proof}

$k_PP+\sum_i k_iH_i$. Its existence and the fact that it
has only vertical zeroes are the exact direct-image
calculation in \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.38}. Adjunction on one leaf gives
\[
                  K_H=\OO_H(-aJ),\qquad
                  a=k_H-k_P+1\in\Z.                      \tag{C.AS.6}\hypertarget{tag-00AV}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.6}
\]
We classify this equality on the actual pair $(H,J)$,
including the full secondary deck group.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  Take a normal primary cyclic subgroup of the Hopf deck
group $\Gamma$. Its generator $F$ is central: conjugation
can send it only to $F$ or $F^{-1}$, while the nonzero
logarithm of the modulus of its derivative determinant
excludes the latter. This is the exact normal-core
argument of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.43}. We therefore have a finite
unramified primary cover $H'\to H$, and the full inverse
image $D$ of $J$ is a disjoint union of smooth elliptic
curves. The finite quotient acts transitively on these
curves, since $J$ is connected. Pullback gives
\[
                           K_{H'}=-aD.                  \tag{C.AS.7}\hypertarget{tag-00AW}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.7}
\]

of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.38} gives its unique axis, and the full

nonlinear quotient in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}--\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}.
The invariant form $dz\wedge dw/w^{r+1}$ has divisor
$-(r+1)J$, on the quotient as well. Since $\OO_H(J)$ has
infinite order, \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.6} forces $a=r+1$.


\item  Consider a diagonal primary contraction. Its invariant
curve computation can be read directly from an equation
on $\C^2$. Closure across the origin and removal of the
nonconstant unit in its transformation give an eigenfunction
of $F$. Comparison of its power-series monomials gives
the axes in the absence of a multiplicative resonance.
In that case the complete centralizer is diagonal, so
it cannot interchange the axes. Thus $D$ is one axis.
If, for example, it is $w=0$, the exact automorphy
characters in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.7} give
$\alpha\beta=\beta^a$, which is the resonance
$\alpha=\beta^{a-1}$. The contraction moduli make

resonance and accounts for that case through an actual
character equality.

subgroup to remove the finite root-of-unity discrepancy.
Its generator has the form
\[
                 F(z,w)=(\gamma^p z,\gamma^q w),
       \qquad p,q\ge1,\quad\gcd(p,q)=1,\quad |\gamma|<1 .
                                                               \tag{C.AS.8}\hypertarget{tag-00AX}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.8}
\]

weighted homogeneous polynomial factors into these
binomials over $\C$. Its irreducible factor is unique
because $p,q$ are coprime. The curves are smooth away
from the origin, as required for the elliptic curves
on $H'$.

\[
                              ampq=p+q.                 \tag{C.AS.9}\hypertarget{tag-00AY}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.9}
\]

extend across the origin, and their nonzero value there
forces the identical character. In particular $a>0$.

or $q\mid p$, also impossible. In this case the
centralizer preserves each axis, so an orbit containing

would require $amr=r+1$, hence $r\mid1$.
The only possibility is the weight-one axis $w=0$,

Commuting with $(\gamma^rz,\gamma w)$ gives exactly
\[

On its affine complement, averaging gives a

\[

\begin{lemma}[Compact insertion with prescribed Hopf leaves]\hypertarget{tag-P353}{}\label{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}

 p^{(i)}=P-s^R\frac{\bar a_i}{a_i}Z,\qquad

$\mathcal B_i\to\Delta_s$, take the weighted blowup of

\begin{equation}

                    \qquad \zeta^{n_i}=1.                \hypertarget{tag-012B}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.9}
\end{equation}
on $(\C^2_{z,w}\setminus\{0\})\times\C_x$.
It is free: a nonzero $w$ or $x$ makes $\zeta=1$,
and when both vanish, $z\ne0$ and $\gcd(r_i,n_i)=1$
has the same consequence. Equivalently, the order-$r_i$
weighted inertia in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.7} acts faithfully
on this line because of that coprimality. Thus the coarse
nonzero line space is smooth.

Choose the given $n_i$th root $\beta_i$ of $\gamma_i$.
The lift of the last period in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.17} is
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 (z,w,x)\longmapsto\bigl(&
   \beta_i^{r_i}(z+d_i x^{R-r_i}w^R),\\
   &\beta_iw,\ \beta_i^{-1}x\bigr).
 \end{split}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AP}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.18}
\hypertarget{tag-0123}{}
\hypertarget{tag-00TK}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.10}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.19}}
\end{equation}
The monomial $x^{R-r_i}w^R$ has weighted degree $r_i$,
so this map commutes with the finite action. It fixes
$s=xw$ and changes $p$ by exactly $d_i s^R$.
On $x=0$, equality $R=r_i$ gives the nonlinear contraction
after $Z=z/(\beta_i^{r_i}d_i)$; strict inequality gives
the diagonal contraction. On $w=0$ it is always
$(z,x)\mapsto(\beta_i^{r_i}z,\beta_i^{-1}x)$.
Thus its main-component chart is
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4} and its leaf is the prescribed
primary or secondary surface.

We prove uniform properness of this quotient with its
varying line. On a closed smaller base disc, solve
\[
 \operatorname{Re}\bigl(Z_{ij}(s)-c_i(s)P_{ij}(s)\bigr)=0,
 \qquad j=1,2.
\]
The real period matrix is invertible, so the solution
$c_i(s)$ is smooth and bounded. The norm
$|\ell|\exp(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)p))$ is invariant
under the two line-factor identifications. The last
period multiplies it by
\[
 \varrho_i(s)=|\gamma_i|
              \exp\bigl(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)d_i s^R)\bigr).
\]
After shrinking, $0<\varrho_-\le\varrho_i(s)\le\varrho_+<1$
uniformly for all marked indices.

For the exceptional line, use the weighted norm
comparison \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.9} with $r=r_i$.
Uniform flat metrics on $B_{i,s}$ give
\[
 d(p+j d_i s^R,p_i^0)\le d(p,p_i^0)+C|j||s|^{r_i}
\]
for every integer $j$, since $R\ge r_i$.
The same inequality for the inverse translation gives
the reverse comparison. The $j$th lift on $\OO(n_iE_i)$
therefore changes its norm by a factor between
$C^{-1}(1+|j|)^{-n_i/r_i}$ and
$C(1+|j|)^{n_i/r_i}$, exactly the $n_i$th tensor power
of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.10}. This comparison extends over
the exceptional divisor by continuity of the positive
line-norm ratio. Multiplication by $\varrho_i(s)^j$
makes the full norm tend uniformly to zero as
$j\to+\infty$ and to infinity as $j\to-\infty$.
Any two compact sets have line norms bounded above and
away from zero, proving proper discontinuity. A fixed
point of a nonzero power would be fixed by arbitrarily
large powers, contradicting these limits, so the action
is free, including after its finite quotient.

Choose one positive integer $N$ such that the $N$th
iterate decreases every line norm. Its norm ratio has
a positive minimum $c_N$ over the compact weighted base
above a closed base disc. Every orbit meets
$c_N\le\|\ell\|\le1$, a compact annulus there.
The quotient $\mathcal Y_i\to\Delta_s$ is therefore a
smooth proper local family.

Outside its exceptional Hopf component, the canonical
section of $\OO(n_iE_i)$ trivializes that factor and gives
\begin{equation}
       \mathcal Y_i\setminus H_i
            \simeq \mathcal T|_{\Delta_s}\setminus F_i,
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TM}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.20}
\end{equation}
where the right side is the compact torus family restricted
to the same disc, with its marked central fibre curve removed.
In the normalized line gauge the torus-family flat coordinate is
$W=x^{-n_i}$. On the main component its other coordinate
is $u=z^{n_i}$, and
$u=p_{\rm loc}^{n_i}W^{r_i}$, $X=p_{\rm loc}^kW^l$ are precisely the inverse
maps in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}, with its base coordinate
identified with $p_{\rm loc}$. On $s\ne0$ the map and
its inverse are the period quotient of
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}.

For simultaneous replacement, choose a compact fundamental
domain on each Hopf component. Along a sequence approaching
it, $z,w$ remain bounded and not both zero, while $x\to0$.
The torus-family flat coordinate $x^{-n_i}$ is put into a fixed
compact norm annulus by $O(1+|\log|x||)$ deck iterates;
this follows from the uniform exponential bounds and
their polynomial factors. The total base displacement is
\begin{equation}
                   O\bigl(|s|^R(1+|\log|x||)\bigr)
                          \longrightarrow0,
                         \qquad s=xw.                   \hypertarget{tag-00AQ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.19}
\end{equation}
because $s=xw$ and $w$ is bounded. The initial base
coordinate $p_{\rm loc}=p-p_i^0=x^{r_i}z$ also tends to zero.
Consequently every cluster point of the images of this
sequence lies on $F_i$ in the original torus family.

Choose disjoint relatively compact neighbourhoods $W_i$
of the $F_i$ in a smaller closed tube. The subsets
$H_i\cup\Psi_i^{-1}(W_i\setminus F_i)$ of $\mathcal Y_i$,
where $\Psi_i$ is \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.20}, are open by the
cluster property. Glue them to the torus family with
the $F_i$ deleted by the same isomorphisms. A pair of
distinct limiting points in different pieces could only
arise from a cluster on one of the $F_i$; those loci have
been deleted from the torus piece and are disjoint for
different $i$. The gluing graphs are thus closed and
the glued space is Hausdorff.
Choose smaller closed neighbourhoods inside the $W_i$.
Their inverse images under $\Psi_i$, together with $H_i$,
are closed subsets of the proper $\mathcal Y_i$ over a
closed base disc and hence compact. Together with the
compact unmodified complement they cover the inverse
image of that disc. This proves properness of the glued
family. All maps are biholomorphic on the overlaps,
so its total space is smooth.

On the central main component the gluing reverses the
same inverse-transform maps used to define $T_0$.
It therefore recovers the original $P$ with every
analytic transition. The chosen fibre-period basis
preserves the linear part of each marked normal cover.
The maps $(z,w)\mapsto(a^{r_i}z,aw)$ commute with both
contractions and with the finite action; as $a$ varies,
they realize every constant translation of the marked
axis. They therefore preserve the given remaining gluing
constants. The full local equation is $s=xw$ in the
free coarse charts, so all central components have
multiplicity one and meet transversely as the given $S$.

Outside this tube the compact family
\eqref{eq:II:compact-twistor-lattice}, pulled back by
$t=s^R$, is unchanged. The proper local replacement and
that compact complement give a smooth compact threefold
over $\PP^1$. Every nonzero fibre is the original smooth
connected two-torus. The central quasibundle has Euler
number zero by \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic};
\cref{lem:II:hopf-curve-restriction} gives Euler number zero
for the Hopf leaves, and each double curve is elliptic. Additivity gives $e(S)=0$, completing
the construction.
\end{proof}

old_text:
\begin{proof}\leavevmode\par



 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=0pt,labelsep=.5em]
\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The canonical identity on an arbitrary Hopf leaf.}
We first use an actual reduced smoothing. Let the divisor
of a local canonical evaluation generator be
$k_PP+\sum_i k_iH_i$. Its existence and the fact that it
has only vertical zeroes are the exact direct-image
calculation in \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.38}. Adjunction on one leaf gives
\[
                  K_H=\OO_H(-aJ),\qquad
                  a=k_H-k_P+1\in\Z.                      \tag{C.AS.6}\hypertarget{tag-00AV}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.6}
\]
We classify this equality on the actual pair $(H,J)$,
including the full secondary deck group.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  Take a normal primary cyclic subgroup of the Hopf deck
group $\Gamma$. Its generator $F$ is central: conjugation
can send it only to $F$ or $F^{-1}$, while the nonzero
logarithm of the modulus of its derivative determinant
excludes the latter. This is the exact normal-core
argument of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.43}. We therefore have a finite
unramified primary cover $H'\to H$, and the full inverse
image $D$ of $J$ is a disjoint union of smooth elliptic
curves. The finite quotient acts transitively on these
curves, since $J$ is connected. Pullback gives
\[
                           K_{H'}=-aD.                  \tag{C.AS.7}\hypertarget{tag-00AW}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.7}
\]


\item  For a nonlinear primary contraction the curve computation
of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.38} gives its unique axis, and the full
centralizer computation of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.43} gives exactly the
nonlinear quotient in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}--\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}.
The invariant form $dz\wedge dw/w^{r+1}$ has divisor
$-(r+1)J$, on the quotient as well. Since $\OO_H(J)$ has
infinite order, \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.6} forces $a=r+1$.


\item  Consider a diagonal primary contraction. Its invariant
curve computation can be read directly from an equation
on $\C^2$. Closure across the origin and removal of the
nonconstant unit in its transformation give an eigenfunction
of $F$. Comparison of its power-series monomials gives
the axes in the absence of a multiplicative resonance.
In that case the complete centralizer is diagonal, so
it cannot interchange the axes. Thus $D$ is one axis.
If, for example, it is $w=0$, the exact automorphy
characters in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.7} give
$\alpha\beta=\beta^a$, which is the resonance
$\alpha=\beta^{a-1}$. The contraction moduli make
$a-1>0$. This contradicts the assumed absence of a
resonance and accounts for that case through an actual
character equality.


\item  In the resonant case pass to a further central cyclic
subgroup to remove the finite root-of-unity discrepancy.
Its generator has the form
\[
                 F(z,w)=(\gamma^p z,\gamma^q w),
       \qquad p,q\ge1,\quad\gcd(p,q)=1,\quad |\gamma|<1 .
                                                               \tag{C.AS.8}\hypertarget{tag-00AX}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.8}
\]
Here the axes have defining weights $p,q$, and every
other irreducible curve has equation $z^q=cw^p$ of
weight $pq$. This follows from the same eigenfunction
calculation: after an axis monomial is removed, a
weighted homogeneous polynomial factors into these
binomials over $\C$. Its irreducible factor is unique
because $p,q$ are coprime. The curves are smooth away
from the origin, as required for the elliptic curves
on $H'$.


\item  The canonical weight is $p+q$. If $D$ is an orbit of
$m$ non-axis curves, \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.7} therefore gives
\[
                              ampq=p+q.                 \tag{C.AS.9}\hypertarget{tag-00AY}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.9}
\]
The same calculation with a single axis replaces $mpq$
by $p$ or $q$. These are genuine character equalities:
a purported extra holomorphic unit and its inverse
extend across the origin, and their nonzero value there
forces the identical character. In particular $a>0$.


\item  For $p,q>1$, coprimality gives $pq>p+q$, so \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.9}
is impossible. A single axis would require $p\mid q$
or $q\mid p$, also impossible. In this case the
centralizer preserves each axis, so an orbit containing
both axes cannot occur. For $p=r>1,q=1$, the curves
$z=cw^r$, including $z=0$, all have weight $r$.
The triangular centralizer can permute these curves;
an orbit of $m$ of them has total weight $mr$ and
would require $amr=r+1$, hence $r\mid1$.
The only possibility is the weight-one axis $w=0$,
and then $a=r+1$.


\item  We retain the full deck group in this last calculation.
Commuting with $(\gamma^rz,\gamma w)$ gives exactly
\[
              (z,w)\longmapsto(Az+Cw^r,Bw).             \tag{C.AS.10}\hypertarget{tag-00AH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.10}
\]
Its induced action on $z/w^r$ is affine. The central
cyclic subgroup acts trivially there; hence the image
is a finite affine group. Averaging the orbit of zero
gives an actual common fixed point. The corresponding
coordinate change $z\mapsto z-cw^r$ makes every element
diagonal, while retaining the marked axis. Equation
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.6} then says, for every deck element,
$AB=B^{r+1}$, so $A=B^r$. Thus $\Gamma$ is the
weighted scalar group with an infinite contracting
generator $\beta$ and finite roots of unity
$\mu_n$. Freeness on the marked axis gives
$\gcd(r,n)=1$. This is exactly the diagonal pair in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}--\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}.


\item  It remains to check the scalar case $p=q=1$,
where the full secondary group need not initially
be diagonal. Every component of $D$ lifts to a
line, and \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.7} gives $am=2$. If $m=1$,
the finite projective group fixes that line.
On its affine complement, averaging gives a
second fixed point, so the linear group becomes
diagonal in coordinates retaining the first line.
The character equality $AB=B^2$ forces $A=B$
for every element. We obtain the case $r=1$
of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}, with scalar finite action.
If $m=2$, then $a=1$ and an element of the full
deck group interchanges the two lines. Choose
them as the two coordinate axes. The unique
log-canonical form up to a constant is
\[
                             \frac{dz}{z}\wedge\frac{dw}{w}.
                                                               \tag{C.AS.11}\hypertarget{tag-00AI}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.11}
\]
Every such interchange multiplies this form
by $-1$. A form with exactly the same divisor
differs by a nowhere-zero holomorphic function
on the compact primary Hopf surface, hence by
a constant. It therefore cannot descend.
This contradicts the actual equality
$K_H+J=0$ in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.6}. Thus this last orbit
does not satisfy \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.6}. We have proved,
without an a priori restriction on the secondary
group, precisely the leaf-pair list \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1},
and in every surviving case
\[
                              k_i-k_P=r_i\ge1.          \tag{C.AS.12}\hypertarget{tag-00AJ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.12}
\]


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The central component is forced into the stated class.}
Adjunction on $P$ now gives the exact effective
canonical divisor
\[
                         K_P=\sum_i(r_i-1)J_i .         \tag{C.AS.13}\hypertarget{tag-00AK}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.13}
\]
Thus $\kappa(P)\ge0$ and $p_g(P)\ge1$.
\ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.28} gives $p_g(P)=1$. The surface $P$
is minimal. Indeed, a $(-1)$-curve is rational,
so is distinct from every elliptic $J_i$.
Its intersections with all of them are
nonnegative, contradicting $K_P\cdot E=-1$
and \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.13}.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  We now specify the covering comparison needed
to apply \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.31} to this original component.
Its full-fibre multiplicity is one. In the
normalized root base change $t=s^N$, a generic
chart is $x=s^N$ after a holomorphic unit is
absorbed. There is exactly one strict covering
component and its map to $P$ has degree one.
Equivalently, the total generic degree of the
strict component covers is the original
multiplicity, as calculated in \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.36}.
After resolution it remains birational to $P$.
Both minimal models are therefore the same
smooth surface. The actual root-cover conclusion
of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.31} thus applies to $P$ itself:
it is a two-torus, or a fixed-Jacobian,
identity-monodromy elliptic quasi-bundle over
a curve of genus at most one, with only smooth
multiple fibres. In the latter description
$p_g(P)=g(B)$, so the base is elliptic.
No assertion about an arbitrary quotient
component has been substituted for this
degree-one comparison.


\item  We also verify that all the given curves
$J_i$ are fibres of one such fibration.
On a torus, an embedded elliptic curve is a
translate of an elliptic subgroup: lift its
map to universal covers and differentiate;
the derivative is periodic and holomorphic,
hence constant. Two elliptic subgroups with
distinct tangent lines give a surjective
isogeny from their product to the two-torus.
Every two translates then meet. The disjoint
$J_i$ consequently have one common tangent
line and are fibres of the actual elliptic
quotient.


\item  In the quasi-bundle description over an
elliptic base the canonical divisor is
$\sum(m-1)F_{\rm red}$, by the exact root
chart calculation in \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49}.
If a multiple fibre occurs, a horizontal
$J_i$ would have positive intersection with
this canonical divisor. But its torsion
normal line gives $J_i^2=0$, and adjunction
gives $K_P\cdot J_i=0$. Thus every $J_i$
is vertical. If no multiple fibre occurs,
we have a principal elliptic bundle.
A nonzero integral Chern vector excludes
a horizontal elliptic curve: its finite
unramified map to the base would pull the
bundle back to one with a section, while
its Chern vector would be multiplied by
the nonzero covering degree. If that Chern
vector is zero, the exact Cech lattice
calculation (C.NS.14) identifies $P$ with
a torus, reducing to the preceding argument.
This proves \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.3} with every marked
curve retained.


\item  The normal of the leaf axis has exact
torsion order $r_i$, including its finite
secondary character by (C.SN.3)--(C.SN.4).
Normal duality in the reduced smoothing
therefore gives full marked fibre $r_iJ_i$
on $P$. Subtracting the marked terms of
its canonical root-chart formula from
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.13} leaves an effective sum of
unmarked multiple fibres linearly
equivalent to zero. Such a nonzero
effective divisor on a compact connected
complex surface cannot be principal:
its defining meromorphic function would
have no poles and hence be constant.
Consequently there are no unmarked
multiple fibres.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The exact topology and the one period shared by all leaves.}
The primary and secondary inverse-transform
charts (C.SN.3)--(C.SN.6) apply to both
contractions in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}: they use their
identical axis normal character. For a
nonlinear leaf the explicit deformation
of its resonant coefficient to zero gives
the relative smooth-pair comparison
proved in \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49}. For a diagonal leaf
the product complement is already exact.
Thus every Hopf complement kills the
same displayed complementary meridian,
and each oriented core two-torus becomes
the ordinary fibre class of the actual
inverse transform $T_0\to B$.
The nearby smoothing is its underlying
four-manifold. Its fundamental group is
the principal-bundle presentation
(C.NS.13), with the unaltered integer
Chern vector. A two-torus has abelian
fundamental group; the injected fibre
lattice in that presentation therefore
forces \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.4}.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  Let $\gamma$ be this one transported
integral core class. Divide the relative
canonical generator by $t^{k_P}$.
On the $i$th Hopf core its leading
term is $t^{r_i}\eta_i$, with
\[
                   \eta_i=c_i\,\frac{dz\wedge dw}{w^{r_i+1}},
                          \qquad c_i\ne0.               \tag{C.AS.14}\hypertarget{tag-00AL}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.14}
\]
This is the actual coefficient calculation
of (C.NS.11), together with \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.12}.
Put $U=z/w^{r_i}$ and $V=\log w$.
The primitive angular period of the
secondary quotient is $(0,2\pi i/n_i)$.
For a nonlinear leaf the other period is
$(\beta_i^{-r_i},\log\beta_i)$, so
\[
       \int_{\gamma}\omega_t
          =t^{r_i}\left(\frac{\pm2\pi i c_i\beta_i^{-r_i}}{n_i}
                         +O(t)\right).                 \tag{C.AS.15}\hypertarget{tag-00AM}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.15}
\]
Its coefficient is nonzero. For a diagonal
leaf the other period is
$(0,\log\beta_i)$: the core lies at
constant $U$, and $c_i\,dU\wedge dV$
has zero integral there. Consequently
\[
                         \int_\gamma\omega_t=O(t^{r_i+1})
                  \quad\hbox{at a diagonal leaf}.        \tag{C.AS.16}\hypertarget{tag-00AN}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.16}
\]
These are periods of the same actual
class in the same nearby fibre. They
are holomorphic functions: integration
of a closed relative holomorphic form
over the transported compact cycle is
holomorphic by differentiation and
Stokes' theorem. The displayed leading
terms also give their holomorphic
extension at zero.


\item  If a nonlinear leaf occurs, \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.15}
gives one finite vanishing order $R$.
Every nonlinear $r_i$ equals it, and
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.16} gives $r_i<R$ for every
diagonal leaf. If all leaves are
diagonal, no finite vanishing order
is asserted for the given smoothing;
the explicit numerical test \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.5}
is satisfied by choosing
$R=1+\max_i r_i$. This proves its
necessity without imposing an unproved
nonzero period on that family.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{One compact construction realizes all the specified data.}
We now use data \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}--\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.5}.
The zero-Chern inverse transform is
the actual torus $T_0$ with its marked
fibres, by (C.NS.14). Take its explicit
compact $\OO_{\PP^1}(1)^{\oplus2}$
twistor family (C.NS.15), and pull it
back by $t=s^R$. For the $i$th marked
curve the exact four-period coordinate
change (C.NS.16)--(C.NS.18), with
$\gamma_i=\beta_i^{n_i}$, gives
\[
 \mathcal T_s=M_{i,s}^{\times}/
   \langle(p,\ell)\mapsto(p+d_i s^R,\gamma_i\ell)\rangle,
                    \qquad d_i\ne0 .                  \tag{C.AS.17}\hypertarget{tag-00AO}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}
\]
The non-torsion flat line and every
original primitive fibre direction
are retained by these actual period
maps.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  At this marked point use weight
$(r_i,1)$ and tensor the flat line
by $\OO(n_iE_i)$, where $E_i$ is
the weighted exceptional divisor.
The same free coarse quotient as
(C.SN.9) has coordinates
$p-p_i=x^{r_i}z$, $s=xw$.
The exact infinite deck map is now
\[
 \begin{split}
 (z,w,x)\longmapsto\bigl(&
   \beta_i^{r_i}(z+d_i x^{R-r_i}w^R),\\
   &\beta_iw,\ \beta_i^{-1}x\bigr).
 \end{split}                                             \tag{C.AS.18}\hypertarget{tag-00AP}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.18}
\]
The exponent $R-r_i$ is nonnegative.
The added monomial has weighted degree
$r_i$, so this map commutes with the
finite action of weights
$(r_i,1,-1)$ modulo $n_i$. It preserves
$s=xw$ and changes the original base
coordinate by exactly $d_i s^R$.
Thus \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.18} is the actual lift
of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}.


\item  On $x=0$, equality $R=r_i$ gives the
specified nonlinear contraction after
$Z=z/(\beta_i^{r_i}d_i)$. Strict
inequality $R>r_i$ gives the specified
diagonal contraction. On $w=0$ the
map is always
$(z,x)\mapsto(\beta_i^{r_i}z,\beta_i^{-1}x)$,
so the main component and its outer
trivialization are exactly
(C.SN.4)--(C.SN.5), independently of
$R$. Every given central component
and every marked normal cover is
therefore the one prescribed.


\item  We record the analytic bounds to
verify the simultaneous compact
replacement in this varying-weight
case. On a small closed disc,
$|s|^R\le C|s|^{r_i}$ for every $i$.
The weighted norm comparison of
(C.NH.9)--(C.NH.10) consequently
gives at most
$C(1+|j|)^{n_i/r_i}$ distortion
for the $j$th translation lift.
The unitary flat metric used in
\ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.50} has scalar multiplier
$|\gamma_i|\exp(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)d_i s^R))$,
uniformly less than one after
shrinking the disc. Its exponential
contraction dominates that polynomial.
The same compact norm annulus proves
properness and freeness of the
infinite quotient. Coprimality in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1} makes its finite coarse
quotient smooth.


\item  Outside the new Hopf component the
canonical exceptional section gives
the actual isomorphism with the
original twistor family minus its
marked central elliptic curve.
In a compact Hopf fundamental domain,
$z,w$ remain bounded and $x\to0$.
The old flat coordinate is proportional
to $x^{-n_i}$. Putting it in a compact
norm annulus uses
$O(1+|\log|x||)$ iterates, with total
base displacement
\[
                   O\bigl(|s|^R(1+|\log|x||)\bigr)
                          \longrightarrow0,
                         \qquad s=xw.                   \tag{C.AS.19}\hypertarget{tag-00AQ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.19}
\]
All cluster points consequently lie
on the specified original central
elliptic curve. The disjoint-curve
gluing proof of (C.NS.20) therefore
applies to all these insertions
simultaneously. It proves a smooth
Hausdorff proper local family, and
the unchanged compact twistor
complement makes the total space
compact over $\PP^1$.


\item  The central main component is
precisely $P$, because all its
analytic torsor transitions have
been reversed by the exact inverse
charts. The diagonal automorphisms
$(z,w)\mapsto(a^{r_i}z,aw)$ commute
with either contraction and with
its finite action; they retain
every specified constant in the
axis gluing. The linear parts were
already retained by the chosen
normal-cover lattice bases.
Thus the full central support is
the specified $S$. Its equations
are $xw=s$ in the free coarse
charts, so every component has
multiplicity one. All other fibres
are the original smooth two-tori.
The Euler number of the central
support is zero by additivity:
each quasi-bundle, Hopf leaf and
double elliptic curve has Euler
number zero.


\item  The exact symbolic checks in
\path{code/root_mixed_hopf_stars.py}
retain the weighted base map, its
Jacobian, the finite-action weights
and the common period exponent.
The finite integer search there
checks the degree exclusions in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.9}; the preceding integer
argument proves them for all weights.



\end{enumerate}

\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\subsection{Canonical divisors on Hopf leaf pairs}\label{subsec:II:hopf-leaf-pairs}

\begin{lemma}[A canonical divisor supported on one Hopf curve]\hypertarget{tag-P352}{}\label{lem:II:hopf-single-canonical-curve}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:hopf-single-canonical-curve}{proved}{P352}{\cref{lem:II:hopf-curves,lem:II:hopf-curve-restriction,lem:II:central-primary-hopf-cover,lem:II:reduced-anticanonical-hopf,lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary}; \cref{cdp:eq:C.SH.3,cdp:eq:C.SH.4}}
Let $H$ be a compact primary or secondary Hopf surface and
$J\subset H$ a connected smooth curve. An identity
$K_H\simeq\OO_H(-aJ)$ with $a\in\Z$ holds exactly for
the marked pairs in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}, with the full
deck actions \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}; in these coordinates
$a=r+1$. The isomorphism marks $J$ as the image of $w=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The curve $J$ is elliptic by \cref{lem:II:hopf-curves}.
By \cref{lem:II:hopf-curve-restriction} and Serre duality,
$H^0(H,K_H)=0$. For $a\le0$ the canonical section of
$\OO_H(-aJ)$ would be nonzero, so $a>0$.
Apply \cref{lem:II:reduced-anticanonical-hopf} with the
effective divisor $aJ$. Its reduced alternative has two
distinct curve images and cannot equal this single-curve
support. Its other alternative gives $a\ge2$ and a finite
unramified central primary cover $\pi:H'\to H$ on which
$D=\pi^{-1}(J)$ is one marked curve. The unramified
differential and divisor pullback give
\begin{equation}
                           K_{H'}=-aD.                  \hypertarget{tag-00AW}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.7}
\end{equation}
The primary-cover clause of that lemma gives either the
nonlinear contraction $(\beta_0^rz+w^r,\beta_0w)$ or the
diagonal contraction $(\gamma^rz,\gamma w)$, with
$D=\{w=0\}$ and $a=r+1$. Its weight comparison
\cref{cdp:eq:C.AS.8,cdp:eq:C.AS.9} and its logarithmic
form \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.11} are on this same central-cover
construction; thus all inverse images of the marked curve
and all divisor coefficients are fixed in this application.

In the nonlinear case use the full centralizer map
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SH.3} for this same central contraction.
Every member of the full deck group commutes with it.
The quotient and splitting maps \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SH.4}
therefore identify $H$ with
$H_r(\beta)/\mu_n$, with finite action
$(z,w)\mapsto(\zeta^rz,\zeta w)$ and $\gcd(r,n)=1$.
Here $\beta$ is the second-coordinate multiplier of the
primitive contracting generator in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SH.4};
the central generator with multiplier $\beta_0$ is a positive
power of it times a finite deck element. The rescaling of
$z$ used there keeps $w=0$, and the
nonlinear primary curve is unique, so these maps carry
its image precisely to the given $J$.

For the diagonal central contraction, every deck lift
preserves its marked axis. For $r\ge2$, this contraction is
class $\mathrm{III}$ of \cite[arXiv v2, Theorem~2.1(3), p.~5]{Khaled2024Hopf}.
Its source parameters $(a,b,d)=(A,C,B)$ give
\begin{equation}
              (z,w)\longmapsto(Az+Cw^r,Bw).             \hypertarget{tag-00AH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.10}
\end{equation}
with $A,B\ne0$. For $r=1$, class $\mathrm{IV}$ in the same
theorem gives $\operatorname{GL}(2,\C)$; preservation of
$w=0$ sets its lower-left matrix entry to zero and gives
the same formula. Its action on
$z/w^r$ is affine. The central contraction acts trivially
on that coordinate, so the induced affine group is finite.
The average of its finite orbit of zero is a common fixed
point $c$. The maps $z'=z-cw^r$, $w'=w$ and
$z=z'+c(w')^r$, $w=w'$ conjugate the whole group to
diagonal maps while preserving the marked curve and
commuting with the central contraction.

The invariant form $dz\wedge dw/w^{r+1}$ trivializes
$K_{H'}((r+1)D)$. The section pulled back from
$K_H(aJ)$ differs from it by a constant, since $H'$ is
compact and connected. Invariance under every diagonal
deck element gives $AB=B^{r+1}$, hence $A=B^r$.
The full group is consequently the weighted scalar group
given by its second-coordinate multipliers. It has a
cyclic subgroup of finite index, so it is generated by
one contracting multiplier $\beta$, together with its
finite subgroup $\mu_n$. Freeness on $w=0$ gives
$\gcd(r,n)=1$: a root with $\zeta^r=1$ would fix a
nonzero point of that axis. Thus its quotient is exactly
the diagonal pair of \cref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1,cdp:eq:C.AS.2},
with the same marked curve.

Conversely, for each displayed pair the invariant form
and infinite order of $\OO_H(J)$ in the proof of
\cref{lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary} give
$K_H=-(r+1)J$ and uniqueness of the integer $a$.
This proves both directions with the stated pair maps.
\end{proof}
