\begin{proof}\leavevmode\par



 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=0pt,labelsep=.5em]
\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The actual inverse transform.}
We first define the operation whenever the marked
multiplicity is $r_i$ and the two normal lines are dual.
Write the Hopf axis as $\C^*/\beta_i^{r_i\Z}$, with
coordinate $z$. Its normal has multiplier $\beta_i$.
The matching neighborhood in $P$ has the precise model
\[
 p=x^{r_i}z,\qquad
 (z,x)\sim(\beta_i^{r_i}z,\beta_i^{-1}x).
                                                        \tag{C.NS.1}\hypertarget{tag-00TA}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.1}
\]
Indeed, normalize the $r_i$-th root of $q$ at this fibre.
The result is a smooth principal $F$-bundle over a disc,
hence is trivial there. The free root action is an
order-$r_i$ translation on $F$, together with the
primitive normal character. A finite averaging gauge
makes that translation independent of the root
parameter. The dual-normal isomorphism identifies this
connected cyclic cover with the one coming from the
Hopf axis. In multiplicative coordinates the cover is
$z=w^{r_i}$, $x=u/w$, with deck $w\mapsto\beta_i w$;
its quotient is exactly \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.1}, with $p=u^{r_i}$.
This also proves that the normal of a smooth
multiple fibre has exact order its multiplicity.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  On the punctured base disc the map
\[
       (z,x)\longmapsto(p,w)=(x^{r_i}z,x^{-1}),
       \qquad z=pw^{r_i},
       \qquad [w]\in F_i=\C^*/\beta_i^{\Z}
                                                        \tag{C.NS.2}\hypertarget{tag-00TL}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}
\]
is an actual product trivialization. Replace \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.1}
by $F_i\times\Delta_p$ through \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}, at every
marked point. The original torsor on the complement
and these exact transition maps define
\[
                             q_0:T_0\longrightarrow B.
                                                        \tag{C.NS.3}\hypertarget{tag-00TN}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.3}
\]
When there are no unmarked multiple fibres, this is a
smooth principal $F$-bundle. All identifications of
$F_i$ with $F$ are the ones furnished by the given
normal covers and the original torsor.


\item  The construction is independent of the permitted local
choices. Two dual-normal isomorphisms differ by a
nonzero holomorphic function on the compact elliptic
axis and hence by a constant. This changes $w$ by a
constant translation of $F_i$, which extends over the
product disc. An automorphism of a root-trivialized
principal $F$-bundle that extends across its central
curve is a holomorphic translation there, followed by
a fixed linear automorphism. If it preserves the
specified normal cover, that translation is invariant
under the root action and descends to a holomorphic
translation on the ordinary disc. It again extends
over the product filling. The specified axis map
fixes the remaining linear identification. Thus
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.3} retains the full holomorphic torsor class;
it is not defined merely by a rational Chern number.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The integral boundary matrix and the smoothing topology.}
We compute all meridians before applying a smoothing
argument. In \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.1}, let $a$ be the positive angular
loop of $z$, let $b$ be its deck loop, and let
$\mu_P$ be the positive angular loop of $x$. On the
punctured product \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}, let $\delta$ be the
positive base loop with $w$ fixed, $e$ the angular
loop of $w$, and $h$ its $\beta_i$-deck loop. Then
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}a&b&\mu_P\end{pmatrix}_{(\delta,e,h)}
       =
 \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0&r_i\\
  0&0&-1\\
  0&1&0
 \end{pmatrix};
 \qquad
 a=\delta,\quad b=h,\quad \mu_P=r_i\delta-e.
                                                        \tag{C.NS.4}\hypertarget{tag-00TO}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.4}
\]
The matrix is integral of determinant one. For example,
holding $p$ fixed while $w$ winds once gives
$x=w^{-1}$ and $z=pw^{r_i}$, proving
$e=r_i a-\mu_P$. The formulas retain the normal
character, not just its order.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  The nonlinear Hopf pair is smoothly equivalent, for
this boundary calculation, to the diagonal pair with
contraction $(\beta_i^{r_i}z,\beta_i w)$. One exact
comparison on the complement is
\[
 U=\frac{z}{w^{r_i}},\qquad
 V=U-\frac{\beta_i^{-r_i}}{\log|\beta_i|}\log|w|.
                                                        \tag{C.NS.5}\hypertarget{tag-00TP}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.5}
\]
The deck map sends $U$ to $U+\beta_i^{-r_i}$ and
$w$ to $\beta_iw$, so $V$ is invariant. This gives
$H_i\setminus J_i\simeq\C_V\times F_i$ smoothly.
The map
$z\mapsto z-\beta_i^{-r_i}w^{r_i}\log|w|/\log|\beta_i|$
extends continuously as the identity on the axis and
preserves orientation; it is smooth on every boundary
torus. Equivalently, vary the resonant coefficient from
one to zero in the contraction and use a uniform
compact fundamental annulus. This is a smooth proper
family of pairs, so the same integral boundary
identification follows by relative Ehresmann.


\item  Let $\mu_H$ be the Hopf normal meridian. The
smoothing equation is $xw=t$, so
$\mu_H=-\mu_P$. The regular fibre cycles on the
Hopf side are
\[
                   e_H=r_i a+\mu_H=e,\qquad h_H=b=h.
                                                        \tag{C.NS.6}\hypertarget{tag-00TQ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.6}
\]
The complementary solid torus $F_i\times D^2$ in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.5} kills $a=\delta$. Consequently replacing
the tubular neighborhood in $P$ by the Hopf
complement is precisely the inverse logarithmic
transform \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}, with its indicated integral
framing.


\item  For completeness, this calculation applies to every
actual SNC smoothing of the specified support.
Remove small tubular neighborhoods of the disjoint
double curves. On each remaining compact component
core the original map is a submersion through zero;
Ehresmann with boundary identifies that core with
its nearby copy. On the collars the local equations
are exactly $xw=t$ after absorbing a holomorphic
unit. The product of the two normal lines is
trivialized by this same function. Two such
trivializations along a compact double curve differ
by a constant in $\C^*$, whose rotation is isotopic
to the identity. Thus the nearby four-manifold is
the indicated tubular plumbing, and \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.4}--\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.6}
identify it with the underlying four-manifold of
$T_0$. Under this identification, the oriented
generator of $H_2(H_i\setminus J_i,\Z)$ is the
ordinary fibre class of $q_0$, for every $i$.
The identifications between the normal covers are
holomorphic elliptic isomorphisms, hence have degree
one and preserve that orientation. In particular all
these transported core cycles are the same integral
two-cycle in the nearby fibre, even when their
primitive angular directions in $\Lambda_F$ differ.


\item  Here is an explicit global version of the Chern test.
Trivialize the principal $F$-bundle on the punctured
base and compare that trivialization with \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}
around the $i$-th disc. Let $\nu_i\in\Lambda_F$ be
the winding of its translation transition, with
positive disc-boundary orientation. Then
\[
 c(T_0)=\sum_i\nu_i,\qquad
 \mu_{P,i}=r_i\delta_{\rm ext}
                    +(r_i\nu_i-e_i).
                                                        \tag{C.NS.7}\hypertarget{tag-00TR}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.7}
\]
The first equality is the integral obstruction to
extending these boundary trivializations over the
discs. It can alternatively be used as the sign
convention for the Chern vector. The second equality
is \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.4} after $\delta_i=\delta_{\rm ext}+\nu_i$.
Thus the rational Seifert vector in this convention
is $\sum_i(\nu_i-e_i/r_i)$, and the inverse transform
adds exactly $\sum_i e_i/r_i$. The holomorphic
transition functions themselves, rather than only
their windings, remain in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.3}.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Canonical orders, the elliptic base, and equal resonance.}
Suppose first that $S$ occurs as in assertion (1).
The equation $xw=t$ proves duality of the normal
lines. Their exact torsion orders then give the
marked multiplicities $r_i$.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  Choose a generator of the rank-one direct image of
the relative canonical line over the disc. Its
evaluation has a vertical divisor
$k_PP+\sum_i k_iH_i$. It is nowhere zero on every
nonzero torus fibre. Adjunction on the Hopf component
and $P|_{H_i}=J_i$, $H_i|_{H_i}=-J_i$ give
\[
 (k_P-k_i)J_i=K_{H_i}+J_i=-r_iJ_i,
       \qquad k_i-k_P=r_i.
                                                        \tag{C.NS.8}\hypertarget{tag-00TS}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.8}
\]
The last equality is an equality of integers:
$\OO_{H_i}(J_i)$ has infinite order, since a
positive effective divisor on a compact complex
surface cannot have a trivial positive tensor power.
Adjunction on $P$ now gives the actual line equality
\[
                         K_P=\OO_P\Bigl(\sum_i(r_i-1)J_i\Bigr).
                                                        \tag{C.NS.9}\hypertarget{tag-00TT}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.9}
\]


\item  For the given quasi-bundle the root charts give
$q_*K_P=K_B$ and
$K_P=q^*K_B+\sum_{\text{all multiple fibres}}(m-1)J$.
Indeed, the local form is the base differential
wedged with the invariant elliptic differential;
on the root chart its exact zero is $(m-1)J$,
and taking the fibrewise constant Laurent
coefficients gives the displayed pushforward.
Equation \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.9} implies $h^0(K_P)\ge1$, so
$g(B)\ge1$. Subtracting the marked terms from
the two canonical formulas gives
\[
 q^*K_B+\sum_{\text{unmarked multiple fibres}}(m-1)J=0
                    \quad\hbox{as a line bundle}.       \tag{C.NS.10}\hypertarget{tag-00TB}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.10}
\]
For $g(B)\ge2$ a nonzero canonical section on $B$
has a nonzero effective divisor, and its pullback
together with the other terms would be a nonzero
effective divisor linearly equivalent to zero on
the compact surface. This is impossible. Therefore
$B$ is elliptic, and the same argument in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.10}
removes every unmarked multiple fibre.


\item  Let $\omega_t$ be the evaluated relative two-form
divided by $t^{k_P}$. On a compact core of $H_i\setminus J_i$
its leading term is $t^{r_i}\eta_i$, where
\[
 \eta_i=c_i\,\frac{dz\wedge dw}{w^{r_i+1}},
                         \qquad c_i\ne0.                \tag{C.NS.11}\hypertarget{tag-00TC}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.11}
\]
To verify this exact pole order, write the total
canonical evaluation in a double chart as
$x^{k_i}w^{k_P}$ times a holomorphic unit and a
coordinate three-form, then divide by $dt$ with
$t=xw$. Equation \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.8} gives \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.11}.
The resulting coefficient on the entire Hopf
component is a nowhere-zero section of
$K_{H_i}((r_i+1)J_i)=\OO_{H_i}$, so it is the
nonzero constant $c_i$.


\item  On the logarithmic cover of $H_i\setminus J_i$,
put $U=z/w^{r_i}$ and $W=\log w$. Its two deck
periods are
$(0,2\pi i)$ and $(\beta_i^{-r_i},\log\beta_i)$.
Thus the integral of $\eta_i=c_i\,dU\wedge dW$
on its oriented core torus is
$\pm2\pi i c_i\beta_i^{-r_i}\ne0$.
Transport that compact torus through the
submersion near the core. By \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.6} all such
cycles are the same class $\gamma$ in the
nearby fibre. Therefore the single holomorphic
period satisfies, for every $i$,
\[
        \int_\gamma\omega_t
             =t^{r_i}\bigl(\pm2\pi i c_i\beta_i^{-r_i}
                              +O(t)\bigr).              \tag{C.NS.12}\hypertarget{tag-00TD}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.12}
\]
Its vanishing order is simultaneously every
$r_i$. Hence all resonances equal $r$.
This uses the transported two-cycle; it makes
no assumption about parallel primitive angular
directions or an elliptic quotient of the
nearby complex torus.


\item  By the plumbing comparison the underlying
four-manifold of $T_0$ is a real four-torus.
For a principal elliptic bundle over the
elliptic curve, the homotopy sequence injects
$\Lambda_F$ into its fundamental group, and
the exact presentation is
\[
 \langle a,b,e,h:\ e,h\text{ central},\
             [a,b]=e^{c_1}h^{c_2}\rangle,
                         \quad(c_1,c_2)=c(T_0).          \tag{C.NS.13}\hypertarget{tag-00TE}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.13}
\]
Its fundamental group is abelian only if
$c(T_0)=0$. This proves every necessity in (3).


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The inverse transform is then an actual torus.}
Assume (3). The sheaf sequence
$0\to\Lambda_F\to\OO_B\to F\to0$ lifts the
principal torsor class of $T_0$ to $H^1(B,\OO_B)$
because its connecting class is precisely
$c(T_0)=0$. On $B=\C/\Gamma_B$ represent this
class by a constant $(0,1)$-form. Integrating it
on the universal cover gives the actual
translation lattice
\[
 (p,z)\mapsto(p+\gamma,z+a\bar\gamma),\quad
 (p,z)\mapsto(p,z+\lambda),
       \qquad \gamma\in\Gamma_B,\quad\lambda\in\Lambda_F.
                                                        \tag{C.NS.14}\hypertarget{tag-00TF}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.14}
\]
Changes of the chosen Cech cocycle are fibre
translations and give an isomorphism with the
original torsor, exactly as in (C.KX.14).
The lattice is discrete of real rank four.
Consequently $T_0$ is a complex two-torus,
with its specified principal elliptic quotient
and all the marked fibres retained.


\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{A compact twistor family with the exact local period presentations.}
Write $T_0=\C^2/\Lambda$ in coordinates $(p,z)$
so that the common elliptic fibre direction is
$p=0$. On the affine $t$-chart of $\PP^1$ put
\[
 \ell_t(p,z)=(p+t\bar z,\ z-t\bar p).
                                                        \tag{C.NS.15}\hypertarget{tag-00TG}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.15}
\]
This is real-linear and invertible for every
$t$, since its inverse has denominator
$1+|t|^2$. The values $\ell_t(v)$ for
$v\in\Lambda$ are holomorphic sections of
$\OO_{\PP^1}(1)^{\oplus2}$: on the other chart
they are $(s p+\bar z,s z-\bar p)$, $s=t^{-1}$.
Translate the vector bundle by these sections
and take the quotient. Each fibre lattice has
real rank four. The inverse real-linear maps
give local uniform fundamental parallelepipeds
over the compact base, proving a free proper
action and a smooth compact quotient
$\mathcal T\to\PP^1$. Its fibres are two-tori
and its fibre at zero is the actual $T_0$.
Pull this family back by $t=s^r$; the pullback
remains smooth and compact because the
original map is a submersion.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  For the $i$-th Hopf identification choose the
oriented fibre-lattice basis
$\lambda_i=(0,a_i)$, $\mu_i=(0,b_i)$ so that
$\beta_i=\exp(2\pi i b_i/a_i)$. This is the
basis supplied by \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}, not a replacement
of the given Hopf modulus. On the vector
space with coordinates $(P,Z)$ after
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.15}, define
\[
 p_i=P-s^r\frac{\bar a_i}{a_i}Z,\qquad
 z_i=\frac{2\pi i}{a_i}Z.
                                                        \tag{C.NS.16}\hypertarget{tag-00TH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.16}
\]
The $\lambda_i$-period is $(0,2\pi i)$ and
the $\mu_i$-period is
\[
   \bigl(\delta_i(s),\log\beta_i\bigr),\qquad
   \delta_i(s)=s^r
        \left(\bar b_i-\frac{\bar a_i b_i}{a_i}\right).
                                                        \tag{C.NS.17}\hypertarget{tag-00TI}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.17}
\]
The coefficient is nonzero because $a_i,b_i$
are an oriented real basis of a complex line.


\item  Complete this pair to an integral basis of
$\Lambda$ by two lifts of the base lattice.
Their $p_i$-periods define a smooth local
family of elliptic curves $B_{i,s}$, and
their exponentiated $z_i$-periods define a
holomorphic family of flat degree-zero line
bundles $M_i$ on $B_{i,s}$. Thus, on a
sufficiently small disc, the actual torus
family has the exact presentation
\[
 \mathcal T_s
   =M_{i,s}^{\times}/\langle g_i\rangle,\qquad
 g_i(p,\ell)=(p+\delta_i(s),\beta_i\ell).
                                                        \tag{C.NS.18}\hypertarget{tag-00TJ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.18}
\]
This equality follows by quotienting the
same four displayed lattice generators,
first by the three excluding $\mu_i$.
It retains the flat part of the torsor,
even when that part is not torsion.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The local weighted insertion with the varying flat line.}
At the marked point of $B_{i,0}$ perform
the weight-$(r,1)$ blowup of the relative
elliptic surface $B_i\to\Delta_s$, and replace
$M_i$ by its pullback tensored with
$\OO(R_i)$. The nonzero line has the same
smooth coarse chart as (C.NH.6)--(C.NH.7).
If $\delta_i(s)=d_i s^r$, the lifted deck
map in a flat local frame is exactly
\[
 (z,w,x)\mapsto
   \bigl(\beta_i^r(z+d_iw^r),
              \beta_iw,\beta_i^{-1}x\bigr),
           \qquad p-p_i=x^rz,\quad s=xw.
                                                        \tag{C.NS.19}\hypertarget{tag-00TK}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.19}
\]
The change $Z=z/(\beta_i^r d_i)$ gives
the specified $H_r(\beta_i)$ on $x=0$.
On $w=0$ the chart is precisely \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.1};
hence the other component is obtained
from $T_0$ by the inverse of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  We check properness with the varying
flat line. On a small closed base disc,
choose smoothly varying unitary flat
metrics on $M_{i,s}$. If its period
characters are $e^{Z_j(s)}$ and base
periods $P_j(s)$, solve the two real
equations
$\operatorname{Re}(Z_j-c(s)P_j)=0$.
Their determinant is nonzero, so $c(s)$
is smooth and bounded. In the resulting
metric, the norm multiplier of the flat
lift in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.18} is
$|\beta_i|\exp(-\operatorname{Re}(c(s)\delta_i(s)))$.
It is uniformly less than one after
shrinking the disc. The additional
exceptional line has the two-sided
polynomial distortion (C.NH.9)--(C.NH.10).
Exponential contraction still dominates
that polynomial uniformly on the closed
disc. The compact-annulus proof of
(C.NH.11) therefore gives a smooth
proper filling $\mathcal Y_i\to\Delta_s$.
Its infinite cyclic action is free,
and every prescribed $\beta_i$ is
retained.


\item  Off the exceptional divisor the canonical
section of $\OO(R_i)$ identifies the new
line with $M_i$, equivariantly for the
two deck maps. Consequently there is
the actual isomorphism
\[
       \mathcal Y_i\setminus H_i
            \simeq \mathcal T|_{\Delta_s}\setminus F_i,
                                                        \tag{C.NS.20}\hypertarget{tag-00TM}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.20}
\]
where $F_i$ is the marked central
elliptic fibre in $T_0$. On the remaining
central component this is exactly the
punctured product map \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Simultaneous replacement and compactness.}
The central curves $F_i$ are disjoint.
We justify that \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.20} allows
independent replacements near them,
although its generic tori need not
have an elliptic quotient.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  If a sequence approaches $H_i$ in
$\mathcal Y_i$, use a compact Hopf
fundamental domain in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.19}.
Then $z,w$ stay bounded, do not
simultaneously approach zero, and
$x\to0$. Its image in the original
line presentation has
$p-p_i=x^rz$, $s=xw$, and flat
line coordinate proportional to $x^{-1}$.
To put that coordinate in a fixed
compact norm annulus requires
$O(1+|\log|x||)$ deck iterates.
Their total base displacement is
$O(|s|^r(1+|\log|x||))$, which
tends to zero. Hence every cluster
point of the images lies in $F_i$.
Conversely properness of $\mathcal Y_i$
shows that images approaching a point
outside $F_i$ have only their unique
inverse-image limit outside $H_i$.


\item  Choose disjoint relatively compact
neighborhoods $W_i$ of $F_i$ in
$\mathcal T$ over a small base disc.
The set consisting of $H_i$ and the
inverse image of $W_i\setminus F_i$
under \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.20} is open, by the
cluster-set calculation. Glue these
open replacements to
$\mathcal T\setminus\bigcup_i F_i$.
Their identification graphs are
relatively closed by that same
calculation, and the replacements
have disjoint central neighborhoods.
Thus the finite gluing is Hausdorff
and smooth. Nested compact
neighborhoods inside the $W_i$,
properness of each $\mathcal Y_i$,
and the compact original complement
cover every closed inverse image
of a sufficiently small base disc.
The resulting map is proper.


\item  The central main component is exactly
$P$: outside the marked fibres its
torsor is unchanged, and at every
marked fibre \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.19} reverses
the precise map \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}.
The Hopf components are the prescribed
$H_i$. Any constant axis translation
in their identification is realized
by the Hopf automorphism
$(z,w)\mapsto(a^rz,aw)$; the linear
part has already been retained in
the chosen fibre-lattice basis.
Thus all specified elliptic gluing
maps, not just their degrees, are
the original ones. The full central
equations are $xw=s$, so the fibre
is reduced SNC.


\item  Finally carry out these replacements
inside the compact pulled-back
twistor family over $\PP^1$ and
leave its complement unchanged.
The preceding proper local gluing
and the original compact complement
give a smooth compact total space.
Every fibre away from zero remains
the original two-torus. The central
support has Euler number zero since
each elliptic quasi-bundle, Hopf
component, and double elliptic curve
has Euler number zero. We have
proved (3)$\Rightarrow$(2), including
the full compact-total-space and
torsor comparisons. Assertion
(2)$\Rightarrow$(1) is restriction
to a disc, completing the equivalence.



\end{enumerate}

\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}\begin{proof}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=*]
\item We give every change to the exact maps of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49}.
Fix one leaf and suppress its index. Choose integers
$k,l$ with
\[
                         rk-nl=1,\qquad \gamma=\beta^n.
                                                        \tag{C.SN.3}\hypertarget{tag-0125}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.3}
\]
On the primary cover of the paired $P$ neighborhood
use $p=x^rz$, the infinite deck
$(z,x)\mapsto(\beta^rz,\beta^{-1}x)$, and the finite
action $(z,x)\mapsto(\zeta^rz,\zeta^{-1}x)$.
The following are genuine invariant coarse coordinates:
\[
 u=z^n,\qquad X=xz^k,\qquad
 p=X^ru^{-l},\qquad
 (u,X)\sim(\gamma^ru,\gamma^lX).
                                                        \tag{C.SN.4}\hypertarget{tag-0126}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.4}
\]
Here $u\ne0$. Since $rk-1=nl$, both coordinates
are finite-group invariant, and the finite quotient
map has no ramification. Conversely, a root of $u$
recovers $z$ and $x=Xz^{-k}$; all choices are exactly
the original finite action. Thus \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4} is the
actual coarse neighborhood, not a formal coordinate
substitution.

\item The normal of $J$ in $P$ has multiplier $\gamma^l$
over $\C^*/\gamma^{r\Z}$. Its order is exactly $r$,
since $\gcd(l,r)=1$. On the normal root cover write
$u=y^r$, $X=s y^l$; then $p=s^r$.
The generator $(y,s)\mapsto(\zeta y,\zeta^{-l}s)$
preserves these coordinates. Normalize its normal
character to $\zeta$: the fibre translation is then
$y\mapsto\zeta^n y$, because $-ln\equiv1\pmod r$.
This proves the exact torsion-character comparison,
including its dependence on $n$.
The dual normal on the secondary Hopf axis is
the inverse character, so its normal-root
identification with the given $P$ gives precisely
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4}.

\item The punctured product map used for the inverse
transform is
\[
 (u,X)\longmapsto(p,W)
       =(X^ru^{-l},\,X^{-n}u^k),\qquad
 u=p^nW^r,\quad X=p^kW^l,\qquad
                       F=\C^*/\gamma^{\Z}.               \tag{C.SN.5}\hypertarget{tag-0127}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}
\]
In the ordered variables $(u,X)$ and $(p,W)$, the exponent
matrix is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-l&r\\k&-n\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
and has determinant $nl-rk=-1$, hence is unimodular.
Consequently these are inverse holomorphic maps
on the punctured chart. On the primary cover
they are $W=x^{-n}$ and $u=z^n=p^nW^r$.
Replacing the chart by $F\times\Delta_p$ through
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5} defines the actual principal torsor $T_0$.
It retains the original analytic transitions
exactly as in (C.NS.3).

\item Let $a$ be the primitive positive angular loop of
$u$ with $X$ fixed, $b$ the infinite deck loop,
and $\mu_P$ the normal loop of $X$. In the
punctured product basis $(\delta,e,h)$,
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5} gives the full integral matrix
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}a&b&\mu_P\end{pmatrix}_{(\delta,e,h)}
   =
 \begin{pmatrix}
   -l&0&r\\
    k&0&-n\\
    0&1&0
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \delta=n a+k\mu_P,\quad e=r a+l\mu_P,\quad h=b.
                                                        \tag{C.SN.6}\hypertarget{tag-0128}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.6}
\]
Its determinant is one. In particular the normal
meridian is $r\delta-ne$ and is primitive even
when $n>1$.

\item On the Hopf side the invariant normal coordinate
is $Y=wz^{-k}$. Its normal-line multiplier is $\gamma^{-l}$,
and the diagonal reference pair has reciprocal
base coordinate $Y^ru^l=w^r/z$ and fibre coordinate
$w^n=Y^nu^k$. The complementary solid torus
therefore has meridian $n a-k\mu_H$ and fibre
cycles $(r a-l\mu_H,b)$. The actual smoothing
identifies $\mu_H=-\mu_P$. Formula \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.6}
then identifies its meridian with $\delta$
and its fibre cycles with $(e,h)$. This proves
the inverse-transform topology and the common
integral fibre-cycle identification for every
secondary leaf. Substituting
$\delta_i=\delta_{\rm ext}+\nu_i$ proves \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.2}.
The nonlinear-to-diagonal comparison (C.NS.5)
is finite-group invariant, so its boundary
calculation applies to this actual quotient.

\item The canonical form
$dz\wedge dw/w^{r+1}$ is invariant under both
the infinite contraction and $\mu_n$. It gives
$K_H=-(r+1)J$ on the quotient. Thus the
canonical-order calculation, the effectivity
argument forcing elliptic $B$ and no unmarked
multiple fibres, and the Chern-zero necessity
are unchanged. The only change to the core
period is explicit. In $U=z/w^r$, $V=\log w$,
the two primitive periods are
\[
             (0,2\pi i/n),\qquad
             (\beta^{-r},\log\beta).
                                                        \tag{C.SN.7}\hypertarget{tag-0129}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.7}
\]
The leading two-form has core integral
$\pm2\pi i c\beta^{-r}/n$, still nonzero.
All cores are the same integral fibre class
by \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.6}, so their one global period
again forces all resonances $r_i$ to coincide.
The finite orders $n_i$ need not coincide.

\item For compact sufficiency perform the exact
inverse transformations and use their
Chern-zero torsor $T_0$, which is an actual
torus by (C.NS.14). In the twistor family
(C.NS.15), choose the $i$-th fibre basis
so that its multiplicative modulus is
$\gamma_i=\beta_i^{n_i}$. After $t=s^r$,
the same four-period calculation gives
\[
 \mathcal T_s=M_{i,s}^{\times}/
   \langle(p,\ell)\mapsto
        (p+d_i s^r,\gamma_i\ell)\rangle,\qquad d_i\ne0.
                                                        \tag{C.SN.8}\hypertarget{tag-012A}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.8}
\]
At the marked point perform the weight-$(r,1)$
blowup, but now tensor the flat line by
$\OO(n_iR_i)$. Its local line coordinate
has weight $-n_i$. Setting it equal to one
leaves the finite action
\[
 (z,w,x)\mapsto
      (\zeta^{r}z,\zeta w,\zeta^{-1}x),
                    \qquad \zeta^{n_i}=1.                \tag{C.SN.9}\hypertarget{tag-012B}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.9}
\]
It is free: a nonzero $w$ or $x$ forces
$\zeta=1$, and if both vanish then $z\ne0$
and $\gcd(r,n_i)=1$ forces the same conclusion.
This proves directly that the coarse nonzero
line is smooth. Equivalently the weighted
orbifold inertia has order $r$ and acts
on the line with the faithful weight $n_i$.

\item Choose the given $n_i$-th root $\beta_i$
of $\gamma_i$. The infinite line deck
lifts to the exact map
\[
 (z,w,x)\mapsto
   \bigl(\beta_i^r(z+d_iw^r),\beta_iw,\beta_i^{-1}x\bigr)
                                                        \tag{C.SN.10}\hypertarget{tag-0123}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.10}
\]
on \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.9}. It commutes with the finite
action. Its exceptional component is
exactly $H_r(\beta_i)/\mu_{n_i}$ after
$Z=z/(\beta_i^r d_i)$.
Off that component the flat-line
coordinate is $W=x^{-n_i}$; consequently
the remaining central chart and its
outer product are exactly
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4}--\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}.

\item The polynomial norm distortion is now
$C(1+|j|)^{n_i/r}$ for the $j$-th
translation lift. The flat-line
contraction multiplier is
$|\gamma_i|\exp(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)d_i s^r))$,
uniformly less than one on a small disc.
It still dominates that polynomial.
The same compact norm annulus proves
properness, and comparison with arbitrarily
large powers proves freeness of the
infinite cyclic quotient. Thus there
is again an actual isomorphism of the
complement of the new Hopf component
with the original twistor tube minus
its marked central elliptic curve.

\item In the cluster calculation the original
flat coordinate is $x^{-n_i}$, so only
$O(1+|\log|x||)$ deck iterates are
needed. Their base displacement remains
$O(|s|^r(1+|\log|x||))$. All cluster
points therefore lie on the prescribed
central fibre curve. The simultaneous
disjoint replacements and compact gluing
of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49} apply with these exact
coarse maps. The main component is the
original $P$, and the finite diagonal
actions commute with the axis-translation
automorphisms used there. Every original
gluing map is retained. The full
central equations are still $xw=s$;
the finite action preserves this
function and is free, so the full
fibre remains reduced SNC.
This proves the equivalence and
compact realization asserted here.

\end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\subsection{Elliptic star data and inverse transforms}\label{subsec:II:elliptic-star-data}

\begin{definition}[Marked elliptic stars and inverse transforms]\hypertarget{tag-P350}{}\label{def:II:elliptic-star-data}
\StatementRecord{def:II:elliptic-star-data}{proved}{P350}{\cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic}}
The leaf pairs are
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 (H^{\rm diag}_{r_i}(\beta_i)/\mu_{n_i},J_i),\qquad
 (H^{\rm nl}_{r_i}(\beta_i)/\mu_{n_i},J_i),\\
 r_i\ge1,\qquad 0<|\beta_i|<1,\qquad \gcd(r_i,n_i)=1 ,
 \end{gathered}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AG}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}
\hypertarget{tag-0122}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.1}}
\end{equation}
with marked axis $J_i=\{w=0\}$ and contractions and finite action
\begin{equation}
 (z,w)\longmapsto(\beta_i^{r_i}z,\beta_iw),\qquad
 (z,w)\longmapsto(\beta_i^{r_i}z+w^{r_i},\beta_iw),
 \quad
 \zeta(z,w)=(\zeta^{r_i}z,\zeta w),                         \hypertarget{tag-00AR}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}
\end{equation}
A marked elliptic star consists of these pairs, a smooth compact
complex surface with a connected elliptic quasibundle
\begin{equation}
                         q:P\longrightarrow B             \hypertarget{tag-00AS}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.3}
\end{equation}
over a smooth compact connected curve $B$, and pairwise distinct
marked fibres with full divisors $r_iJ_i$. Here a quasibundle has
only positive multiples of smooth elliptic curves as fibres.
Its integral $H_1$ monodromy is the identity, and its smooth
fibres are torsors under one fixed elliptic curve $F$.
The data include the isomorphism from each marked leaf axis to
the corresponding $J_i\subset P$ and a duality between their
normal lines. These identifications form the reduced surface
$S=P\cup H_1\cup\cdots\cup H_n$, with $n\ge1$, disjoint
double curves and no other intersections.

For one marked fibre suppress the index and choose integers $k,l$ with
\begin{equation}
                         rk-nl=1,\qquad \gamma=\beta^n.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-0125}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.3}
\end{equation}
The paired neighbourhood in $P$, in the axis coordinate $z$
of the leaf cover, has the invariant coordinates
\begin{equation}
 u=z^n,\qquad X=xz^k,\qquad
 p=X^ru^{-l},\qquad
 (u,X)\sim(\gamma^ru,\gamma^lX).
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-0126}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.4}
\hypertarget{tag-00TA}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.1}}
\end{equation}
Here $u\ne0$. Its punctured product map and inverse are
\begin{equation}
 (u,X)\longmapsto(p,W)
       =(X^ru^{-l},\,X^{-n}u^k),\qquad
 u=p^nW^r,\quad X=p^kW^l,\qquad
                       F=\C^*/\gamma^{\Z}.               \hypertarget{tag-0127}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}
\hypertarget{tag-00TL}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}}
\end{equation}
Replace each marked neighbourhood by the product $F\times\Delta_p$
through this punctured isomorphism, keeping every transition map
of $P$ away from the marked values. The resulting map is the
\emph{inverse logarithmic transform}
\begin{equation}
                             q_0:T_0\longrightarrow B.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TN}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.3}
\end{equation}
If there are no unmarked multiple fibres, it is a holomorphic
principal $F$-torsor. Its integral Chern vector is the connecting
class $c(T_0)\in H^2(B,\Lambda_F)$ of the sheaf sequence in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.KX.13}, with $F_1=F$.
The transform preserves the full analytic torsor transition maps
and is independent, up to an isomorphism over $B$, of the
compatible local coordinates used in its construction.
\end{definition}
\begin{proof}
Every vertical prime of a quasibundle is elliptic, so it has
no vertical exceptional curve of the first kind and is relatively
minimal. The normalized root of a smooth full fibre $mJ$ is a
smooth elliptic product over a disc by
\cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic}. In its fixed integral
marking, the cyclic deck map has the form
$(s,v)\mapsto(\zeta_m s,v+\tau(s))$.
Its central translation has exact order $m$, because this cyclic
action is free. Lift $\tau(s)$ near its central value to
$t(s)\in\C$, and put $\upsilon(s)=t(s)-t(0)$. The cyclic law gives
$\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\upsilon(\zeta_m^j s)=0$. The holomorphic change
$v'=v+h(s)$, where
\[
 h(s)=-\frac1m\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}j\,\upsilon(\zeta_m^j s),
 \qquad h(\zeta_m s)-h(s)=-\upsilon(s),
\]
makes the translation constant. Thus the germ is the quotient
of $F\times\Delta_s$ by a fixed order-$m$ translation of $F$
and the primitive normal character $s\mapsto\zeta_m s$.
The associated normal line on $J$ has exact order $m$:
a trivial power would pull back to a nowhere-zero holomorphic
function on the compact elliptic cover, hence a constant,
and its character would have to be trivial. Its unit-frame
cover identifies this cyclic elliptic cover and its normal
character.

For the marked Hopf pair, the finite quotient acts on the axis
and a transverse coordinate by $(z,x)\mapsto
(\zeta^r z,\zeta^{-1}x)$ on the paired side.
The invariant monomials are $u=z^n$, $X=xz^k$, because
$rk-1=nl$. They have the deck factors in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4}, and $p=x^r z=X^r u^{-l}$.
Conversely, every choice of an $n$th root $z$ of $u$ gives
$x=Xz^{-k}$; the $n$ choices are exactly the finite orbits.
This proves the coordinate isomorphism, including its inverse.
The marked curve is $\C^*/\gamma^{r\Z}$, and its paired
normal has factor $\gamma^l$. On the normal bundle of the Hopf axis, the invariant
fibre coordinate is $Y=wz^{-k}$, with factor $\gamma^{-l}$.
The relation $rk-nl=1$ gives $\gcd(l,r)=1$, so these dual
normal lines have exact order $r$.

In the normalized root write $u=y^r$, $X=s y^l$;
then $p=s^r$. The deck action from the root is
$(y,s)\mapsto(\xi y,\xi^{-l}s)$, $\xi^r=1$,
and the infinite period is $y\mapsto\gamma y$.
Writing its positive normal character as $s\mapsto\zeta s$
gives $y\mapsto\zeta^n y$, since $-nl\equiv1\pmod r$.
The unit-frame cover of the dual normal line is therefore
precisely the cyclic elliptic cover of the preceding paragraph.
The given axis and normal-line maps identify the two quotients,
so this is a chart of the given quasibundle germ.

The exponent matrix of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5} is
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-l&r\\k&-n\end{smallmatrix}\right)$,
with determinant $nl-rk=-1$. Direct substitution gives
$u=p^nW^r$, $X=p^kW^l$, so the maps are mutually inverse.
The infinite deck map sends $W$ to $\gamma W$ and fixes $p$.
They are consequently product isomorphisms over the punctured
disc. For a primary leaf, $n=1,k=0,l=-1$, these are exactly
the coordinates and product maps in
\cref{cdp:eq:C.NS.1,cdp:eq:C.NS.2}.

The product pieces glue to the unchanged outside of $P$ by
these isomorphisms. A finite cover of the compact base by
smaller discs and their compact complement gives compact
inverse images, because every local product and every
unchanged quasibundle piece is proper. The resulting map
is therefore proper. It is smooth at the replaced fibres,
and all its remaining fibre models are those of $q$.
If they are smooth, its overlap maps preserve the integral
marking and hence have identity linear part; it is the
stated principal torsor.

Changing the integers to $k'=k+na$, $l'=l+ra$ changes
$X$ to $X'=Xu^a$ and leaves $p$ and $W$ unchanged in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}. More generally, two compatible root
trivializations differ by a holomorphic translation in the
elliptic product and a constant origin-preserving linear map.
The marked axis and normal cover identify that linear map.
The remaining translation is invariant under the root group,
so descends to a holomorphic translation on the ordinary
$p$-disc. The same map extends across its centre in the
replacement product. Ratios of two normal dualities are
nowhere-zero holomorphic functions on the compact axis,
thus nonzero constants, and give the same extending
translation comparison. These maps glue with the unchanged
outside transitions and have inverse translations. They
prove the asserted choice independence while preserving the
analytic torsor class.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The reduced Hopf-star criterion}\label{subsec:II:reduced-hopf-star-criterion}

\begin{proposition}[Reduced Hopf stars with torus smoothings]
\hypertarget{tag-01DY}{}\label{cdp:st:C.2.UN.53}
\StatementRecord{cdp:st:C.2.UN.53}{proved}{01DY}{\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data,lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary,lem:II:hopf-single-canonical-curve,lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion,cdp:st:C.2.UN.17,cdp:st:C.2.UN.28,cdp:st:C.2.UN.31,lem:II:cyclic-component-cover,lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor}}
\hypertarget{tag-01DT}{}\label{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49}
\StatementRecord{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49}{proved}{01DT}{}
\hypertarget{tag-01DV}{}\label{cdp:st:C.2.UN.50}
\StatementRecord{cdp:st:C.2.UN.50}{proved}{01DV}{}
Let $S$ be a compact connected SNC surface with
smooth components $P,H_1,\ldots,H_n$, $n\ge1$, where each
$H_i$ is a primary or secondary Hopf surface. Its intersection
with $P$ is one connected smooth curve $J_i$, the $J_i$ are
disjoint on $P$, and there are no other intersections.
The following assertions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $S$ is the full reduced central fibre of a proper
degeneration of connected two-tori with smooth total threefold.
\item $S$ is the full fibre over zero of a proper map from
a smooth compact complex threefold to $\PP^1$, every other
fibre being a smooth connected two-torus.
\item The leaf pairs are the marked pairs
\cref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1,cdp:eq:C.AS.2}, their normal lines
are dual across every $J_i$, and $P$ admits the
quasibundle \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.3} over an elliptic curve,
with fixed Jacobian and identity integral monodromy.
Its marked full fibres are $r_iJ_i$ and it has no
unmarked multiple fibres. The inverse transform of
\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data} has the zero Chern vector
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.4}, and its leaf exponents satisfy
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.5} for a positive integer $R$.
\end{enumerate}
All components, finite secondary actions, analytic torsor
parameters, primitive angular directions and given
elliptic identifications are preserved in the compact
realization. Every reduced support there has Euler number zero.

When a fixed-Jacobian identity-monodromy quasibundle $q:P\to B$
with the $J_i$ as distinct reduced fibre supports is part
of the given data, the same tests use that given $q$.
For exclusively nonlinear leaves they say that $B$ is
elliptic, every marked full fibre is $r_iJ_i$, there are
no other multiple fibres, the normals are dual, all $r_i$
equal one integer $r$, and the inverse-transform Chern vector
is zero. Arbitrary secondary orders $n_i$ satisfying
$\gcd(r_i,n_i)=1$ remain allowed. The primary specialization
is $n_i=1$, with the local identifications
$k=0,l=-1,u=z,X=x,W=x^{-1}$ in
\cref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4,cdp:eq:C.SN.5}.
If every leaf is diagonal, one can take
$R=1+\max_i r_i$. A nonlinear leaf determines $R=r_i$,
and every diagonal leaf then has strictly smaller exponent.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Assume the local occurrence. Along each double curve the
defining function has local product equation $xy=t$.
Its bilinear normal term identifies
$N_{J_i/P}\otimes N_{J_i/H_i}$ with $\OO_{J_i}$,
so the given curve identifications have dual normal lines.
Apply the evaluation construction
of \cref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.17} to this proper disc map, with
all full-fibre multiplicities one. Write its canonical
divisor as $k_PP+\sum_i k_iH_i$.
The principal central fibre and adjunction on a leaf give
\begin{equation}
                  K_H=\OO_H(-aJ),\qquad
                  a=k_H-k_P+1\in\Z.                      \hypertarget{tag-00AV}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.6}
\end{equation}
Apply \cref{lem:II:hopf-single-canonical-curve} to this
same $H_i$, its connected curve $J_i$, and
$a=k_i-k_P+1$. It gives the full marked pair
\cref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1,cdp:eq:C.AS.2}, with
$k_i-k_P=r_i\ge1$.
Adjunction on $P$ gives exactly
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.9}. Its effective canonical divisor
makes $\kappa(P)\ge0$ and $p_g(P)\ge1$.
The compact-component bound \cref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.28},
applied to this same fibre and its smooth component $P$,
gives $p_g(P)=1$.
The surface $P$ is minimal: an exceptional rational curve
$E$ is distinct from all the elliptic $J_i$ and intersects
them nonnegatively, whereas adjunction gives $K_P\cdot E=-1$.
This contradicts \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.9}.

To identify its fibration, apply the component-cover construction
\cref{lem:II:cyclic-component-cover}. The multiplicity of $P$
in this full fibre is one. In a generic chart of a normalized
root base change $t=s^N$, its equation is $x=s^N$ after
absorbing a unit. There is one strict covering component,
whose map to $P$ has degree one. Its subsequent resolution
remains birational to $P$. The smooth minimal model is
therefore this same $P$, by uniqueness of the minimal model
in nonnegative Kodaira dimension. Thus the cover conclusion
of \cref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.31} applies through this degree-one
map: $P$ is a two-torus or it has a fixed-Jacobian,
identity-monodromy elliptic quasibundle over a curve of
genus at most one. In the latter case
$p_g(P)=g(B)$ by \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic},
so $B$ is elliptic.

We choose this fibration so that all marked curves are fibres.
On a two-torus an embedded elliptic curve is a translate of
an elliptic subgroup: a lift to universal covers has periodic
holomorphic derivative, which is constant. Two such subgroups
with distinct tangent lines have a surjective product map
to the torus with finite kernel. Every two translates would
then meet. The disjoint $J_i$ have one common tangent line
and are therefore fibres of the quotient by that elliptic
subgroup; its connected quotient is an elliptic curve.

For the quasibundle over an elliptic base, use the canonical
map \eqref{eq:II:quasibundle-canonical}.
If there is a multiple fibre, its effective contribution
makes the intersection with every horizontal $J_i$ positive.
But normal duality gives $J_i^2=0$, because the leaf normal
has finite order, and adjunction gives $K_P\cdot J_i=0$.
Thus every $J_i$ is vertical.
If the quasibundle is smooth, it is a principal elliptic
torsor. For a nonzero Chern vector, a horizontal elliptic
curve would map to the elliptic base by a finite unramified
map of nonzero degree. Pullback to that curve has the
diagonal section $j\mapsto(j,j)$ and hence zero Chern class;
on $H^2(B,\Lambda_F)$ the same pullback multiplies the
Chern vector by the degree, a contradiction.
For zero Chern vector, \cref{lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor}
identifies this same total space with a two-torus through
its full analytic cocycle. The preceding subgroup argument
then supplies its quotient with all $J_i$ as fibres.

If a quasibundle with these marked fibre supports was already
given, keep that map throughout. Its relative minimality
follows from its smooth elliptic fibre supports, and
\cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic} gives
$g(B)=p_g(P)=1$ directly. Thus this case has the same
elliptic-base conclusion for the given $q$.

For either resulting map, the normal-order comparison in
\cref{lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary} gives full marked
fibres $r_iJ_i$. Subtracting \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.9}
from its canonical formula leaves
\begin{equation}
 q^*K_B+\sum_{\text{unmarked multiple fibres}}(m-1)J=0
                    \quad\hbox{as a line bundle}.       \hypertarget{tag-00TB}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.10}
\end{equation}
Since $B$ is elliptic, this is an effective sum of unmarked
multiple fibres linearly equivalent to zero. A nonzero
such divisor would be the divisor of a holomorphic function
on the compact connected $P$, which must be constant.
There are therefore no unmarked multiple fibres.

The inverse transform is now a principal elliptic torsor
over $B$. The core and collar map of
\cref{lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary} identifies its underlying
four-manifold with a nearby torus, using the unimodular
matrices \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.6} and the full analytic maps
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}. Its injected fibre lattice in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.13} forces \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.4}.
All oriented Hopf core classes are the same integral
class $\gamma_{\rm core}$. The holomorphic period of the divided
canonical generator therefore has the expansions
\cref{cdp:eq:C.AS.15,cdp:eq:C.AS.16} at every leaf.
A nonlinear leaf gives a nonzero leading coefficient and
finite vanishing order $R=r_i$. Every other nonlinear
leaf has that order, and every diagonal leaf has
$r_i<R$. When all leaves are diagonal, the integer
$1+\max_i r_i$ satisfies \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.5}.
This proves every test in the third assertion.

Conversely, use the given leaf presentations, quasibundle,
axis identifications and normal dualities as the marked
star data of \cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data}.
The third assertion supplies exactly the elliptic-base,
zero-Chern and exponent hypotheses of
\cref{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}.
Its explicit inverse-transform maps recover the same $P$,
its weighted charts recover each given leaf, and its
axis translations preserve the given gluing maps. It gives
the second assertion with all other fibres smooth tori
and all support Euler numbers zero. Restricting that
proper map to a disc about zero gives the first assertion.

For exclusively nonlinear data, \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.5}
is the common-resonance identity $r_i=r=R$.
The matrix \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.6} and meridian
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.2} preserve each full secondary integer
$n_i$. For $n_i=1$, the substitutions in the statement
identify those maps with
\cref{cdp:eq:C.NS.1,cdp:eq:C.NS.2,cdp:eq:C.NS.4,cdp:eq:C.NS.7};
the period \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.15} becomes
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.12}, and the compact deck map
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.18} becomes \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.19}.
These are the complete primary and secondary nonlinear
specializations for the given quasibundle and surface.
\end{proof}
reason: The all-diagonal value R=1+max r_i satisfies all strict inequalities. A nonlinear leaf fixes the finite vanishing order by its nonzero core integral. No nonzero period is imposed on an all-diagonal given family.

\subsection{Compact insertion of elliptic stars}\label{subsec:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}

\begin{lemma}[Compact insertion with prescribed Hopf leaves]\hypertarget{tag-P353}{}\label{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}{proved}{P353}{\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data,lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor,lem:II:logarithmic-period-family,cdp:st:C.2.UN.42}; \cref{cdp:eq:C.NH.6,cdp:eq:C.NH.7,cdp:eq:C.NH.9,cdp:eq:C.NH.10}}
Let a marked elliptic star have elliptic base $B$, no unmarked
multiple fibres, and
\begin{equation}
                         c(T_0)=0\in H^2(B,\Lambda_F).     \hypertarget{tag-00AT}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.4}
\end{equation}
Suppose there is a positive integer $R$ with
\begin{equation}
 \begin{cases}
 r_i=R,&H_i\text{ is of the nonlinear form in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}},\\
 r_i<R,&H_i\text{ is of the diagonal form in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}}.
 \end{cases}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AU}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.5}
\end{equation}
Then its given reduced surface $S$ is the full fibre over
zero of a proper map $f:Y\to\PP^1$, where $Y$ is a smooth
compact complex threefold and every other fibre is a smooth
connected two-torus. The central main component is the given
$P$, with its entire analytic torsor and marked normal covers;
each leaf and each elliptic gluing map is the prescribed one.
Every reduced fibre support has Euler characteristic zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor} to the
principal torsor $q_0:T_0\to B$ of
\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data}, using $F_1=F$ and its
zero Chern class. Use the coordinate change
$(z,w)_{\mathrm{KX}}=(p,z)$, with
$\Gamma=\Gamma_B$ and $\Lambda_{F_1}=\Lambda_F$.
The resulting full lattice presentation is exactly
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.14}. The local translations by the
zero-cochain in that lemma and their inverse translations
identify this quotient with the original analytic torsor
over the same $B$. Write it as $T_0=\C^2/\Lambda_0$, with
the fibre direction $p=0$ and the disjoint marked fibres $F_i$.

Apply the full rank-four clause of
\cref{lem:II:logarithmic-period-family} to this exact lattice
$\Lambda_0$, and pull its compact family back by $t=s^R$.
Its periods are $V_{s^R}(\Lambda_0)$ and its central fibre
is the same $T_0$. For the $i$th marked fibre, the product
map \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5} identifies its elliptic curve with
$\C^*/\gamma_i^{\Z}$, where $\gamma_i=\beta_i^{n_i}$.
Choose the corresponding oriented fibre-period basis
$\lambda_i=(0,a_i)$, $\mu_i=(0,b_i)$, with
$\gamma_i=\exp(2\pi i b_i/a_i)$. The projection of
$\Lambda_0$ onto the base lattice is surjective with this
fibre lattice as kernel, so these two periods extend to
an integral basis of all four periods.
In the vector coordinates $(P,Z)$ after $V_{s^R}$, set
\begin{equation}
 p^{(i)}=P-s^R\frac{\bar a_i}{a_i}Z,\qquad
 z_i=\frac{2\pi i}{a_i}Z.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.16}
\end{equation}
The period $\lambda_i$ becomes $(0,2\pi i)$, and $\mu_i$ becomes
\begin{equation}
   \bigl(\delta_i(s),\log\gamma_i\bigr),\qquad
   \delta_i(s)=s^R
        \left(\bar b_i-\frac{\bar a_i b_i}{a_i}\right).
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TI}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.17}
\end{equation}
where $d_i=\overline b_i-\overline a_i b_i/a_i\ne0$ by
the real independence of $a_i,b_i$.
The two remaining periods have coordinates
$(P_{ij}(s),Z_{ij}(s))$, $j=1,2$.
At zero their first coordinates are a base-period basis,
so remain real-linearly independent on a smaller disc.
They define the elliptic curve
$B_{i,s}=\C/\langle P_{i1}(s),P_{i2}(s)\rangle$ and the
degree-zero line $M_{i,s}$ with constant factors
$\exp Z_{ij}(s)$.
Quotienting first by these two periods and by $(0,2\pi i)$,
then by the last period, gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_s=M_{i,s}^{\times}/
   \langle(p,\ell)\mapsto(p+d_i s^R,\gamma_i\ell)\rangle,
                    \qquad d_i\ne0 .                  \hypertarget{tag-00AO}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}
\hypertarget{tag-012A}{}
\hypertarget{tag-00TJ}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.8}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.18}}
\end{equation}
This is an isomorphism of holomorphic families: the first
quotient uses $(p,z)\mapsto(p,e^z)$ and the two constant
line factors, and the last quotient uses exactly the
remaining period. The inverse is given by local logarithms
modulo those same four generators. All four periods and
their original flat torsor parameters are therefore preserved.
The line $M_{i,s}$ may be any degree-zero line. In particular
when $T_0=F\times B$ and its complementary periods have zero
fibre coordinate, $M_{i,0}$ is trivial.

Write $p=p^{(i)}$ in this presentation, and choose a constant
lift $p_i^0$ of its marked central base point. At that point
of the smooth elliptic surface family
$\mathcal B_i\to\Delta_s$, take the weighted blowup of
weights $(r_i,1)$ in $(p-p_i^0,s)$ and denote its exceptional
divisor by $E_i$. Pull back $M_i$ and tensor by
$\OO(n_iE_i)$. The weighted presentation
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.6}, with $r=r_i$, is
$p_{\rm loc}=p-p_i^0=x^{r_i}z$, $s=xw$, with weights
$(r_i,1,-1)$ on $(z,w,x)$.
The extra line coordinate $\ell$ has weight $-n_i$.
Choose $\lambda$ with $\lambda^{n_i}=\ell$ and apply the
weighted action to set $\ell=1$. Two choices differ exactly
by the action below; its inverse sends a finite orbit to
the weighted orbit represented with $\ell=1$.
The residual finite action is
\begin{equation}
 (z,w,x)\mapsto
      (\zeta^{r_i}z,\zeta w,\zeta^{-1}x),
                    \qquad \zeta^{n_i}=1.                \hypertarget{tag-012B}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.9}
\end{equation}
on $(\C^2_{z,w}\setminus\{0\})\times\C_x$.
It is free: a nonzero $w$ or $x$ makes $\zeta=1$,
and when both vanish, $z\ne0$ and $\gcd(r_i,n_i)=1$
has the same consequence. Equivalently, the order-$r_i$
weighted inertia in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.7} acts faithfully
on this line because of that coprimality. Thus the coarse
nonzero line space is smooth.

Choose the given $n_i$th root $\beta_i$ of $\gamma_i$.
The lift of the last period in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.17} is
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 (z,w,x)\longmapsto\bigl(&
   \beta_i^{r_i}(z+d_i x^{R-r_i}w^R),\\
   &\beta_iw,\ \beta_i^{-1}x\bigr).
 \end{split}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AP}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.18}
\hypertarget{tag-0123}{}
\hypertarget{tag-00TK}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.10}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.19}}
\end{equation}
The monomial $x^{R-r_i}w^R$ has weighted degree $r_i$,
so this map commutes with the finite action. It fixes
$s=xw$ and changes $p$ by exactly $d_i s^R$.
On $x=0$, equality $R=r_i$ gives the nonlinear contraction
after $Z=z/(\beta_i^{r_i}d_i)$; strict inequality gives
the diagonal contraction. On $w=0$ it is always
$(z,x)\mapsto(\beta_i^{r_i}z,\beta_i^{-1}x)$.
Thus its main-component chart is
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4} and its leaf is the prescribed
primary or secondary surface.

We prove uniform properness of this quotient with its
varying line. On a closed smaller base disc, solve
\[
 \operatorname{Re}\bigl(Z_{ij}(s)-c_i(s)P_{ij}(s)\bigr)=0,
 \qquad j=1,2.
\]
The real period matrix is invertible, so the solution
$c_i(s)$ is smooth and bounded. The norm
$|\ell|\exp(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)p))$ is invariant
under the two line-factor identifications. The last
period multiplies it by
\[
 \varrho_i(s)=|\gamma_i|
              \exp\bigl(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)d_i s^R)\bigr).
\]
After shrinking, $0<\varrho_-\le\varrho_i(s)\le\varrho_+<1$
uniformly for all marked indices.

For the exceptional line, use the weighted norm
comparison \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.9} with $r=r_i$.
Uniform flat metrics on $B_{i,s}$ give
\[
 d(p+j d_i s^R,p_i^0)\le d(p,p_i^0)+C|j||s|^{r_i}
\]
for every integer $j$, since $R\ge r_i$.
The same inequality for the inverse translation gives
the reverse comparison. The $j$th lift on $\OO(n_iE_i)$
therefore changes its norm by a factor between
$C^{-1}(1+|j|)^{-n_i/r_i}$ and
$C(1+|j|)^{n_i/r_i}$, exactly the $n_i$th tensor power
of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.10}. This comparison extends over
the exceptional divisor by continuity of the positive
line-norm ratio. Multiplication by $\varrho_i(s)^j$
makes the full norm tend uniformly to zero as
$j\to+\infty$ and to infinity as $j\to-\infty$.
Any two compact sets have line norms bounded above and
away from zero, proving proper discontinuity. A fixed
point of a nonzero power would be fixed by arbitrarily
large powers, contradicting these limits, so the action
is free, including after its finite quotient.

Choose one positive integer $N$ such that the $N$th
iterate decreases every line norm. Its norm ratio has
a positive minimum $c_N$ over the compact weighted base
above a closed base disc. Every orbit meets
$c_N\le\|\ell\|\le1$, a compact annulus there.
The quotient $\mathcal Y_i\to\Delta_s$ is therefore a
smooth proper local family.

Outside its exceptional Hopf component, the canonical
section of $\OO(n_iE_i)$ trivializes that factor and gives
\begin{equation}
       \mathcal Y_i\setminus H_i
            \simeq \mathcal T|_{\Delta_s}\setminus F_i,
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TM}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.20}
\end{equation}
where the right side is the compact torus family restricted
to the same disc, with its marked central fibre curve removed.
In the normalized line gauge the torus-family flat coordinate is
$W=x^{-n_i}$. On the main component its other coordinate
is $u=z^{n_i}$, and
$u=p_{\rm loc}^{n_i}W^{r_i}$, $X=p_{\rm loc}^kW^l$ are precisely the inverse
maps in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}, with its base coordinate
identified with $p_{\rm loc}$. On $s\ne0$ the map and
its inverse are the period quotient of
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}.

For simultaneous replacement, choose a compact fundamental
domain on each Hopf component. Along a sequence approaching
it, $z,w$ remain bounded and not both zero, while $x\to0$.
The torus-family flat coordinate $x^{-n_i}$ is put into a fixed
compact norm annulus by $O(1+|\log|x||)$ deck iterates;
this follows from the uniform exponential bounds and
their polynomial factors. The total base displacement is
\begin{equation}
                   O\bigl(|s|^R(1+|\log|x||)\bigr)
                          \longrightarrow0,
                         \qquad s=xw.                   \hypertarget{tag-00AQ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.19}
\end{equation}
because $s=xw$ and $w$ is bounded. The initial base
coordinate $p_{\rm loc}=p-p_i^0=x^{r_i}z$ also tends to zero.
Consequently every cluster point of the images of this
sequence lies on $F_i$ in the original torus family.

Choose disjoint relatively compact neighbourhoods $W_i$
of the $F_i$ in a smaller closed tube. The subsets
$H_i\cup\Psi_i^{-1}(W_i\setminus F_i)$ of $\mathcal Y_i$,
where $\Psi_i$ is \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.20}, are open by the
cluster property. Glue them to the torus family with
the $F_i$ deleted by the same isomorphisms. A pair of
distinct limiting points in different pieces could only
arise from a cluster on one of the $F_i$; those loci have
been deleted from the torus piece and are disjoint for
different $i$. The gluing graphs are thus closed and
the glued space is Hausdorff.
Choose smaller closed neighbourhoods inside the $W_i$.
Their inverse images under $\Psi_i$, together with $H_i$,
are closed subsets of the proper $\mathcal Y_i$ over a
closed base disc and hence compact. Together with the
compact unmodified complement they cover the inverse
image of that disc. This proves properness of the glued
family. All maps are biholomorphic on the overlaps,
so its total space is smooth.

On the central main component the gluing reverses the
same inverse-transform maps used to define $T_0$.
It therefore recovers the original $P$ with every
analytic transition. The chosen fibre-period basis
preserves the linear part of each marked normal cover.
The maps $(z,w)\mapsto(a^{r_i}z,aw)$ commute with both
contractions and with the finite action; as $a$ varies,
they realize every constant translation of the marked
axis. They therefore preserve the given remaining gluing
constants. The full local equation is $s=xw$ in the
free coarse charts, so all central components have
multiplicity one and meet transversely as the given $S$.

Outside this tube the compact family
\eqref{eq:II:compact-twistor-lattice}, pulled back by
$t=s^R$, is unchanged. The proper local replacement and
that compact complement give a smooth compact threefold
over $\PP^1$. Every nonzero fibre is the original smooth
connected two-torus. The central quasibundle has Euler
number zero by \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic};
\cref{lem:II:hopf-curve-restriction} gives Euler number zero
for the Hopf leaves, and each double curve is elliptic. Additivity gives $e(S)=0$, completing
the construction.
\end{proof}

ring is specified. We use $B=\PP^1_t$, $(p_1,p_2,p_0)=(0,1,\infty)$,
the ordered lattice
$\Lambda=\Z\langle\widehat\gamma,\widehat u,\widehat w,\widehat\delta\rangle$,
and the marked periods, writing $\beta_c=\beta^{\rm part}+c$,
\[
\Pi_c=\begin{pmatrix}6\mu&\tau&1&0\\\beta^{\rm part}+c&\mu&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad w=e^{-\pi i c},\qquad (\beta^{\rm part}+\tau)(p_0)=0.
\]
Let $\pi:\mathfrak H\to B\setminus\{p_0\}$ be the marked
$(3,4,\infty)$ orbifold uniformization, with marked deck generators
$g_1,g_2$ of orders three and four. Let $z_j\in\mathfrak H$
be the fixed point of $g_j$ above $p_j$. Thus
$\pi(z_j)=p_j$, $g_jz_j=z_j$,
$\rho=\tau(z_1)=e^{\pi i/3}$ and $\tau(z_2)=i$.
The marked values are
$\mu(z_1)=(2-\rho)/3$ and $\mu(z_2)=(1-i)/2$
(\SeriesRef{fam:src:C.1.1}). The local roots are
$r^3=t\circ\pi$ at $z_1$ and $s^4=(t-1)\circ\pi$ at $z_2$.
We take $r>0$ on $0<t<1$, where $\tau$ follows the unit-circle
arc from $\rho$ to $i$. At $z_2$ we use the branch with
$\operatorname{Im}\mu_s(0)>0$ and
\[
 \tau=i+\frac{i}{\pi\sqrt{E_4(i)}}s^2+O(s^4),
\]
where $E_4$ is the normalized Eisenstein series of weight four;
on the marked arc $t>1$ one has $\tau=iy$, $y>1$
(\SeriesRef{I:def:finite-coordinates}).
Base meridians are counterclockwise. The analytic root decks are clockwise,
$s_j(g_jz)=e^{-2\pi i/m_j}s_j(z)$, with $g_1g_2g_0=1$;
the resulting homology monodromies are $A_1,A_2,M_0$.
The primitive invariant vectors are
$\varepsilon=(1,2,-4,0)^t$ and
$\varepsilon'=(1,3,-3,0)^t$.
For an admissible finite affine datum, with $3\nmid l_1$ and
$2\nmid l_2$, we write
$v_1=l_1\varepsilon+k_1\widehat\delta$ and
$v_2=l_2\varepsilon'+k_2\widehat\delta$, using the coefficients
$l_1,l_2$ of the peripheral presentation.
Define
\[
 D_{\rm part}=\operatorname{Im}\beta^{\rm part}
       -\frac{6(\operatorname{Im}\mu)^2}{\operatorname{Im}\tau},
 \qquad M=\max_{B\setminus\{p_0\}}D_{\rm part}
       =-\frac3\pi\log6.
\]
The admissible parameter inequality is $\operatorname{Im}c<-M$;
the maximum of $D_{\rm part}$ is attained only at $t=1$, as proved in \SeriesRef{fam:src:C.2.3}.
The standard multiplicities are $m_1=3,m_2=4$,
$f^*p_j=m_jS_j$, and $W=f^{-1}(p_0)$ is reduced, with normalization
$\eta:\mathrm dP_6\to W$.
Let $\gamma:\Lambda\to\Z$ be the first coordinate and
$\Lambda_{\rm tor}=\Z\langle\widehat w,\widehat\delta\rangle$.
For the cusp collar section $\sigma$, define
$l_0=\gamma(c(\sigma))$, where
$c(\sigma)=[\lambda_\sigma]\in\Lambda/\Lambda_{\rm tor}$ is determined
by a holomorphic lift $\widetilde\sigma$ on the cusp cover:
\[
 t^{-1}=e^{2\pi i s_0},\qquad
 \widetilde\sigma(s_0+1)-\widetilde\sigma(s_0)
     =\Pi_c(s_0+1)\lambda_\sigma.
\]
Changing the lift adds $(I-M_0^{-1})\lambda$ to $\lambda_\sigma$;
this lies in $\Lambda_{\rm tor}$, on which $\gamma$ vanishes.
This is the winding convention of
\cite[Definition~6.6 and Proposition~6.7, pp.~39--40]{AC26}.
Since $\gamma(v_j)=l_j$, the peripheral presentation in
\cite[Theorem~7.17, p.~57]{AC26}, using the clockwise analytic
generators, gives
\[
 p=12l_0-4l_1-3l_2,\qquad \pi_1(X)\simeq\Z/|p|\Z.
\]
Those peripheral generators lift the inverses of our
counterclockwise base meridians. The standard fixed data are
those of \SeriesRef{fam:src:A.5.1}; the arbitrary affine vectors
and full cusp collar section are those of
\SeriesRef{fam:src:B.2.1}.
An unqualified fibre is its full Cartier scheme; its reduction is always
specified explicitly. The coefficient group is displayed in each homology or cohomology group.
Complex manifolds carry their complex orientations.
\end{definition}

Choose a projective embedding $X\hookrightarrow\PP^N$.
Apply \cite[published version, (0.1)(1), p.~208; Theorem~1.6
and Remarks~1.7(2), pp.~215--216]{BierstoneMilman1997}
first to this reduced algebraic $X$, obtaining
$\rho:X_1\to X$ with $X_1$ smooth, and then to the reduced
divisor $D=((f\circ\rho)^{-1}\{0,\infty\})_{\rm red}$
in $X_1$. Denote the second composite by $\sigma:X_2\to X_1$.
The first centers lie over $\operatorname{Sing}X$, which is
contained in the two central fibres; the second centers lie
over $D$. Every blowup is algebraic and projective.
Thus $X_2$ is smooth and projective, the reduced inverse image
of $D$ is SNC, and $f\circ\rho\circ\sigma$ restricts to the
same quotient family over $\PP^1\setminus\{0,\infty\}$.

\section{Euler sign and equality for arbitrary torus fibres}\hypertarget{tag-034C}{}\label{sec:II:all:12}


\begin{theorem}[The Euler sign for every degeneration and its equality criterion]
\hypertarget{tag-01BZ}{}\label{cdp:st:C.2.G.1}
\StatementRecord{cdp:st:C.2.G.1}{proved}{01BZ}{\SeriesRef{cdp:st:D.1.9}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:A.3.4}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:A.5.2}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:A.5.3}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.MH.1}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.MH.2}, \SeriesRef{night:P4.26}, \SeriesRef{night:P4.32}, \SeriesRef{night:P4.36}, \SeriesRef{night:P4.37}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.INT.1}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.INT.2}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.INT.3}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C2a}; \cite[Proposition~2.1 and Theorem~2.2, pp.~842--843]{Peters2021}}

Let $Y$ be a connected smooth compact complex threefold with
$b_1(Y)=b_2(Y)=0$, and let $f:Y\to B$ be a proper surjective
holomorphic map with connected fibres to a smooth compact curve.
Assume that the smooth general fibre is a complex two-torus.
The full fibres may have arbitrary positive component multiplicities
and their reduced supports may have arbitrary singularities. Then
\begin{equation}
 B\simeq\PP^1,\qquad
 c_3(Y)=e(Y)\in\{0,2\},\qquad b_3(Y)=2-c_3(Y).
 \hypertarget{tag-00KW}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.G.1}
\end{equation}
Every reduced fibre support has nonnegative Euler number.
An irreducible singular support with rational normalization
resolution has Euler number two; every other irreducible support
has Euler number zero.

The equality $c_3(Y)=0$ holds exactly when every support has one
of the following descriptions. A smooth irreducible support has
a finite unramified torus cover. A singular irreducible support
has smooth minimal elliptic ruled or smooth minimal Hopf
normalization. A reducible support has normalization a disjoint
union of smooth minimal Hopf or non-K\"ahler elliptic surfaces;
its reduced conductor image and inverse image are disjoint
unions of smooth elliptic curves, and the conductor branch maps
are finite unramified covers. These are the normalization
and resolution maps of each full fibre, with its given
component and conductor multiplicities.
\end{theorem}


\begin{proof}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{The base and the finite character.}
The beginning of connected-fibre Leray injects
$H^1(B,\Q)$ into $H^1(Y,\Q)=0$, so $B=\PP^1$.
Proposition~\SeriesRef{cdp:st:D.1.9} supplies an integral section
of $R^1f_*\Z$ which restricts nontrivially to each reduced
support and to each nearby torus. On a small disc its
Leray lift is an integral class on the entire tube.
Reduction modulo a prime which does not divide its fibre
restriction gives the finite cyclic character used in
\ref{cdp:st:C.2.MH.2}, on the full Cartier fibre $f^*(b)$.

\item \textbf{Smooth supports.}
Proposition~\SeriesRef{cdp:st:A.5.2} excludes a singular normal
support. For a smooth support $S$ in a full fibre $mS$,
the normalized change $t=s^m$ is, in a local equation
$t=uz^m$, the map
\[
 w^m=u,\qquad s=wz.
\]
These charts give a finite unramified central cover of $S$
and a proper holomorphic submersion over the new disc,
as in \SeriesRef{cdp:st:A.3.4}. Its nearby fibre is the
original torus. Smooth proper transport gives $b_1=4$
and rational first Chern class zero on the central cover.
It is K\"ahler by the even-$b_1$ criterion in
\cite[Proposition~2.1, p.~842]{Peters2021}.
Its rationally trivial canonical class excludes an exceptional
curve, whose canonical intersection would be $-1$.
Every effective pluricanonical divisor has zero K\"ahler area
and hence is empty, so every nonzero pluricanonical space has
dimension one. In the classification of
\cite[Theorem~2.2, p.~843]{Peters2021}, the remaining
Kodaira-dimension-zero case with $b_1=4$ is a torus;
the ruled alternative has canonical intersection $-2$ with
a ruling fibre and is excluded by the same Chern class.
The degree-$m$ unramified central cover therefore gives
$e(S)=e(S')/m=0$, where $S'$ denotes that cover.

\item \textbf{Normalization resolutions.}
Write $Z\to T\to S$ for the minimal resolution of the
normalization. The canonical evaluation and
\SeriesRef{cdp:st:A.5.3} give a nonempty effective divisor $D$
with $K_Z+D$ torsion. A positive pluricanonical section,
raised to a power killing this torsion, would give a
nonzero holomorphic function vanishing along a positive
multiple of $D$. Compactness excludes that function.
Hence $\kappa(Z)=-\infty$. The classification in
\cite[Theorem~2.2, p.~843]{Peters2021} gives a rational
resolution, a resolution ruled over a curve of positive
genus, or a resolution of class VII. We apply the following
results to these same maps $Z\to T\to S$.

\item \textbf{Irreducible supports.}
For a rational resolution,
\ref{cdp:st:C.2.MH.2} gives $e(S)=2$. For a resolution
ruled over a curve of genus $g\ge1$, the same proposition
gives $e(S)=2-2g$. The local irreducible inequality in
\SeriesRef{night:P4.26} gives $e(S)\ge0$, and therefore $g=1$
and $e(S)=0$. The irreducible-support assertion of that
proposition uses the effective conductor, local trace
inequality and fundamental group of this same $S$. The zero-Euler
comparison in \SeriesRef{night:P4.32} then identifies $T$ as
a smooth minimal elliptic ruled surface.

For a class-VII resolution, \SeriesRef{night:P4.37} excludes
every minimal model with positive second Betti number
by its saturated-foliation Chern identity and the
negative-definite curve form. The curve-free Inoue
case cannot carry the nonempty effective conductor.
The remaining Hopf case is treated by
\SeriesRef{night:P4.36}: its derivative and foliation
calculations make $T$ smooth and minimal, with $e(S)=0$.
These are the single-support conclusions for the
normalization map $T\to S$ fixed in step~3.

\item \textbf{Reducible supports.}
For each normalization resolution, an adjacent global
component gives a nonzero effective divisor with

with the stated component types and classifies marked Hopf, ruled
and elliptic supports with their full multiplicities.

canonical-order reduction and finite rooted generation, ending with
the Euler sign and equality criterion for arbitrary torus fibres in

\item Consider a component $T$ meeting a known elliptic
boundary $C$ whose normal line is torsion. It has
$C^2=0$. A minimal rational surface contains no
such elliptic curve. On $\PP^2$ a smooth elliptic
curve has degree three and square nine. On a
Hirzebruch surface write an irreducible elliptic
curve as $aC_0+bf$, with $a>0$. Its arithmetic
genus equation is
\begin{equation}
           (a-1)(2b-na-2)=2.
\hypertarget{tag-00RG}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.MR.9}
\end{equation}
It is distinct from $C_0$ and has $b\ge na$.
The only possibilities have $a=2$, $b=n+2$,
$n\le2$, with square eight, or $a=3,n=1,b=3$,
with square nine. These include $\mathbb F_1$.
None has square zero. On a ruled surface over
a base of genus at least two an elliptic curve
cannot be horizontal by Riemann--Hurwitz, and
cannot be contained in a rational ruling fibre.
Those components are excluded as well.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  Suppose that $T\to E$ is ruled over an elliptic
curve. Its finite map $C\to E$ is unramified.
Pull the ruling back along this map and write $p:T'\to C$ for the resulting bundle. The diagonal section $C\subset T'$ has the same normal line $L$, since $T'\to T$ is finite unramified. Put $W=p_*\OO_{T'}(C)$. Fibrewise evaluation gives a surjection $p^*W\to\OO_{T'}(C)$ and hence, with the lines convention, an isomorphism $T'\simeq\PP_C(W^*)$. Pushing forward the section restriction sequence gives $0\to\OO_C\to W\to L\to0$, because $H^1(\PP^1,\OO)=0$ on every ruling fibre. Dualize and tensor by $L$: the bundle $V=W^*\otimes L$ has the exact sequence
\begin{equation}
     0\longrightarrow\OO_C\longrightarrow V
                         \longrightarrow L\longrightarrow0.
\hypertarget{tag-00R2}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.MR.10}
\end{equation}
The dual evaluation on the section is the inclusion $L^{-1}\hookrightarrow W^*$, so tensoring identifies the diagonal section with $\PP_C(\OO_C)\subset\PP_C(V)$.
If $L\ne\OO_C$, its extension group is
$H^1(C,L^{-1})=H^0(C,L)^*=0$, so it splits.
If $L=\OO_C$, the complement of this section
is the additive torsor of the extension
class in $H^1(C,\OO_C)$.


\item  There is a second boundary curve on $T$.
Otherwise \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.64} would make this terminal pair
a section leaf: its connected anticanonical
bisection over an elliptic ruling base is
excluded by the residue/finite-trace map.
It would already have been contracted.
Pull a second boundary back and normalize
one component. It is a compact curve mapping
finitely onto $C$ and lying in the complement
of the section. It supplies a section of
the pulled-back additive torsor. Finite
trace composed with pullback on $H^1(\OO)$
is multiplication by its positive degree,
so the original additive class is zero.
Thus \eqref{cdp:eq:C.MR.10} splits in this case also.


\item  Kill the torsion $L$ by a further finite
\'etale cover. The resulting surface
is $E'\times\PP^1$, with its finite Galois
covering map to $T$. The base cover is
an isogeny after selecting origins; its
deck group acts by translations on $E'$.
A deck map on the product is a translation
on $E'$ and a holomorphic map
$E'\to\operatorname{PGL}_2(\C)$ on the
projective fibre. The latter is constant:
$\operatorname{PGL}_2$ is affine, so its
coordinate functions are constant on the
compact elliptic curve. These constants
give a finite action on $\PP^1$.
Taking its quotient constructs
\begin{equation}
        T=(E'\times\PP^1)/G
                         \longrightarrow\PP^1/G.
\hypertarget{tag-00R3}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.MR.11}
\end{equation}
Its regular connected fibre is $E'/K$,
where $K$ is the kernel of the projective
action. All fibre actions are translations.
At a projective stabilizer the base action
on $E'$ is free, so the local quotient
is exactly the smooth multiple chart
of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.QT.2}. This proves fixed Jacobian
and identity integral monodromy directly.


\item  Every other boundary pulls back to a
compact curve disjoint from the fixed
section of $E'\times\PP^1$. Its second
coordinate is a holomorphic function
with values in the affine complement
of that section, and is constant.
It is therefore a constant section.
Consequently every original boundary
is a fibre support of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.MR.11}, with
its normal-root cover retained.


\end{enumerate}

elliptic curve is either a nonlinear
leaf, or is an elliptic Hopf component

occur here, by the exact characters

quotient in this use of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.31}.

translation-root differential gives

pluricanonical pushdown. Since
$C$ is elliptic and $C^2=0$,
adjunction gives $K_T\cdot C=0$.

vertical. Every disjoint boundary
is also vertical, since a horizontal
curve meets this entire fibre support.

multiple fibres, so $q_0$ is a
principal elliptic torsor. A horizontal
$C$ maps finitely and unramifiedly
onto $B_0$ and gives a section after
that base pullback. The integral
Chern vector therefore pulls back to
zero. Pullback is multiplication by
the positive covering degree on the
free lattice group $H^2(B_0,\Lambda_F)$,
so this vector is zero. Apply \cref{lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor} with $(E_1,B,F_1)=(T,B_0,F)$ and this vanishing integral Chern class. Its cocycle/cochain isomorphism identifies this principal torsor, over the same $B_0$, with a complex two-torus. This is already
the preceding torus case. If $C$ is
vertical there is nothing to change.

\begin{equation}

                       (2,4,4),\quad(2,3,6).
\hypertarget{tag-00R5}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.MR.13}
\end{equation}
There is an elliptic covering
$E\to\PP^1$ with precisely these
ramification indices. For four
specified double points it is the
double cover branched at those
points. For the three-point lists
it is the elliptic quotient by
the cyclic group of order three,
four or six, with the three
branch values moved to the
specified points by a projective
coordinate. These are the quotient maps and stabilizer lists
in \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.33}.


\item  Normalize the pullback of $T$ by
this map. In each chart \eqref{cdp:eq:C.QT.2}
it is the finite \'etale surface
map $F\times\Delta_s\to
(F\times\Delta_s)/\mu_{m_i}$;
the free translation removes
the multiple fibre. Thus the
global pullback $T'\to T$ is
a finite \'etale Galois
cover and $T'\to E$ is a
principal fixed-elliptic torsor.
The pullback components of this horizontal $C$ are elliptic and map finitely to $E$.
A component of that pullback maps unramifiedly to the elliptic $E$ and supplies a section after its base pullback. The Chern class of $T'\to E$ is therefore killed by its positive covering degree in the free lattice $H^2(E,\Lambda_F)$, hence is zero. Apply \cref{lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor} with $(E_1,B,F_1)=(T',E,F)$. Its isomorphism preserves this pulled-back torsor and proves that $T'$ is a two-torus.


\item  The preimage of $C$ in $T'$ is
a finite disjoint union of
parallel elliptic translates.
The deck group preserves their
elliptic subtorus and therefore
acts on its elliptic quotient.
The descended map
\begin{equation}
 T=T'/G\longrightarrow
                  (T'/F')/G
\hypertarget{tag-00R6}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.MR.14}
\end{equation}
has connected elliptic fibres.
Indeed the kernel on the base
acts by translations on $F'$:
a nontranslation finite elliptic
automorphism would have a fixed
point on a fibre, contradicting
the \'etale surface action.
The same argument at a base
stabilizer gives precisely
smooth multiple fibres.
The curve $C$ is one such
fibre support, and every
disjoint boundary is vertical.
Apply \cref{lem:II:vertical-elliptic-alignment} to this descended connected map on the same component $T$, with every boundary just proved vertical. The component is minimal, so the relative contraction is the identity. This proves identity integral monodromy and \eqref{cdp:eq:C.MR.8} for precisely the map \eqref{cdp:eq:C.MR.14}.


\end{enumerate}
