\begin{lemma}[Compact insertion with prescribed Hopf leaves]\hypertarget{tag-P353}{}\label{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}{proved}{P353}{\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data,lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor,lem:II:logarithmic-period-family,cdp:st:C.2.UN.42}; \cref{cdp:eq:C.NH.6,cdp:eq:C.NH.7,cdp:eq:C.NH.9,cdp:eq:C.NH.10}}
Let a marked elliptic star have elliptic base $B$, no unmarked
multiple fibres, and
\begin{equation}
                         c(T_0)=0\in H^2(B,\Lambda_F).     \hypertarget{tag-00AT}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.4}
\end{equation}
Suppose there is a positive integer $R$ with
\begin{equation}
 \begin{cases}
 r_i=R,&H_i\text{ is of the nonlinear form in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}},\\
 r_i<R,&H_i\text{ is of the diagonal form in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}}.
 \end{cases}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AU}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.5}
\end{equation}
Then its given reduced surface $S$ is the full fibre over
zero of a proper map $f:Y\to\PP^1$, where $Y$ is a smooth
compact complex threefold and every other fibre is a smooth
connected two-torus. The central main component is the given
$P$, with its entire analytic torsor and marked normal covers;
each leaf and each elliptic gluing map is the prescribed one.
Every reduced fibre support has Euler characteristic zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor} to the
principal torsor $q_0:T_0\to B$ of
\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data}, using $F_1=F$ and its
zero Chern class. Use the coordinate change
$(z,w)_{\mathrm{KX}}=(p,z)$, with
$\Gamma=\Gamma_B$ and $\Lambda_{F_1}=\Lambda_F$.
The resulting full lattice presentation is exactly
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.14}. The local translations by the
zero-cochain in that lemma and their inverse translations
identify this quotient with the original analytic torsor
over the same $B$. Write it as $T_0=\C^2/\Lambda_0$, with
the fibre direction $p=0$ and the disjoint marked fibres $F_i$.

Apply the full rank-four clause of
\cref{lem:II:logarithmic-period-family} to this exact lattice
$\Lambda_0$, and pull its compact family back by $t=s^R$.
Its periods are $V_{s^R}(\Lambda_0)$ and its central fibre
is the same $T_0$. For the $i$th marked fibre, the product
map \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5} identifies its elliptic curve with
$\C^*/\gamma_i^{\Z}$, where $\gamma_i=\beta_i^{n_i}$.
Choose the corresponding oriented fibre-period basis
$\lambda_i=(0,a_i)$, $\mu_i=(0,b_i)$, with
$\gamma_i=\exp(2\pi i b_i/a_i)$. The projection of
$\Lambda_0$ onto the base lattice is surjective with this
fibre lattice as kernel, so these two periods extend to
an integral basis of all four periods.
In the vector coordinates $(P,Z)$ after $V_{s^R}$, set
\begin{equation}
 p^{(i)}=P-s^R\frac{\bar a_i}{a_i}Z,\qquad
 z_i=\frac{2\pi i}{a_i}Z.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.16}
\end{equation}
The period $\lambda_i$ becomes $(0,2\pi i)$, and $\mu_i$ becomes
\begin{equation}
   \bigl(\delta_i(s),\log\gamma_i\bigr),\qquad
   \delta_i(s)=s^R
        \left(\bar b_i-\frac{\bar a_i b_i}{a_i}\right).
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TI}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.17}
\end{equation}
where $d_i=\overline b_i-\overline a_i b_i/a_i\ne0$ by
the real independence of $a_i,b_i$.
The two remaining periods have coordinates
$(P_{ij}(s),Z_{ij}(s))$, $j=1,2$.
At zero their first coordinates are a base-period basis,
so remain real-linearly independent on a smaller disc.
They define the elliptic curve
$B_{i,s}=\C/\langle P_{i1}(s),P_{i2}(s)\rangle$ and the
degree-zero line $M_{i,s}$ with constant factors
$\exp Z_{ij}(s)$.
Quotienting first by these two periods and by $(0,2\pi i)$,
then by the last period, gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_s=M_{i,s}^{\times}/
   \langle(p,\ell)\mapsto(p+d_i s^R,\gamma_i\ell)\rangle,
                    \qquad d_i\ne0 .                  \hypertarget{tag-00AO}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}
\hypertarget{tag-012A}{}
\hypertarget{tag-00TJ}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.8}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.18}}
\end{equation}
This is an isomorphism of holomorphic families: the first
quotient uses $(p,z)\mapsto(p,e^z)$ and the two constant
line factors, and the last quotient uses exactly the
remaining period. The inverse is given by local logarithms
modulo those same four generators. All four periods and
their original flat torsor parameters are therefore preserved.
The line $M_{i,s}$ may be any degree-zero line. In particular
when $T_0=F\times B$ and its complementary periods have zero
fibre coordinate, $M_{i,0}$ is trivial.

Write $p=p^{(i)}$ in this presentation, and choose a constant
lift $p_i^0$ of its marked central base point. At that point
of the smooth elliptic surface family
$\mathcal B_i\to\Delta_s$, take the weighted blowup of
weights $(r_i,1)$ in $(p-p_i^0,s)$ and denote its exceptional
divisor by $E_i$. Pull back $M_i$ and tensor by
$\OO(n_iE_i)$. The weighted presentation
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.6}, with $r=r_i$, is
$p_{\rm loc}=p-p_i^0=x^{r_i}z$, $s=xw$, with weights
$(r_i,1,-1)$ on $(z,w,x)$.
The extra line coordinate $\ell$ has weight $-n_i$.
Choose $\lambda$ with $\lambda^{n_i}=\ell$ and apply the
weighted action to set $\ell=1$. Two choices differ exactly
by the action below; its inverse sends a finite orbit to
the weighted orbit represented with $\ell=1$.
The residual finite action is
\begin{equation}
 (z,w,x)\mapsto
      (\zeta^{r_i}z,\zeta w,\zeta^{-1}x),
                    \qquad \zeta^{n_i}=1.                \hypertarget{tag-012B}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.9}
\end{equation}
on $(\C^2_{z,w}\setminus\{0\})\times\C_x$.
It is free: a nonzero $w$ or $x$ makes $\zeta=1$,
and when both vanish, $z\ne0$ and $\gcd(r_i,n_i)=1$
has the same consequence. Equivalently, the order-$r_i$
weighted inertia in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.7} acts faithfully
on this line because of that coprimality. Thus the coarse
nonzero line space is smooth.

Choose the given $n_i$th root $\beta_i$ of $\gamma_i$.
The lift of the last period in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.17} is
\begin{equation}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.10}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.19}}
 \begin{split}
 (z,w,x)\longmapsto\bigl(&
   \beta_i^{r_i}(z+d_i x^{R-r_i}w^R),\\
   &\beta_iw,\ \beta_i^{-1}x\bigr).
 \end{split}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AP}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.18}
\hypertarget{tag-0123}{}
\hypertarget{tag-00TK}{}
\end{equation}
The monomial $x^{R-r_i}w^R$ has weighted degree $r_i$,
so this map commutes with the finite action. It fixes
$s=xw$ and changes $p$ by exactly $d_i s^R$.
On $x=0$, equality $R=r_i$ gives the nonlinear contraction
after $Z=z/(\beta_i^{r_i}d_i)$; strict inequality gives
the diagonal contraction. On $w=0$ it is always
$(z,x)\mapsto(\beta_i^{r_i}z,\beta_i^{-1}x)$.
Thus its main-component chart is
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4} and its leaf is the prescribed
primary or secondary surface.

We prove uniform properness of this quotient with its
varying line. On a closed smaller base disc, solve
\[
 \operatorname{Re}\bigl(Z_{ij}(s)-c_i(s)P_{ij}(s)\bigr)=0,
 \qquad j=1,2.
\]
The real period matrix is invertible, so the solution
$c_i(s)$ is smooth and bounded. The norm
$|\ell|\exp(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)p))$ is invariant
under the two line-factor identifications. The last
period multiplies it by
\[
 \varrho_i(s)=|\gamma_i|
              \exp\bigl(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)d_i s^R)\bigr).
\]
After shrinking, $0<\varrho_-\le\varrho_i(s)\le\varrho_+<1$
uniformly for all marked indices.

For the exceptional line, use the weighted norm
comparison \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.9} with $r=r_i$.
Uniform flat metrics on $B_{i,s}$ give
\[
 d(p+j d_i s^R,p_i^0)\le d(p,p_i^0)+C|j||s|^{r_i}
\]
for every integer $j$, since $R\ge r_i$.
The same inequality for the inverse translation gives
the reverse comparison. The $j$th lift on $\OO(n_iE_i)$
therefore changes its norm by a factor between
$C^{-1}(1+|j|)^{-n_i/r_i}$ and
$C(1+|j|)^{n_i/r_i}$, exactly the $n_i$th tensor power
of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.10}. This comparison extends over
the exceptional divisor by continuity of the positive
line-norm ratio. Multiplication by $\varrho_i(s)^j$
makes the full norm tend uniformly to zero as
$j\to+\infty$ and to infinity as $j\to-\infty$.
Any two compact sets have line norms bounded above and
away from zero, proving proper discontinuity. A fixed
point of a nonzero power would be fixed by arbitrarily
large powers, contradicting these limits, so the action
is free, including after its finite quotient.

Choose one positive integer $N$ such that the $N$th
iterate decreases every line norm. Its norm ratio has
a positive minimum $c_N$ over the compact weighted base
above a closed base disc. Every orbit meets
$c_N\le\|\ell\|\le1$, a compact annulus there.
The quotient $\mathcal Y_i\to\Delta_s$ is therefore a
smooth proper local family.

Outside its exceptional Hopf component, the canonical
section of $\OO(n_iE_i)$ trivializes that factor and gives
\begin{equation}
       \mathcal Y_i\setminus H_i
            \simeq \mathcal T|_{\Delta_s}\setminus F_i,
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TM}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.20}
\end{equation}
where the right side is the compact torus family restricted
to the same disc, with its marked central fibre curve removed.
In the normalized line gauge the torus-family flat coordinate is
$W=x^{-n_i}$. On the main component its other coordinate
is $u=z^{n_i}$, and
$u=p_{\rm loc}^{n_i}W^{r_i}$, $X=p_{\rm loc}^kW^l$ are precisely the inverse
maps in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}, with its base coordinate
identified with $p_{\rm loc}$. On $s\ne0$ the map and
its inverse are the period quotient of
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}.

For simultaneous replacement, choose a compact fundamental
domain on each Hopf component. Along a sequence approaching
it, $z,w$ remain bounded and not both zero, while $x\to0$.
The torus-family flat coordinate $x^{-n_i}$ is put into a fixed
compact norm annulus by $O(1+|\log|x||)$ deck iterates;
this follows from the uniform exponential bounds and
their polynomial factors. The total base displacement is
\begin{equation}
                   O\bigl(|s|^R(1+|\log|x||)\bigr)
                          \longrightarrow0,
                         \qquad s=xw.                   \hypertarget{tag-00AQ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.19}
\end{equation}
because $s=xw$ and $w$ is bounded. The initial base
coordinate $p_{\rm loc}=p-p_i^0=x^{r_i}z$ also tends to zero.
Consequently every cluster point of the images of this
sequence lies on $F_i$ in the original torus family.

Choose disjoint relatively compact neighbourhoods $W_i$
of the $F_i$ in a smaller closed tube. The subsets
$H_i\cup\Psi_i^{-1}(W_i\setminus F_i)$ of $\mathcal Y_i$,
where $\Psi_i$ is \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.20}, are open by the
cluster property. Glue them to the torus family with
the $F_i$ deleted by the same isomorphisms. A pair of
distinct limiting points in different pieces could only
arise from a cluster on one of the $F_i$; those loci have
been deleted from the torus piece and are disjoint for
different $i$. The gluing graphs are thus closed and
the glued space is Hausdorff.
Choose smaller closed neighbourhoods inside the $W_i$.
Their inverse images under $\Psi_i$, together with $H_i$,
are closed subsets of the proper $\mathcal Y_i$ over a
closed base disc and hence compact. Together with the
compact unmodified complement they cover the inverse
image of that disc. This proves properness of the glued
family. All maps are biholomorphic on the overlaps,
so its total space is smooth.

On the central main component the gluing reverses the
same inverse-transform maps used to define $T_0$.
It therefore recovers the original $P$ with every
analytic transition. The chosen fibre-period basis
preserves the linear part of each marked normal cover.
The maps $(z,w)\mapsto(a^{r_i}z,aw)$ commute with both
contractions and with the finite action; as $a$ varies,
they realize every constant translation of the marked
axis. They therefore preserve the given remaining gluing
constants. The full local equation is $s=xw$ in the
free coarse charts, so all central components have
multiplicity one and meet transversely as the given $S$.

Outside this tube the compact family
\eqref{eq:II:compact-twistor-lattice}, pulled back by
$t=s^R$, is unchanged. The proper local replacement and
that compact complement give a smooth compact threefold
over $\PP^1$. Every nonzero fibre is the original smooth
connected two-torus. The central quasibundle has Euler
number zero by \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic};
\cref{lem:II:hopf-curve-restriction} gives Euler number zero
for the Hopf leaves, and each double curve is elliptic. Additivity gives $e(S)=0$, completing
the construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[One-mark elliptic quasibundles]\hypertarget{tag-P370}{}\label{lem:II:one-mark-elliptic-torsor}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:one-mark-elliptic-torsor}{proved}{P370}{\cref{def:II:elliptic-root-curve,lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic}}
Let $q:T\to\PP^1$ be an identity-monodromy elliptic quasibundle
with fixed Jacobian $F=\C/\Lambda_F$. Mark a fibre with full divisor
$mJ$ over infinity, and suppose every other fibre is smooth and reduced.
The marked surface is either $(F\times\PP^1,F\times\{\infty\})$,
with $m=1$, or a diagonal Hopf surface
$H_m^{\rm diag}(\beta)/\boldsymbol\mu_n$ with marked axis $W=0$,
where $n>0$ and $\gcd(m,n)=1$. The isomorphism is determined by
the torsor class, a primitive oriented fibre basis and the marked
root-chart identification. In this description $n$ is the full
root-line degree.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The root charts of \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic} identify
$q$ with a principal $F$-torsor on the root curve
\begin{equation}
                 \mathcal B=\PP^1[(\infty,m)].
\hypertarget{tag-00VH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.1}
\end{equation}
For an oriented basis $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ of $\Lambda_F$, the
sheaves of holomorphic functions, units and $F$-valued maps fit into
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
0\longrightarrow\OO_{\mathcal B}
\xrightarrow{\ a\mapsto
 (e^{2\pi i\lambda_2a},e^{-2\pi i\lambda_1a})\ }
(\OO_{\mathcal B}^{*})^2
\xrightarrow{\ \Phi\ }F_{\mathcal B}\longrightarrow0,\\
\Phi(u,v)=\frac{\lambda_1\log u+\lambda_2\log v}{2\pi i}
                              \pmod{\Lambda_F}.
\end{gathered}
\hypertarget{tag-00VR}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.2}
\end{equation}
A change of logarithm adds a lattice period, so $\Phi$ is well-defined.
Local logarithms make it surjective. For a pair in its kernel, adjust
these logarithms by integral periods; their weighted sum is then zero,
which gives the displayed additive kernel. This kernel is injected:
$\lambda_1a,\lambda_2a\in\Z$ implies $a=0$, since
$\lambda_2/\lambda_1$ is nonreal.

Finite stabilizer averaging gives
$H^j(\mathcal B,\OO)=H^j(\PP^1,\OO)=0$ for $j=1,2$.
The canonical root line satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal B)=\Z[\mathcal R],\qquad
               \mathcal R^m=\OO_{\PP^1}(\infty).
\hypertarget{tag-00VS}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.3}
\end{equation}
Indeed subtracting the stabilizer weight of a line, as a power of
$\mathcal R$, makes that line descend to $\PP^1$. The displayed
relation then gives its unique integral power of $\mathcal R$.
The cohomology sequence of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.2} identifies the
torsor class with a vector in $\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal B)^2=\Z^2$.

The zero vector gives $F\times\mathcal B$. The connected root cover
of a smooth multiple fibre is unramified over the surface tube by
\cref{def:II:elliptic-root-curve}. Its inertia therefore acts freely
on the total torsor. In the product this inertia acts trivially on
$F$, so it is trivial: $m=1$ and $T=F\times\PP^1$.

For a nonzero vector, an oriented integral basis change sends it to
$(-n,0)$, with $n>0$. The inverse basis change identifies its primitive
direction with the original fibre basis. Push out
$(\mathcal R^{-n},\OO)$ through \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.2} and gauge the
second line coordinate to one. Its remaining ambiguity multiplies
the first coordinate by powers of
$\gamma=\exp(2\pi i\lambda_2/\lambda_1)$, with $|\gamma|<1$.
Thus the surface is
\begin{equation}
                  (\mathcal R^{-n})^\times/\gamma^{\Z}.
\hypertarget{tag-00VT}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.4}
\end{equation}
Write $\mathcal B=\PP(m,1)$, with coarse coordinate $Z/W^m$.
Its nonzero line has the presentation
\begin{equation}
 [((\C^2\setminus0)\times\C^*_\ell)/
  \lambda\cdot(Z,W,\ell)
     =(\lambda^mZ,\lambda W,\lambda^{-n}\ell)].
\hypertarget{tag-00VU}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.5}
\end{equation}
The gauge $\ell=1$ leaves $\boldsymbol\mu_n$ with weights $(m,1)$.
Choosing $\beta^n=\gamma$ lifts the infinite action to
$(Z,W)\mapsto(\beta^mZ,\beta W)$. Freeness on the axis $W=0$
is equivalent to $\gcd(m,n)=1$; on $W\ne0$ it follows from the
weight one. Changing the root $\beta$ multiplies this lift by an
element of the same finite group. These maps give the asserted
marked Hopf isomorphism and its inverse through \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.5}.
The integer $n$, together with the inverse integral basis change,
recovers the complete torsor class in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.3}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Two-mark elliptic quasibundles]\hypertarget{tag-P371}{}\label{lem:II:two-mark-elliptic-torsor}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:two-mark-elliptic-torsor}{proved}{P371}{\cref{lem:II:one-mark-elliptic-torsor}}
Let $q:T\to\PP^1$ be an identity-monodromy elliptic quasibundle
with fixed Jacobian $F$, whose multiple fibres are among two marked
fibres of orders $a,b$. As a surface with both marked curves and
fibre maps, $T$ is a diagonal primary or secondary Hopf surface, or
an elliptic ruled surface $\PP(\OO_E\oplus L)$ with its two sections,
where $L$ has finite order. The following root-line and quotient
maps determine the full torsor and both marked identifications.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $g=\gcd(a,b)$, $A=a/g$ and $B=b/g$. The map
\begin{equation}
 \PP^1[(0,A),(\infty,B)]
   \longrightarrow\PP^1[(0,a),(\infty,b)],\qquad t=z^g
\hypertarget{tag-00VW}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.7}
\end{equation}
is representable and finite \'etale. At zero its root uniformizers
have map $v=u$ and inertia inclusion $\boldsymbol\mu_A\subset
\boldsymbol\mu_a$; the analogous description holds at infinity.
Since $\gcd(A,B)=1$, its source is $\PP(B,A)$, with coarse coordinate
$z=X^A/Y^B$. The two root divisors have classes $B$ and $A$.
B\'ezout's identity therefore identifies its Picard group with
$\Z[\OO(1)]$. Finite averaging gives the vanishing of its higher
coherent cohomology.

Apply \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.2} to this pullback root curve. The pulled
back torsor is represented by an integral vector. For a nonzero
vector use the oriented basis change to $(-n,0)$ and the gauge
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.5}, with weights $(B,A)$ in place of $(m,1)$.
The resulting cover has contraction
$(X,Y)\mapsto(\beta^BX,\beta^AY)$ and finite action
$\boldsymbol\mu_n(B,A)$. Its inertia acts freely exactly when
$\gcd(n,A)=\gcd(n,B)=1$. Cyclic descent preserves the two axes.
On a central primary cover a lift commuting with the contraction
and preserving each axis is $(Xf(X,Y),Yh(X,Y))$. Equivariance
makes $f,h$ invariant under the contraction, hence constant by
iteration to the origin. The finite quotient preserving the axes
is cyclic: its character on either axis is injective by freeness.
These coordinate maps identify the descended marked surface with
a diagonal primary or secondary Hopf surface.

For the zero vector, free inertia gives $A=B=1$ and the pulled back
surface is $F\times\PP^1$. Descent acts by
$(y,z)\mapsto(y+\tau,\zeta_gz)$, since its translation part is a
holomorphic map $\PP^1\to F$ and hence constant. The principal
$F$-action fixes its linear part. Freeness at zero and infinity
makes $\tau$ have exact order $g$. Taking the quotient gives
\begin{equation}
 \PP(\OO_E\oplus L),\qquad
 E=F/\langle\tau\rangle,\qquad
 L=(F\times\C)/((y,v)\sim(y+\tau,\zeta_gv)).
\hypertarget{tag-00VX}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.8}
\end{equation}
The map from $F\times\PP^1$ is the projectivization of the displayed
line quotient. It identifies the axes with the two sections, gives
$L$ exact order $g$, and descends the fibre map $q=z^g$.
All these identifications use the original torsor transition maps.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Leaf pruning and boundary groups]\hypertarget{tag-P372}{}\label{lem:II:elliptic-tree-pruning}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:elliptic-tree-pruning}{proved}{P372}{\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data,lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary,lem:II:one-mark-elliptic-torsor,lem:II:two-mark-elliptic-torsor,lem:II:normal-product-collars}}
Let $S$ have a rooted-tree or unicyclic incidence graph. Give its
elliptic components identity-monodromy quasibundle maps, with
all their multiple fibres among the double curves, and give every
nonlinear Hopf component one marked axis as a leaf. All nonroot
vertices off the cycle have base $\PP^1$. The double-curve
identifications and normal dualities determine successive inverse
logarithmic transforms, from the leaves toward the root or cycle.
Every terminal step is a Hopf pair or the product pair
$(F\times\PP^1,F\times\{\infty\})$. The resulting root or marked
cycle, with its torsor atlas, is independent up to marked
isomorphism of the order of disjoint steps. The full integer
secondary framings and primitive fibre bases determine inverse
maps recovering each removed pair.

Replacing the filled leaf complement by its inverse product tube
induces an isomorphism of fundamental groups, equal to the identity
on the unchanged exterior and on its fibre generators. The same
comparison holds for compressed normal-product collars $uv=s^h$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a Hopf leaf of normal order $m$ and secondary integer $n$, set
$r=m$ in \cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data}. Its connected root cover
is identified with the parent's root cover by the given axis map
and dual normal lines. Choose $k,l$ with $mk-nl=1$.
The coordinate map \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.6}, together with the quotient
in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4}, gives
$p=X^mu^{-l}$, $W=X^{-n}u^k$ and the inverse
$u=p^nW^m$, $X=p^kW^l$. Replace this punctured chart by
$\Delta_p\times(\C^*/\gamma^{\Z})$ using that map.
The proof of \cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data} proves properness of
this replacement and extends every compatible coordinate change
as a translation over the product disc. It also identifies changes
$k\mapsto k+na$, $l\mapsto l+ma$ by $X\mapsto Xu^a$ while fixing
$p,W$. Thus the given gluing translation, primitive basis and
integer $n$ remain in the transition atlas.

A product cap is removed by the identity product-disc map on its
parent. At any other terminal vertex, removing its children has
removed their multiple fibres and changed no other chart.
Only the parent mark can remain multiple. Apply
\cref{lem:II:one-mark-elliptic-torsor} to this modified quasibundle;
it is exactly one of the two terminal pairs. This proves that the
procedure continues to the root or cycle. Operations in disjoint
base discs glue to the same complementary atlas and commute.
The same holds in disjoint subtrees. Every order processes a parent
after its children, and any two such orders differ by these
commutations. The resulting isomorphisms fix every remaining mark.
For a cycle, \cref{lem:II:two-mark-elliptic-torsor} identifies each
final component with its marked Hopf or ruled model.

For the group comparison, the diagonal Hopf complement and the
product-cap complement are both $\C\times F$. The smooth-pair
deformation in \cref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49} identifies the nonlinear
Hopf complement and its boundary with the diagonal pair.
Use the primitive boundary basis of
\cref{lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary}. The filling homomorphism is
\begin{equation}
 \Z^3_{\delta,e,h}\longrightarrow\Z^2_{e,h},\qquad
              \delta\longmapsto0,\quad e\longmapsto e,
              \quad h\longmapsto h.
\hypertarget{tag-00VY}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.9}
\end{equation}
Indeed \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.6}, with $r=m$, has columns
$(-l,k,0),(0,0,1),(m,-n,0)$ and determinant one.
It sends the reversed Hopf meridian to $\delta$ and its remaining
generators to $e,h$. The product tube $F\times D^2$ has the same
homomorphism on these same three loops. Van Kampen gives identical
pushout maps from the unchanged exterior and the filling; the
identity on that exterior and on $e,h$ induces the asserted group
isomorphism. Repeat the argument with all remaining collars fixed.
For a smoothing, \cref{lem:II:normal-product-collars} identifies
these collars with its normal-product tubes. In $uv=s^h$, fixing
$s\ne0$ still reverses the normal circle through
$v=s^h/u$; the same boundary maps and group comparison apply.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Compact insertion with prescribed Hopf leaves]\hypertarget{tag-P353}{}\label{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:compact-elliptic-star-insertion}{proved}{P353}{\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data,lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor,lem:II:logarithmic-period-family,cdp:st:C.2.UN.42}; \cref{cdp:eq:C.NH.6,cdp:eq:C.NH.7,cdp:eq:C.NH.9,cdp:eq:C.NH.10}}
Let a marked elliptic star have elliptic base $B$, no unmarked
multiple fibres, and
\begin{equation}
                         c(T_0)=0\in H^2(B,\Lambda_F).     \hypertarget{tag-00AT}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.4}
\end{equation}
Suppose there is a positive integer $R$ with
\begin{equation}
 \begin{cases}
 r_i=R,&H_i\text{ is of the nonlinear form in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}},\\
 r_i<R,&H_i\text{ is of the diagonal form in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}}.
 \end{cases}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AU}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.5}
\end{equation}
Then its given reduced surface $S$ is the full fibre over
zero of a proper map $f:Y\to\PP^1$, where $Y$ is a smooth
compact complex threefold and every other fibre is a smooth
connected two-torus. The central main component is the given
$P$, with its entire analytic torsor and marked normal covers;
each leaf and each elliptic gluing map is the prescribed one.
Every reduced fibre support has Euler characteristic zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{lem:II:zero-chern-elliptic-torsor} to the
principal torsor $q_0:T_0\to B$ of
\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data}, using $F_1=F$ and its
zero Chern class. Use the coordinate change
$(z,w)_{\mathrm{KX}}=(p,z)$, with
$\Gamma=\Gamma_B$ and $\Lambda_{F_1}=\Lambda_F$.
The resulting full lattice presentation is exactly
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.14}. The local translations by the
zero-cochain in that lemma and their inverse translations
identify this quotient with the original analytic torsor
over the same $B$. Write it as $T_0=\C^2/\Lambda_0$, with
the fibre direction $p=0$ and the disjoint marked fibres $F_i$.

Apply the full rank-four clause of
\cref{lem:II:logarithmic-period-family} to this exact lattice
$\Lambda_0$, and pull its compact family back by $t=s^R$.
Its periods are $V_{s^R}(\Lambda_0)$ and its central fibre
is the same $T_0$. For the $i$th marked fibre, the product
map \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5} identifies its elliptic curve with
$\C^*/\gamma_i^{\Z}$, where $\gamma_i=\beta_i^{n_i}$.
Choose the corresponding oriented fibre-period basis
$\lambda_i=(0,a_i)$, $\mu_i=(0,b_i)$, with
$\gamma_i=\exp(2\pi i b_i/a_i)$. The projection of
$\Lambda_0$ onto the base lattice is surjective with this
fibre lattice as kernel, so these two periods extend to
an integral basis of all four periods.
In the vector coordinates $(P,Z)$ after $V_{s^R}$, set
\begin{equation}
 p^{(i)}=P-s^R\frac{\bar a_i}{a_i}Z,\qquad
 z_i=\frac{2\pi i}{a_i}Z.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.16}
\end{equation}
The period $\lambda_i$ becomes $(0,2\pi i)$, and $\mu_i$ becomes
\begin{equation}
   \bigl(\delta_i(s),\log\gamma_i\bigr),\qquad
   \delta_i(s)=s^R
        \left(\bar b_i-\frac{\bar a_i b_i}{a_i}\right).
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TI}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.17}
\end{equation}
where $d_i=\overline b_i-\overline a_i b_i/a_i\ne0$ by
the real independence of $a_i,b_i$.
The two remaining periods have coordinates
$(P_{ij}(s),Z_{ij}(s))$, $j=1,2$.
At zero their first coordinates are a base-period basis,
so remain real-linearly independent on a smaller disc.
They define the elliptic curve
$B_{i,s}=\C/\langle P_{i1}(s),P_{i2}(s)\rangle$ and the
degree-zero line $M_{i,s}$ with constant factors
$\exp Z_{ij}(s)$.
Quotienting first by these two periods and by $(0,2\pi i)$,
then by the last period, gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_s=M_{i,s}^{\times}/
   \langle(p,\ell)\mapsto(p+d_i s^R,\gamma_i\ell)\rangle,
                    \qquad d_i\ne0 .                  \hypertarget{tag-00AO}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}
\hypertarget{tag-012A}{}
\hypertarget{tag-00TJ}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.8}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.18}}
\end{equation}
This is an isomorphism of holomorphic families: the first
quotient uses $(p,z)\mapsto(p,e^z)$ and the two constant
line factors, and the last quotient uses exactly the
remaining period. The inverse is given by local logarithms
modulo those same four generators. All four periods and
their original flat torsor parameters are therefore preserved.
The line $M_{i,s}$ may be any degree-zero line. In particular
when $T_0=F\times B$ and its complementary periods have zero
fibre coordinate, $M_{i,0}$ is trivial.

Write $p=p^{(i)}$ in this presentation, and choose a constant
lift $p_i^0$ of its marked central base point. At that point
of the smooth elliptic surface family
$\mathcal B_i\to\Delta_s$, take the weighted blowup of
weights $(r_i,1)$ in $(p-p_i^0,s)$ and denote its exceptional
divisor by $E_i$. Pull back $M_i$ and tensor by
$\OO(n_iE_i)$. The weighted presentation
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.6}, with $r=r_i$, is
$p_{\rm loc}=p-p_i^0=x^{r_i}z$, $s=xw$, with weights
$(r_i,1,-1)$ on $(z,w,x)$.
The extra line coordinate $\ell$ has weight $-n_i$.
Choose $\lambda$ with $\lambda^{n_i}=\ell$ and apply the
weighted action to set $\ell=1$. Two choices differ exactly
by the action below; its inverse sends a finite orbit to
the weighted orbit represented with $\ell=1$.
The residual finite action is
\begin{equation}
 (z,w,x)\mapsto
      (\zeta^{r_i}z,\zeta w,\zeta^{-1}x),
                    \qquad \zeta^{n_i}=1.                \hypertarget{tag-012B}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.9}
\end{equation}
on $(\C^2_{z,w}\setminus\{0\})\times\C_x$.
It is free: a nonzero $w$ or $x$ makes $\zeta=1$,
and when both vanish, $z\ne0$ and $\gcd(r_i,n_i)=1$
has the same consequence. Equivalently, the order-$r_i$
weighted inertia in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.7} acts faithfully
on this line because of that coprimality. Thus the coarse
nonzero line space is smooth.

Choose the given $n_i$th root $\beta_i$ of $\gamma_i$.
The lift of the last period in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.17} is
\begin{equation}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.10}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.19}}
 \begin{split}
 (z,w,x)\longmapsto\bigl(&
   \beta_i^{r_i}(z+d_i x^{R-r_i}w^R),\\
   &\beta_iw,\ \beta_i^{-1}x\bigr).
 \end{split}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AP}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.18}
\hypertarget{tag-0123}{}
\hypertarget{tag-00TK}{}
\end{equation}
The monomial $x^{R-r_i}w^R$ has weighted degree $r_i$,
so this map commutes with the finite action. It fixes
$s=xw$ and changes $p$ by exactly $d_i s^R$.
On $x=0$, equality $R=r_i$ gives the nonlinear contraction
after $Z=z/(\beta_i^{r_i}d_i)$; strict inequality gives
the diagonal contraction. On $w=0$ it is always
$(z,x)\mapsto(\beta_i^{r_i}z,\beta_i^{-1}x)$.
Thus its main-component chart is
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.4} and its leaf is the prescribed
primary or secondary surface.

We prove uniform properness of this quotient with its
varying line. On a closed smaller base disc, solve
\[
 \operatorname{Re}\bigl(Z_{ij}(s)-c_i(s)P_{ij}(s)\bigr)=0,
 \qquad j=1,2.
\]
The real period matrix is invertible, so the solution
$c_i(s)$ is smooth and bounded. The norm
$|\ell|\exp(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)p))$ is invariant
under the two line-factor identifications. The last
period multiplies it by
\[
 \varrho_i(s)=|\gamma_i|
              \exp\bigl(-\operatorname{Re}(c_i(s)d_i s^R)\bigr).
\]
After shrinking, $0<\varrho_-\le\varrho_i(s)\le\varrho_+<1$
uniformly for all marked indices.

For the exceptional line, use the weighted norm
comparison \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.9} with $r=r_i$.
Uniform flat metrics on $B_{i,s}$ give
\[
 d(p+j d_i s^R,p_i^0)\le d(p,p_i^0)+C|j||s|^{r_i}
\]
for every integer $j$, since $R\ge r_i$.
The same inequality for the inverse translation gives
the reverse comparison. The $j$th lift on $\OO(n_iE_i)$
therefore changes its norm by a factor between
$C^{-1}(1+|j|)^{-n_i/r_i}$ and
$C(1+|j|)^{n_i/r_i}$, exactly the $n_i$th tensor power
of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NH.10}. This comparison extends over
the exceptional divisor by continuity of the positive
line-norm ratio. Multiplication by $\varrho_i(s)^j$
makes the full norm tend uniformly to zero as
$j\to+\infty$ and to infinity as $j\to-\infty$.
Any two compact sets have line norms bounded above and
away from zero, proving proper discontinuity. A fixed
point of a nonzero power would be fixed by arbitrarily
large powers, contradicting these limits, so the action
is free, including after its finite quotient.

Choose one positive integer $N$ such that the $N$th
iterate decreases every line norm. Its norm ratio has
a positive minimum $c_N$ over the compact weighted base
above a closed base disc. Every orbit meets
$c_N\le\|\ell\|\le1$, a compact annulus there.
The quotient $\mathcal Y_i\to\Delta_s$ is therefore a
smooth proper local family.

Outside its exceptional Hopf component, the canonical
section of $\OO(n_iE_i)$ trivializes that factor and gives
\begin{equation}
       \mathcal Y_i\setminus H_i
            \simeq \mathcal T|_{\Delta_s}\setminus F_i,
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TM}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.20}
\end{equation}
where the right side is the compact torus family restricted
to the same disc, with its marked central fibre curve removed.
In the normalized line gauge the torus-family flat coordinate is
$W=x^{-n_i}$. On the main component its other coordinate
is $u=z^{n_i}$, and
$u=p_{\rm loc}^{n_i}W^{r_i}$, $X=p_{\rm loc}^kW^l$ are precisely the inverse
maps in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}, with its base coordinate
identified with $p_{\rm loc}$. On $s\ne0$ the map and
its inverse are the period quotient of
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.17}.

For simultaneous replacement, choose a compact fundamental
domain on each Hopf component. Along a sequence approaching
it, $z,w$ remain bounded and not both zero, while $x\to0$.
The torus-family flat coordinate $x^{-n_i}$ is put into a fixed
compact norm annulus by $O(1+|\log|x||)$ deck iterates;
this follows from the uniform exponential bounds and
their polynomial factors. The total base displacement is
\begin{equation}
                   O\bigl(|s|^R(1+|\log|x||)\bigr)
                          \longrightarrow0,
                         \qquad s=xw.                   \hypertarget{tag-00AQ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.19}
\end{equation}
because $s=xw$ and $w$ is bounded. The initial base
coordinate $p_{\rm loc}=p-p_i^0=x^{r_i}z$ also tends to zero.
Consequently every cluster point of the images of this
sequence lies on $F_i$ in the original torus family.

Choose disjoint relatively compact neighbourhoods $W_i$
of the $F_i$ in a smaller closed tube. The subsets
$H_i\cup\Psi_i^{-1}(W_i\setminus F_i)$ of $\mathcal Y_i$,
where $\Psi_i$ is \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.20}, are open by the
cluster property. Glue them to the torus family with
the $F_i$ deleted by the same isomorphisms. A pair of
distinct limiting points in different pieces could only
arise from a cluster on one of the $F_i$; those loci have
been deleted from the torus piece and are disjoint for
different $i$. The gluing graphs are thus closed and
the glued space is Hausdorff.
Choose smaller closed neighbourhoods inside the $W_i$.
Their inverse images under $\Psi_i$, together with $H_i$,
are closed subsets of the proper $\mathcal Y_i$ over a
closed base disc and hence compact. Together with the
compact unmodified complement they cover the inverse
image of that disc. This proves properness of the glued
family. All maps are biholomorphic on the overlaps,
so its total space is smooth.

On the central main component the gluing reverses the
same inverse-transform maps used to define $T_0$.
It therefore recovers the original $P$ with every
analytic transition. The chosen fibre-period basis
preserves the linear part of each marked normal cover.
The maps $(z,w)\mapsto(a^{r_i}z,aw)$ commute with both
contractions and with the finite action; as $a$ varies,
they realize every constant translation of the marked
axis. They therefore preserve the given remaining gluing
constants. The full local equation is $s=xw$ in the
free coarse charts, so all central components have
multiplicity one and meet transversely as the given $S$.

Outside this tube the compact family
\eqref{eq:II:compact-twistor-lattice}, pulled back by
$t=s^R$, is unchanged. The proper local replacement and
that compact complement give a smooth compact threefold
over $\PP^1$. Every nonzero fibre is the original smooth
connected two-torus. The central quasibundle has Euler
number zero by \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic};
\cref{lem:II:hopf-curve-restriction} gives Euler number zero
for the Hopf leaves, and each double curve is elliptic. Additivity gives $e(S)=0$, completing
the construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact pruning and compact reinsertion classify every reduced all-Hopf support]\hypertarget{tag-01E6}{}\label{cdp:st:C.2.UN.60}
\StatementRecord{cdp:st:C.2.UN.60}{proved}{01E6}{\SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.UN.46}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.UN.50}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.2}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.4}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.UN.43}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.6}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.3}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.UN.58}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.5}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.UN.57}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.UN.54}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.9}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.UN.48}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.10}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.12}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.13}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.14}, \SeriesRef{cdp:eq:C.PR.16}, \SeriesRef{cdp:st:C.2.UN.42}}

Let $S$ be a specified compact connected reduced SNC surface whose
smooth components are primary or secondary Hopf surfaces. Its
elliptic gluing maps are part of the specified surface. The following
finite geometric test is necessary and sufficient for $S$ to occur
as the full central fibre of a proper degeneration of connected
complex two-tori with smooth total space.

\begin{enumerate}
\item The actual normal lines on every double curve are dual, and
the incidence graph has exactly one independent cycle.
\item If a diagonal algebraic-dimension-zero component occurs, the
whole support is its diagonal cycle and its integral lattice product
$M$ is the identity, as in \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.46}.
\item In the remaining case every algebraic-dimension-zero vertex
is a nonlinear leaf. Every other vertex has its actual elliptic
reduction to $\PP^1$, and every multiple fibre of that reduction
is one of its marked double curves.
\item Let $m_e$ be the exact order of either normal line at an edge,
and let $h_v$ be zero on the cycle and the sum of the $m_e$ along
the path from the cycle to $v$. There is an integer $R>0$ such that
every nonlinear leaf has $h_v=R$ and every other vertex has $h_v<R$.
If there is no nonlinear leaf, any $R>\max h_v$ passes this test.
\item Perform the exact leaf-pruning operations specified below,
including the full integer secondary framing and all torsor maps.
The resulting marked Hopf/ruled core cycle has integral
complement-lattice product $M=I$.
\end{enumerate}

In the second case the tests referring to elliptic tree vertices are
unneeded. In the remaining case the pruning operations always exist
under the preceding geometric requirements. Each terminal step is
one of two explicit operations: the inverse logarithmic chart of
\ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.50} for a primary or secondary Hopf pair; or removal of the
product pair $(F\times\PP^1,F\times\{\infty\})$. The latter leaves
the parent surface unchanged. After its children have been removed,
every vertex has exactly one of these two forms. The pruned core
and its test are independent, up to the stated actual marked
isomorphisms, of the order of pruning disjoint branches.

Every support passing the test has a realization over $\PP^1$
with smooth compact total threefold. It retains all the original
components, their analytic torsors and every specified elliptic
gluing map. Its other singular support can be taken to be the
complex conjugate of its pruned core cycle. All reduced fibre
supports have Euler characteristic zero.
\end{proposition}



\begin{proof}\leavevmode\par



 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=0pt,labelsep=.5em]
\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The exact one-point torsor and its marked compact surface.}
We first prove the classification used at a terminal pruning step.
Let $q:T\to\PP^1$ be a fixed-Jacobian, identity-monodromy elliptic
quasi-bundle, with just one possible multiple fibre $mJ$, marked
over infinity. Its actual normal-root charts make it a principal
$F$-torsor on
\[
                 \mathcal B=\PP^1[(\infty,m)].          \tag{C.PR.1}\hypertarget{tag-00VH}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.1}
\]
Choose an oriented period basis $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ of
$F=\C/\Lambda_F$. The exact sheaf sequence used here is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 0\longrightarrow\OO_{\mathcal B}
 \xrightarrow{\ a\mapsto
 (e^{2\pi i\lambda_2a},e^{-2\pi i\lambda_1a})\ }
 (\OO_{\mathcal B}^{*})^2
 \xrightarrow{\ \Phi\ }F_{\mathcal B}\longrightarrow0,\\
 \Phi(u,v)=
 \frac{\lambda_1\log u+\lambda_2\log v}{2\pi i}
                          \pmod{\Lambda_F}.            \tag{C.PR.2}\hypertarget{tag-00VR}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.2}
 \end{gathered}
\]
Changing a logarithm changes the numerator by a lattice period.
Conversely a pair in the kernel can be lifted to logarithms,
adjusted by integral periods, and then lies on the displayed
complex line. The intersection of that line with the integral
two-period lattice is zero because
$\lambda_2/\lambda_1$ is not real. Thus the additive kernel and
every map in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.2} are exact.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  Finite stabilizer invariants are exact in characteristic zero, so
$H^j(\mathcal B,\OO)=H^j(\PP^1,\OO)=0$ for $j=1,2$.
Moreover
\[
 \operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal B)=\Z[\mathcal R],
                 \qquad \mathcal R^m=\OO_{\PP^1}(\infty).
                                                        \tag{C.PR.3}\hypertarget{tag-00VS}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.3}
\]
Indeed every line has a unique stabilizer weight modulo $m$;
subtract that power of the canonical root line and it descends
to $\PP^1$. The displayed relation then gives the asserted
infinite cyclic group, with its canonical sections retained.
The long exact sequence of \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.2} therefore identifies the
actual $F$-torsor class with a unique vector in
$\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal B)^2=\Z^2$.


\item  If this vector is zero, the torsor is the product
$F\times\mathcal B$. The inertia must act freely on its total
space because the actual connected root cover of $mJ$ is
unramified over the original surface tube. A nontrivial inertia
would act trivially on its product fibre. Thus $m=1$ and
$T=F\times\PP^1$, with $J=F\times\{\infty\}$.


\item  For a nonzero vector, choose its primitive direction and an
oriented period basis so that it is $(-n,0)$, $n>0$. This is
an integral change of the actual fibre basis, not removal of
its direction. The torsor is the pushout of
$(\mathcal R^{-n},\OO)$ by \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.2}. Gauge the second nonzero
line coordinate to one. The remaining ambiguity is multiplication
of the first coordinate by
$\gamma^{\Z}$, where
$\gamma=\exp(2\pi i\lambda_2/\lambda_1)$ and $|\gamma|<1$.
Consequently the actual total surface is
\[
                         (\mathcal R^{-n})^\times/\gamma^{\Z}.
                                                        \tag{C.PR.4}\hypertarget{tag-00VT}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.4}
\]
Write $\mathcal B=\PP(m,1)$ with coordinates $(Z,W)$ of
weights $(m,1)$ and coarse coordinate $U=Z/W^m$.
The nonzero total line of $\mathcal R^{-n}$ is
\[
 [((\C^2\setminus0)\times\C^*_\ell)/
              \lambda\cdot(Z,W,\ell)
                =(\lambda^mZ,\lambda W,\lambda^{-n}\ell)].
                                                        \tag{C.PR.5}\hypertarget{tag-00VU}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.5}
\]
Setting $\ell=1$ leaves the finite group $\mu_n$ with weights
$(m,1)$. A scalar multiplication by $\gamma$ lifts, after choosing
$\beta^n=\gamma$, to $(Z,W)\mapsto(\beta^mZ,\beta W)$.
Thus \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.4} is exactly
$H_m^{\rm diag}(\beta)/\mu_n$, with the marked axis $W=0$.
Freeness of the original inertia is exactly
$\gcd(m,n)=1$. Changing the chosen root of $\gamma$ changes
the infinite generator by the already included finite group.
Every primitive fibre basis, the full integer $n$, and the marked
axis identification have been retained.


\item  This also explains why reduction of $n$ modulo $m$ is impermissible:
the entire root-line degree in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.4}, rather than only its
stabilizer character, is the torsor class.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The actual inverse operation at a Hopf leaf.}
For a nonlinear leaf use its full normal form from \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.43};
for an elliptic terminal surface use \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.4}. Both have the
same marked normal-line data. Put $r=m$, choose $k,l$ with
$mk-nl=1$, and write $\gamma=\beta^n$. On the parent the
actual coarse root chart and its inverse product chart are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 (u,X)\sim(\gamma^m u,\gamma^lX),\qquad p=X^m u^{-l},\\
 W=X^{-n}u^k,\qquad
                u=p^nW^m,\quad X=p^kW^l.
 \end{gathered}                                        \tag{C.PR.6}\hypertarget{tag-00VV}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.6}
\]
These are precisely (C.SN.3)--(C.SN.5), with the given dual-normal
map and elliptic gluing used to choose the same connected root
cover. Replace this marked multiple-fibre tube by
$(p,W)\in\Delta\times(\C^*/\gamma^{\Z})$ through the displayed
isomorphism on $p\ne0$. This is the actual inverse logarithmic
transform. Its base point becomes an ordinary elliptic fibre.
Every other chart and transition of the parent is unchanged.
In particular the parent remains the same fixed-Jacobian
identity-monodromy quasi-bundle off this one point, with its full
analytic torsor retained by the displayed transition map.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  The choices do not discard gluing data. A change of a root
trivialization or a normal-product constant changes \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.6} by
a translation gauge extending over the inserted product disc.
The primitive nonzero direction in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.3} fixes the angular
direction; the other period can change by an integral multiple,
which changes the generator by its same finite deck group.
Translations of the marked axis are retained in the transition.
This is the exact choice comparison already proved for the
full inverse torsor in \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49} and \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.50}.


\item  Remove terminal vertices inward from every attached tree.
All original nonterminal vertices have the elliptic reduction
of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.58}. Removing a child removes exactly its marked
multiple fibre by \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.6}, or leaves an ordinary fibre unchanged
in the product-cap case. Hence, after all children of a vertex
are removed, its only possible multiple fibre is its parent
mark. The one-point classification above applies to that
actual modified surface. This proves that every terminal step
has one of the two asserted forms.


\item  Operations in distinct discs of one base keep the same transition
atlas on their complement and hence commute. Operations in disjoint
subtrees do likewise. Every allowable pruning order differs by
interchanging such operations; a parent is processed only after
its children. This proves independence through actual marked
torsor isomorphisms, not merely through the same degree vector.
Keep the entire maps \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.6}, the primitive periods, the integer
$n$ and all remaining marked points as the record of each step.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The exact two-point core models.}
At the end each cycle vertex is still a connected fixed-$F$
quasi-bundle over $\PP^1$, with only its two marked possible
multiple fibres, of orders $a,b$. Put $g=\gcd(a,b)$,
$A=a/g$, $B=b/g$. There is the actual representable finite
etale orbicurve map
\[
 \PP^1[(0,A),(\infty,B)]
       \longrightarrow \PP^1[(0,a),(\infty,b)],
                         \qquad t=z^g .                \tag{C.PR.7}\hypertarget{tag-00VW}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.7}
\]
At zero its root uniformizers have map $v=u$ and inertia
$\mu_A\subset\mu_a$; the infinity chart has the analogous
inclusion. Thus it is etale as a map of these root curves.
The source, since $A,B$ are coprime, is the weighted projective
line $\PP(B,A)$, with coarse coordinate
$z=X^A/Y^B$. Its Picard group is generated by $\OO(1)$:
the two root divisors have classes $B$ and $A$, and Bezout
expresses their generator. Its higher coherent groups vanish.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  Pull back the actual $F$-torsor. The same sequence \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.2}
therefore describes it by an integral vector. A nonzero vector
$(-n,0)$ gives the explicit nonzero line $\OO(-n)$, and the
gauge \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.5}, now of weights $(B,A)$, gives the actual diagonal
Hopf cover with contraction $(\beta^BX,\beta^AY)$ and finite
action $\mu_n(B,A)$. The inertia is free precisely when
$\gcd(n,A)=\gcd(n,B)=1$. Its cyclic descent preserves both
marked axes. Lifts to a central primary cover commute with a
contraction and preserve each axis, so they have the form
$(Xf(X,Y),Yh(X,Y))$; contraction equivariance forces the
nonvanishing units $f,h$ to be constant. Thus the full quotient
is the actual marked diagonal primary or secondary Hopf surface.


\item  For the zero vector, free inertia forces $A=B=1$ and the cover
is $F\times\PP^1$. Its cyclic descent is
$(y,z)\mapsto(y+\tau,\zeta_g z)$: a holomorphic map
$\PP^1\to F$ is constant, and the principal-$F$ action excludes
a linear part. Freeness at $0,\infty$ makes $\tau$ have exact
order $g$. The quotient is exactly
\[
        \PP(\OO_E\oplus L),\quad
        E=F/\langle\tau\rangle,\quad
        L=(F\times\C)/((y,v)\sim(y+\tau,\zeta_gv)).
                                                        \tag{C.PR.8}\hypertarget{tag-00VX}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.8}
\]
This exhibits its two marked sections, the exact torsion order
of $L$, the full fibre map $q=z^g$ on the cover, and both
elliptic identifications. It also gives the actual finite
projective-bundle map from $F\times\PP^1$.
Thus the pruned core is precisely one of the marked diagonal
Hopf/ruled cycles of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.57}, with all its data retained.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{Necessity of the core lattice test through actual group maps.}
For an actual torus degeneration, the graph, normal and height
requirements are \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.54} and \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.58}. It remains to compare
the nearby group to that of the pruned core; no contraction of
the given holomorphic total space is required.


\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=1.3em,labelsep=.5em]
\item  The complement of the marked axis in a terminal diagonal Hopf
pair is exactly $\C\times F$. For a nonlinear pair the explicit
proper smooth-pair deformation of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49} identifies its compact
core and boundary with the diagonal pair. The product ruled cap
has the same complement $F\times\C$. In the primitive boundary
basis of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.50} the actual homomorphism of this compact
piece is
\[
        \Z^3_{\delta,e,h}\longrightarrow\Z^2_{e,h},
                  \delta\longmapsto0,\quad
                  e\longmapsto e,\quad h\longmapsto h. \tag{C.PR.9}\hypertarget{tag-00VY}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.9}
\]
For the Hopf case the exact matrix
$[(-l,k,0),(0,0,1),(m,-n,0)]$ has determinant one;
the normal reversal in $xy=t$ turns the killed Hopf meridian
into precisely $\delta$. The inverse product filling
$F\times D^2$ has the identical homomorphism \eqref{cdp:eq:C.PR.9},
with the same two retained generators. For a product cap this
is the literal product-disc boundary map.


\item  Van Kampen applied to the unchanged exterior and this boundary
gives two pushout diagrams with identical maps. Their resulting
groups are canonically isomorphic by the identity on the exterior
and the two displayed fibre generators. Repeat the comparison,
retaining every remaining collar. The actual tubular comparison
of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.49} carries these maps to an arbitrary original smoothing.
Consequently the nearby group of the core plumbing is the
original $\Z^4$. The exact core calculation of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.57} gives
$\Lambda\rtimes_M\Z$, with $\Lambda$ injected. Its abelianness
forces $M=I$. This proves necessity using the actual maps needed
for the test.


\end{enumerate}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The compact core family with a prescribed remaining period order.}
For sufficiency first handle the all-algebraic-dimension-zero
diagonal branch by \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.48}. Otherwise prune as above and assume
the core test passes. Its components have retained elliptic
quasi-bundles. In the common complement
$G=\C^2/\Lambda$ of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.57} their regular fibres are translates
of the compact elliptic subgroup
\[
       F=(W\cap iW)/(\Lambda\cap W\cap iW),
                     \qquad W=\operatorname{span}_{\R}\Lambda.
                                                        \tag{C.PR.10}\hypertarget{tag-00VI}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.10}
\]
Their lattice is primitive of rank two: their actual quotient
in the open two-boundary component is $\C^*$.

\begin{definition}[Marked collections of surface models]\hypertarget{tag-P368}{}\label{def:II:marked-surface-models}

\item \par\medskip\noindent\textbf{The classified endpoint and inverse maps.}
Every endpoint component and double curve
has topological Euler number zero, so
\(e(S_*)=0\). The exact invariant relative
cohomology frame gives
\(p_g(Z)=g(B)\) for a quasi-bundle. The
common regular Jacobian is retained by
the actual normal-root maps: along an
edge joining two quasi-bundle vertices,
the dual normal lines have the same
exact order, and inversion identifies
their connected root covers of the
elliptic double curve. These are exactly
the two regular elliptic fibres, by
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.QT.2}--\eqref{cdp:eq:C.QT.3}; their translations
are retained in the gluing record.
At a nonlinear Hopf leaf the same root
cover is instead its exact period cover
of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.50}. Such leaves do not interrupt
propagation through the connected
quasi-bundle region, and their actual
leaf periods and finite characters are
retained by that comparison.
The
compact-core bound \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.28} therefore permits
at most one genus-one base. If there is
one, that normalization has \(p_g=1\).

fundamental group onto that of the full
support. The graph-of-spaces comparison
gives a surjection from the support
fundamental group to that of its incidence
graph, and kills the image of this
component's fundamental group.

trivial, so the connected graph is a tree.

fundamental-group comparisons of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.61}
then give its rooted-tree support, with the
actual integral Chern and recursive
period conditions. If there is none,
\ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.62} gives the unicyclic support and
its exact torsor, height and common-period
conditions. Its nonlinear leaves retain
the secondary finite characters of \ref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.50}.

surfaces and gluing maps in the same smoothing.

exceptional set. The graph of each exceptional
tree starts with a rational curve of square
\(-1\) and valence zero. If \(C^2=-b\) and
\(n\) is its valence in this entire exceptional
set, the actual smooth and node blowups give
\begin{equation}
                              n\le b+1.

\end{equation}

coordinates identifying that support with $x=0$ or $xy=0$.
The blowup of $(x,y)$ is the same local point morphism whose
square and valence updates prove \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AP.5}.
A centre off the exceptional support starts a rational
tree at $(b,n)=(1,0)$, which also satisfies the bound.

triple count \(t\) is at most the old valence.

\item We prove the local ring comparison
at every point of $G$.  Let $A$ be the reduced hypersurface
ring, let $B$ be its finite normalization ring, and let $I$
be the conductor.  The ring $B$ is a product of regular
two-dimensional local rings.  Define
\[

\]

step.  There is an inclusion $A\subset A'\subset B$.
The two first rings agree in codimension one by the
ordinary-node calculation, so $A'/A$ has finite length.

Local cohomology of $0\to A\to A'\to A'/A\to0$ injects
$A'/A$ into $H^1_{\mathfrak m}(A)$.  The latter vanishes
because a hypersurface surface ring has depth two.
It follows that $A'=A$, and therefore
$A/I=(B/I)^\iota$.

\begin{definition}[Marked elliptic stars and inverse transforms]\hypertarget{tag-P350}{}\label{def:II:elliptic-star-data}
\StatementRecord{def:II:elliptic-star-data}{proved}{P350}{\cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic}}
The leaf pairs are
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 (H^{\rm diag}_{r_i}(\beta_i)/\mu_{n_i},J_i),\qquad
 (H^{\rm nl}_{r_i}(\beta_i)/\mu_{n_i},J_i),\\
 r_i\ge1,\qquad 0<|\beta_i|<1,\qquad \gcd(r_i,n_i)=1 ,
 \end{gathered}                                             \hypertarget{tag-00AG}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.1}
\hypertarget{tag-0122}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.1}}
\end{equation}
with marked axis $J_i=\{w=0\}$ and contractions and finite action
\begin{equation}
 (z,w)\longmapsto(\beta_i^{r_i}z,\beta_iw),\qquad
 (z,w)\longmapsto(\beta_i^{r_i}z+w^{r_i},\beta_iw),
 \quad
 \zeta(z,w)=(\zeta^{r_i}z,\zeta w),                         \hypertarget{tag-00AR}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}
\end{equation}
A marked elliptic star consists of these pairs, a smooth compact
complex surface with a connected elliptic quasibundle
\begin{equation}
                         q:P\longrightarrow B             \hypertarget{tag-00AS}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.3}
\end{equation}
over a smooth compact connected curve $B$, and pairwise distinct
marked fibres with full divisors $r_iJ_i$. Here a quasibundle has
only positive multiples of smooth elliptic curves as fibres.
Its integral $H_1$ monodromy is the identity, and its smooth
fibres are torsors under one fixed elliptic curve $F$.
The data include the isomorphism from each marked leaf axis to
the corresponding $J_i\subset P$ and a duality between their
normal lines. These identifications form the reduced surface
$S=P\cup H_1\cup\cdots\cup H_n$, with $n\ge1$, disjoint
double curves and no other intersections.

For one marked fibre suppress the index and choose integers $k,l$ with
\begin{equation}
                         rk-nl=1,\qquad \gamma=\beta^n.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-0125}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.3}
\end{equation}
The paired neighbourhood in $P$, in the axis coordinate $z$
of the leaf cover, has the invariant coordinates
\begin{equation}
 u=z^n,\qquad X=xz^k,\qquad
 p=X^ru^{-l},\qquad
 (u,X)\sim(\gamma^ru,\gamma^lX).
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-0126}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.4}
\hypertarget{tag-00TA}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.1}}
\end{equation}
Here $u\ne0$. Its punctured product map and inverse are
\begin{equation}
 (u,X)\longmapsto(p,W)
       =(X^ru^{-l},\,X^{-n}u^k),\qquad
 u=p^nW^r,\quad X=p^kW^l,\qquad
                       F=\C^*/\gamma^{\Z}.               \hypertarget{tag-0127}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}
\hypertarget{tag-00TL}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.2}}
\hypertarget{tag-00VV}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.6}}
\end{equation}
Replace each marked neighbourhood by the product $F\times\Delta_p$
through this punctured isomorphism, keeping every transition map
of $P$ away from the marked values. The resulting map is the
\emph{inverse logarithmic transform}
\begin{equation}
                             q_0:T_0\longrightarrow B.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TN}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.3}
\end{equation}
If there are no unmarked multiple fibres, it is a holomorphic
principal $F$-torsor. Its integral Chern vector is the connecting
class $c(T_0)\in H^2(B,\Lambda_F)$ of the sheaf sequence in
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.KX.13}, with $F_1=F$.
The transform preserves the full analytic torsor transition maps
and is independent, up to an isomorphism over $B$, of the
compatible local coordinates used in its construction.
\end{definition}
\begin{proof}
Every vertical prime of a quasibundle is elliptic, so it has
no vertical exceptional curve of the first kind and is relatively
minimal. Apply \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic} to this

\end{proof}

 \begin{gathered}

\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.PR.6}}
\hypertarget{tag-017U}{}\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.WT.15}}

\begin{lemma}[Boundary maps and canonical periods of elliptic stars]\hypertarget{tag-P351}{}\label{lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary}
\StatementRecord{lem:II:elliptic-star-boundary}{proved}{P351}{\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data,lem:II:normal-product-collars,cdp:st:C.2.UN.17}}
Every leaf pair in \cref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1,cdp:eq:C.AS.2} has
$K_H\simeq\OO_H(-(r+1)J)$, and $\OO_H(J)$ has infinite order.
For a full reduced SNC torus degeneration, let one
component be such a leaf, with its only double curve $J$
on a neighbouring smooth component $P$. The difference
of the canonical evaluation orders and the individual
core expansions are
\cref{cdp:eq:C.NS.8,cdp:eq:C.NS.11,cdp:eq:C.AS.15,cdp:eq:C.AS.16},
with $k_P$ the order of this neighbour. These conclusions
use only that leaf and its double curve; the rest of the
support may contain other components and intersections.
In these expansions $\gamma_{\rm core}$ is the oriented
core of this leaf, and the relative evaluation is divided
by $t^{k_P}$.

For a full star $P\cup_iH_i$ with arbitrary smooth main
component $P$, the main canonical divisor is
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.9}. The global comparison with the
inverse transform and the common core class below use
the following quasibundle and star hypotheses.
Let $q:P\to B$ be a fixed-Jacobian elliptic quasibundle with
identity integral monodromy, and identify the axes of leaf
pairs \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.1} with distinct reduced fibres $J_i$.
Suppose their normal lines are dual. The marked full fibres
are $r_iJ_i$, so these data define the inverse transform of
\cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data}.

For a marked fibre use $r,n,k,l,\gamma$ and $(u,X,p,W)$ from
that definition. Let $a$ be its positive angular $u$-loop,
$b$ its deck-period loop, and $\mu_P$ its positive normal
$X$-loop. Let $\delta$ be the positive $p$-loop at fixed $W$,
and let $e,h$ be the angular and deck-period loops of
$F=\C^*/\gamma^{\Z}$. Their integral comparison is
\begin{equation}
 \begin{pmatrix}a&b&\mu_P\end{pmatrix}_{(\delta,e,h)}
   =
 \begin{pmatrix}
   -l&0&r\\
    k&0&-n\\
    0&1&0
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \delta=n a+k\mu_P,\quad e=r a+l\mu_P,\quad h=b.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-0128}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.6}
\hypertarget{tag-00TO}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.4}}
\end{equation}
In particular $\mu_P=r\delta-ne$ is primitive.
The Hopf complement fills the meridian
$\delta_H=na-k\mu_H$ and carries the fibre loops
$e_H=ra-l\mu_H$, $h_H=b$. The normal-product identification
$\mu_H=-\mu_P$ sends them to $\delta,e,h$ respectively.
For the primary choice $n=1,k=0,l=-1$, this is
\begin{equation}
                   e_H=r_i a+\mu_H=e,\qquad h_H=b=h.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TQ}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.6}
\end{equation}
When there are no unmarked multiple fibres, choose a
trivialization over the complement of small marked
base discs, write $\delta_i=\delta_{\rm ext}+\nu_i$,
where $\nu_i\in\Lambda_F$ is its translation winding.
The integral Chern vector and meridians are
\begin{equation}
       \mu_{P,i}=r_i\delta_{\rm ext}
                         +(r_i\nu_i-n_i e_i),\qquad
                         c(T_0)=\sum_i\nu_i.             \hypertarget{tag-0124}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.2}
\hypertarget{tag-00TR}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.7}}
\end{equation}
Thus the rational Seifert vector before replacement is
$\sum_i(\nu_i-n_ie_i/r_i)$, and the replacements add
$\sum_i n_ie_i/r_i$ while preserving all holomorphic
transition maps.

The canonical line and direct image of this $q$ are
\eqref{eq:II:quasibundle-canonical} in
\cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic}, with
$(E_0,C_b)=(P,J_b)$.
If $S=P\cup_iH_i$ is the full reduced fibre of a proper
two-torus degeneration from a smooth threefold, a nearby
fibre is smoothly identified with $T_0$. Under this
identification every oriented Hopf core two-torus is the
ordinary fibre class $\gamma_{\rm core}$ of $q_0$. For a canonical
evaluation generator with orders $k_P,k_i$ one has
\begin{equation}
 (k_P-k_i)J_i=K_{H_i}+J_i=-r_iJ_i,
       \qquad k_i-k_P=r_i.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TS}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.8}
\hypertarget{tag-00AJ}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.12}}
\end{equation}
On the main component,
\begin{equation}
                         K_P=\OO_P\Bigl(\sum_i(r_i-1)J_i\Bigr).
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TT}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.9}
\hypertarget{tag-00AK}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.13}}
\end{equation}
After division by $t^{k_P}$, the leading relative two-form
on the $i$th Hopf core is $t^{r_i}\eta_i$, where
\begin{equation}
 \eta_i=c_i\,\frac{dz\wedge dw}{w^{r_i+1}},
                         \qquad c_i\ne0.                \hypertarget{tag-00TC}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.11}
\hypertarget{tag-00AL}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.14}}
\end{equation}
For a nonlinear leaf its period is
\begin{equation}
       \int_{\gamma_{\rm core}}\omega_t
          =t^{r_i}\left(\frac{\pm2\pi i c_i\beta_i^{-r_i}}{n_i}
                         +O(t)\right).                 \hypertarget{tag-00AM}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.15}
\hypertarget{tag-00TD}{}
\SsixEquationAliases{\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.12}}
\end{equation}
For a diagonal leaf it satisfies
\begin{equation}
                         \int_{\gamma_{\rm core}}\omega_t=O(t^{r_i+1})
                  \quad\hbox{at a diagonal leaf}.        \hypertarget{tag-00AN}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.AS.16}
\end{equation}
In the full star case with this quasibundle $P$, these are
expansions of its one common holomorphic core period.

When $B$ is elliptic and $q_0$ has no multiple fibres, its
fundamental group has the presentation
\begin{equation}
 \langle a_B,b_B,e,h:\ e,h\text{ central},\
             [a_B,b_B]=e^{c_1}h^{c_2}\rangle,
                         \quad(c_1,c_2)=c(T_0).          \hypertarget{tag-00TE}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.13}
\end{equation}
The fibre subgroup $\langle e,h\rangle\simeq\Lambda_F$
is injected. Consequently, in a two-torus smoothing its
Chern vector is zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic} to the
given quasibundle $q$ and marked full fibre $mJ$.
Its connected root and primitive normal character give
normal order exactly $m$.
The dual Hopf normal has exact order $r$, including its
finite character $\gamma^{-l}$. Hence $m=r$ and the local
maps of \cref{def:II:elliptic-star-data} apply to this quasibundle.

Apply the angular and deck loops to the monomials
$p=X^ru^{-l}$ and $W=X^{-n}u^k$.
The resulting columns are $(-l,k,0)$, $(0,0,1)$,
and $(r,-n,0)$, giving \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.6}.
Its determinant is $rk-nl=1$.
The identities for $\delta,e,h$ follow by multiplying
these columns by the displayed integral coefficients.
They also give $\mu_P=r\delta-ne$ and its primitivity.

On the diagonal reference Hopf pair put $Y=wz^{-k}$ and $u=z^n$.
Then $Y^r u^l=w^r/z$ and $Y^n u^k=w^n$.
Use $U=z/w^r$ as the positive complementary base coordinate;
it is the reciprocal of $Y^r u^l$.
The loops $na-k\mu_H$ and $ra-l\mu_H$ therefore change
$(\arg U,\arg(w^n))$ by $(2\pi,0)$ and $(0,2\pi)$,
respectively. The deck loop is the period $w^n\mapsto
\gamma w^n$. The normal product is $XY=xw=t$, so its
positive normal meridians are opposite. Substitution gives
$\delta_H=\delta$, $e_H=e$ and $h_H=h$, including
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.6} in the primary case.

For a diagonal leaf its complement is
$\C_U\times(\C^*/\langle\beta,\mu_n\rangle)$, and
$[w]\mapsto[w^n]$ identifies the second factor with $F$.
For a nonlinear leaf the smooth coordinates
\begin{equation}
 U=\frac{z}{w^{r_i}},\qquad
 V=U-\frac{\beta_i^{-r_i}}{\log|\beta_i|}\log|w|.
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-00TP}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.NS.5}
\end{equation}
make $V$ invariant under the infinite deck map and under
the finite action. They give the same smooth product
$\C_V\times F$. Its compact core fills the complementary
disc and keeps the two fibre circles just calculated.
The normal framing agrees with the diagonal reference
through a smooth comparison of pairs: vary the resonant
coefficient in $(\beta^r z+c w^r,\beta w)$ from $c=1$ to
$c=0$. Its iterates have a uniform polynomial factor times
a contracting exponential, so one compact annulus meets
every orbit throughout this interval. The quotient is a
smooth proper family of pairs with the axis and its normal
characters fixed. A horizontal vector field tangent to the
axis, extended by a partition of unity, has a complete
flow over the compact parameter interval. Its flow gives
the pair diffeomorphism and fixes the displayed peripheral
maps. The product formula above identifies the fibre
circles in that comparison.

Apply \cref{lem:II:normal-product-collars} to the given
full reduced SNC star. Its double curves have two embedded
branches, its normal-product line maps are the given ones,
and there are no triple points. Its compatible core and
collar diffeomorphisms identify the nearby fibre with the
union of the $P$ core and these Hopf fillings. Each Hopf
filling kills $\delta$ and keeps $e,h$, exactly as the
product inserted by \eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.5}. Gluing these
maps and their inverses gives the claimed diffeomorphism
to $T_0$. Along any path in $B$ joining two marked values
and avoiding the remaining multiple values, the ordinary
elliptic fibres are homologous. Thus all oriented Hopf
cores give the same integral class $\gamma_{\rm core}$.

When $q_0$ is smooth, its translation trivialization on the punctured base gives
$\delta_i=\delta_{\rm ext}+\nu_i$. Substitution into
$\mu_{P,i}=r_i\delta_i-n_ie_i$ gives
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.SN.2}. The obstruction to extending that
trivialization over all base discs is the sum of their
winding vectors, which is the connecting Chern class of
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.KX.13}. This proves both the integral
and rational Seifert comparisons. The full punctured product
maps also preserve the analytic transitions in the preceding
diffeomorphism.

The canonical isomorphism and direct image are the
application of \cref{lem:II:identity-monodromy-elliptic}
to this same $q:P\to B$, its marked and unmarked full
fibres, and its fixed integral elliptic marking.

For any one of the stated leaf occurrences, apply the evaluation construction of
\cref{cdp:st:C.2.UN.17} with all full-fibre multiplicities
equal to one. Its principal fibre identity and adjunction
give $(k_P-k_i)J_i=K_{H_i}+J_i$. The form
$dz\wedge dw/w^{r_i+1}$ is invariant under both deck
groups, for both contractions in \eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.2}.
It gives $K_{H_i}=-(r_i+1)J_i$.
The line $\OO_{H_i}(J_i)$ has infinite order: a trivial
positive power would make its canonical section a
nonconstant holomorphic function on a compact surface.
Thus the coefficient equality is precisely
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.8}. When the entire support is the star, adjunction on its main
component $P$ gives \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.9}.

In a product chart $t=xw$, with $H_i:x=0$ and $P:w=0$,
the total canonical generator is
$x^{k_i}w^{k_P}g\,dz\wedge dw\wedge dx$, with $g$ a
holomorphic unit. Dividing its relative residue by
$t^{k_P}$ gives
$t^{r_i}g\,dz\wedge dw/w^{r_i+1}$.
On the compact leaf, the leading coefficient is a
nowhere-zero section of $K_{H_i}((r_i+1)J_i)$, whose
invariant trivialization just displayed makes it a
nonzero constant. This proves \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.11}.
In the logarithmic variables $(U,\log w)$ the nonlinear
core has primitive periods
\begin{equation}
             (0,2\pi i/n),\qquad
             (\beta^{-r},\log\beta).
                                                        \hypertarget{tag-0129}{}\label{cdp:eq:C.SN.7}
\end{equation}
and its form is $c_i\,dU\wedge d\log w$.
Their determinant is nonzero and gives
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.15}, with the sign fixed by orientation.
For a diagonal leaf both periods have zero $U$-component,
so this leading integral is zero, giving
\eqref{cdp:eq:C.AS.16}. Differentiation under the integral
and Stokes' theorem make the integral over the transported
closed cycle holomorphic; the displayed local expressions
give its holomorphic extension and stated orders at zero.

Finally, for a principal elliptic bundle over an elliptic
base, the homotopy sequence injects $\pi_1(F)=\Lambda_F$
because $\pi_2(B)=0$. Its structure group acts by
translations, so this subgroup is central. Lift the two
generators $a_B,b_B$ of a fundamental polygon for $B$ through a
trivialization over its one-skeleton. The attaching map
of its two-cell is the Chern winding $(c_1,c_2)$ in the
fibre lattice, giving \eqref{cdp:eq:C.NS.13}.
An abelian total group forces $e^{c_1}h^{c_2}=1$;
the injected lattice then gives $c_1=c_2=0$.
The nearby two-torus has abelian fundamental group, so
the conclusion follows through the constructed diffeomorphism.
\end{proof}
